Research Talks: Civic Engagement
Room: Workshop 0
Topic:
Form of presentation: Research Talk
Duration: 90 Minutes
Psychological Willingness and Inhibitions in Stem Cell Donor Registration
Prof. Dr. Katherine Bruns | Fachhochschule des Mittelstands (FHM) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Katherine Bruns | Fachhochschule des Mittelstands (FHM) | Germany
Carlotta Stapenhorst | Fachhochschule des Mittelstands (FHM)
Anna Lindau | Fachhochschule des Mittelstands (FHM)
Prof. Dr. Anett Wolgast | Fachhochschule des Mittelstands (FHM)

Stem cell donation is a life-saving medical intervention, yet donor registration rates remain low. This study examined psychological predictors of young adults’ willingness to register as stem cell donors by integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior with Prospect Theory and the Empathy–Altruism Hypothesis. We tested the effects of altruism, fear of medical procedures, and prior knowledge about stem cell donation on registration behavior, controlling for age, gender, and personal relevance.
In a cross-sectional online survey, 149 young adults aged 18–30 years (73.6% female, Mage = 23.91, SD = 2.84) reported donor registration status and measures of altruism, fear, and knowledge. Data were analyzed using latent variable structural equation modeling with WLSMV estimation.
Altruism was positively associated with donor registration (latent r = 0.266, SE = 0.098, 95% CI [0.073, 0.459]), whereas fear of medical procedures was negatively associated with registration (latent r = −0.260, SE = 0.086, 95% CI [0.428, 0.092]). Prior knowledge showed a strong positive association with registration (latent r = 0.558, SE = 0.088, 95% CI [0.386, 0.731]). Personal relevance also predicted registration (β = 0.234, SE = 0.075, 95% CI [0.088, 0.380]), and gender showed a small effect, with higher registration probability among women (β = 0.157, SE = 0.077, 95% CI [0.050, 0.309]), while age was not significant.
These findings highlight the roles of prosocial motivation, emotional inhibition, and informational factors in stem cell donor registration and underscore the importance of theory-informed, evidence-based recruitment strategies targeting eligible young adults.

Civic Engagement Among Youth: Longitudinal Insights from AID:A Data
Prof. Dr. Susanne Kuger | German Youth Institute (DJI), LMU Munich | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Susanne Kuger | German Youth Institute (DJI), LMU Munich | Germany
Dr. Inga Simm | German Youth Institute (DJI)

Civic engagement is vital for democratic cohesion and social services in clubs, associations, and neighborhoods. Existing research links it to political interest, participation and well-being at the individual level (Barrett & Brunton-Smith, 2017; Müller, 2014). Population-representative studies document prevalence among adolescents and young adults (Fritzsche et al., 2025), but lack depth on personal values, political participation, and longitudinal development.
Using data from the German population study AID:A (2019 and 2023), this study traces individual civic engagement trajectories in a sample of n= 2.142 young people aged 12 to 27 years. The dataset enables analysis of relationships with political attitudes, participation, life satisfaction, self-efficacy and general values.
Longitudinal structure equation modelling reveal moderate stability of civic engagement over time (r=.20) showing differences between different forms of civic engagement. They also show significant albeit low correlations between later engagement and political participation (r=.10) and life satisfaction (r=.08), highlighting interconnected developmental pathways.
These findings contribute insights to the foundations of social cohesion and individual engagement, informing strategies to foster youth involvement in civic and political life to strengthen our democracy.

What Predicted the Participation in Climate Demonstrations? A Systematic Review
Jonathan Kuhlmann | Germany
Show details
Author:
Jonathan Kuhlmann | Germany

The accelerating climate crisis is likely the biggest threat to humanity and nature in the twenty-first century. Facing this threat requires rapid action and a societal transformation. Fridays for Future (FFF), a global youth-led climate movement, peaked in 2019, mobilising millions of protesters. Climate protestors had a worldwide political impact by putting pressure on policymakers to stick to the Paris Agreement. Today, the 1.5 °C limit has been exceeded and climate action faces a backlash. This raises the question of what motivated individuals to participate in climate protests in the first place. This systematic review aims to synthesise relevant studies (January 2000 –February 2025) to identify and analyse psychological factors that influenced individuals’ decisions to participate in climate demonstrations. Using the PRISMA guidelines, I systematically screened N = 2,490 articles from five databases, selected and assessed n = 36 studies with quantitative and qualitative data. Each study was assessed using one of two self-developed quality assessment tools (quantitative: 27 items; qualitative: 19 items) including the evaluation of validity, reliability and objectivity. The findings suggest that social identity processes are likely to be the main psychological driver for participation in climate demonstrations. In line with social identity models (SIMCA; SIMPEA), identification with the movement, feeling empowered to achieve meaningful change together and the role of social norms are important for motivating participation. I discuss implications for future research and the climate movement.

Aktuelle Herausforderungen in der Verkehrspsychologie
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Tibor Petzoldt (TU Dresden)
Room: Workshop +1
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Fachgruppensymposium
Duration: 195 Minutes

Ziel von Verkehrspsychologie ist es, Mobilität sicherer, effizienter und menschengerechter zu gestalten. In diesem Zusammenhang widmet sich das vorliegende Symposium aktuellen Herausforderungen, die sich aus den tiefgreifenden Transformationen des Verkehrssektors ergeben. Ein zentraler Schwerpunkt liegt auf der automatisierten Mobilität: Wie interagieren Fußgänger, Radfahrende und andere Verkehrsteilnehmende mit automatisierten Fahrzeugen? Welche Erwartungen, Unsicherheiten und Anpassungsprozesse prägen diese Begegnungen? Darüber hinaus thematisiert das Symposium Fragen der nachhaltigen Mobilität, insbesondere die Förderung und Sicherheit des Radverkehrs. Eng damit verknüpft sind neuartige Mobilitätsformen wie E-Scooter, die den urbanen Verkehrsraum verändern und neue Konflikte sowie Regelungsbedarfe mit sich bringen. Ein weiterer Beitrag widmet sich dem Einfluss von Kultur und Werten auf das Verkehrsverhalten: Wie prägen gesellschaftliche Normen unser Handeln im Straßenverkehr, und welche Implikationen ergeben sich daraus für Prävention und Intervention?Schließlich greift das Symposium eine hochaktuelle gesellschaftspolitische Entwicklung auf: die Freigabe von Cannabis und die damit verbundenen Fragestellungen zur Fahrtauglichkeit. Das Symposium bietet damit einen umfassenden Einblick in die vielfältigen Schnittstellen von Psychologie, Technologie und Gesellschaft im Mobilitätskontext.

Cannabis im Straßenverkehr – Eine intraindividuelle Untersuchung der Fahrleistung unter dem Einfluss von THC
Finn Rathgeber
Show details
Authors:
Finn Rathgeber
Martin Söllner
Wolfgang Fastenmeier
Matthias Graw
Benno Hartung
Anna-Christina Holzer
Maren Peschke

Mit der (Teil-)Legalisierung von Cannabis in Deutschland drängt sich insbesondere im Kontext Straßenverkehr die Frage nach möglichen sicherheitsrelevanten Konsequenzen auf. Um weitere Erkenntnisse zu diesem Thema zu gewinnen, die über die reine Durchführung von Laborstudien hinausgehen, wurden die unmittelbaren Auswirkungen des Cannabiskonsums auf das Steuern eines Fahrzeugs in realitätsnahem Setting untersucht. In einem Prä-Post-Design absolvierten N = 64 Teilnehmer:innen auf dem Gelände des Fahrsicherheitszentrums Sachsenring vier verschiedene Fahraufgaben sowie vier verschiedene kognitive Leistungstests vor bzw. nach dem Konsum von Cannabis. Die Fahraufgaben wurden jeweils von geschulten Fahrlehrern sowie zusätzlichen Beobachter:innen im Fahrzeug begleitet. Zur engmaschigen Kontrolle der THC-Konzentration (ng/ml) wurden den Teilnehmenden zu verschiedenen Zeitpunkten während des Versuchsablaufs Blutproben entnommen und toxikologisch analysiert. Trotz zum Teil beobachtbarer Ausfallerscheinungen nach dem Konsum, konnte keine eindeutige Konzentrations-Wirkungs-Beziehung zwischen THC ng/ml und der gezeigten Leistung in den verschiedenen Outcome-Variablen nachgewiesen werden. Es werden sowohl Befunde zu der kognitiven Leistungsfähigkeit in den computergestützten Testverfahren als auch zu der tatsächlich erbrachten Leistung in den Fahraufgaben präsentiert. Implikationen der Studie für den Umgang mit Cannabis im Straßenverkehr und insbesondere für die Bewertung geltender gesetzlicher Vorgaben werden diskutiert.

Erfassung subjektiver Sicherheit und Komfort im Radverkehr: Entwicklung und Validierung der SuSi&Ko-Skala
Stefan Bohmann
Show details
Authors:
Stefan Bohmann
Martina Suing
Anna Marie Harkin
Stefan Pliquett
Anja Katharina Huemer

Die Förderung des Radverkehrs erfordert Infrastruktur, die nicht nur objektiv sicher ist, sondern auch als sicher wahrgenommen wird. Umgekehrt können Situationen, die subjektiv sicher wirken, aber objektiv ein erhöhtes Gefahrenpotenzial mit sich bringen, bei ausbleibender erforderlicher Verhaltenskompensation riskanteres Verhalten begünstigen. Vor diesem Hintergrund wurde in einem durch die Bundesanstalt für Straßen- und Verkehrswesen geleiteten Expert:innenkreis ein Fragebogen zur Erfassung subjektiver Sicherheit und Fahrkomfort beim Radfahren entwickelt (SuSi&Ko).
Subjektive Sicherheit beim Radfahren ist die persönliche Einschätzung einer konkreten Radfahrsituation dahingehend, inwiefern sie ungefährlich und bewältigbar ist. Subjektive Sicherheit von Radverkehrsführungen, dem Verkehrsgeschehen und der Interaktion mit anderen Verkehrsteilnehmenden drückt sich aus als persönliche Einschätzung der Übersicht, des Risikos, der Bewältigung, des Risikos für Kinder (als vulnerable Radfahrendengruppe), der Nutzungsbereitschaft sowie des Wohlbefindens. Fahrkomfort ist ein weiterer Aspekt des Erlebens beim Radfahren.
Die Validierung erfolgte anhand einer Online-Videostudie (N = 3.947) mit acht Videoclips als zu bewertende Stimuli zu unterschiedlichen Radinfrastrukturen und Verkehrsbedingungen. Psychometrisch wurde ein hierarchisches Graded-Response-Messmodel geschätzt und theoriegeleitet anhand globaler und lokaler Modellpassung optimiert; aus ursprünglich 42 Items verblieben 20 Items im finalen Messmodell. In einem Strukturgleichungsmodell erklärten die Videovignetten 43,3 % der Varianz der latenten subjektiven Sicherheit und 51,1 % der Varianz des physischen Fahrkomforts. Die Ergebnisse unterstützen SuSi&Ko als Skala zur reliablen und validen Erfassung subjektiver Sicherheit und physischen Komforts zur Bewertung von Radverkehrsinfrastrukturen und damit verbundenen Verkehrsbedingungen.

E-Scooter auf dem Gehweg: Störend, weil sie im Weg stehen – oder weil sie E-Scooter sind?
Tibor Petzoldt
Show details
Author:
Tibor Petzoldt

Leih-E-Scooter stehen häufig in der Kritik, unter anderem weil sie wiederholt als Hindernisse auf Gehwegen wahrgenommen werden. Unklar bleibt jedoch, inwieweit entsprechende negative Reaktionen von Fußgänger:innen auf die tatsächlich durch E-Scooter verursachte physische Beeinträchtigung zurückzuführen sind oder ob darüber hinaus allgemein negative Einstellungen gegenüber diesem Verkehrsmittel eine Rolle spielen. Um diese Frage zu adressieren, untersucht die vorliegende Studie, wie Fußgänger:innen Leih-E-Scooter, Fahrräder sowie Umzugskartons bewerten, die auf Gehwegen entweder randseitig und damit wenig störend oder im Gehbereich und somit behindernd positioniert sind.
In einem Online-Experiment mit 200 Teilnehmer:innen (192 nach Bereinigung) aus zwei Alterskohorten wurden behindernd positionierte Objekte durchgehend als störender bewertet als randseitig platzierte. Leih-E-Scooter erhielten dabei höhere Störungsbewertungen als Fahrräder oder Umzugskartons, jedoch ausschließlich im behindernden Szenario.
Die Bewertungen wurden maßgeblich durch allgemeine Einstellungen gegenüber Leih-E-Scootern beeinflusst: Teilnehmer:innen mit eher negativen Haltungen stuften sämtliche Objekte als störender ein, wobei der stärkste Bias gegenüber Leih-E-Scootern auftrat. Die Ergebnisse legen nahe, dass die Wahrnehmung problematisch geparkter Leih-E-Scooter nicht allein durch das Ausmaß der physischen Beeinträchtigung bestimmt wird, sondern zusätzlich durch einstellungsbasierte bzw. stereotype Biases gegenüber diesem Verkehrsmittel.

Von Werten zu Verhalten: Ein theoretisches Modell zur Rolle der Verkehrssicherheitskultur
Dr. Tina Morgenstern
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Tina Morgenstern
Markus Suren
Jens Schade

Die Europäische Union verfolgt mit der Vision Zero das Ziel, Verkehrsunfälle mit Todesfolge vollständig zu vermeiden, wofür ein sicheres und rücksichtsvolles Miteinander aller Verkehrsteilnehmenden unerlässlich ist. Traditionelle Ansätze der Verkehrssicherheit konzentrieren sich überwiegend auf Erziehung, Überwachung und technische Maßnahmen zur Reduzierung von Unfällen und wurden im Safe-System-Ansatz zu einem systemischen Sicherheitskonzept zusammengeführt. Gleichzeitig zeigt sich jedoch, dass kulturelle Faktoren das Verkehrsverhalten sowie gesellschaftliche und politische Reaktionen maßgeblich prägen. Eine gezielte Untersuchung von Verkehrssicherheitskultur ist daher notwendig, um das Safe-System-Denken weiter zu stärken. Ziel der vorliegenden Arbeit ist es, ein theoretisch fundiertes Modell zu entwickeln, das den Einfluss psychologischer Faktoren – wie geteilter Werte, Überzeugungen, Normen und Einstellungen – auf individuelle Entscheidungen in Bezug auf protektives versus riskantes Verkehrsverhalten erklärt. Diese Faktoren bilden den Kern der Verkehrssicherheitskultur und ermöglichen es, kulturelle Einflüsse auf die Verkehrssicherheit systematisch zu erfassen. Auf Basis statistischer Analysen werden die Zusammenhänge empirisch überprüft und erste Ergebnisse der Modellvalidierung diskutiert. Das Modell wird im Rahmen des EU-geförderten Projekts Roads4All* entwickelt und dient als Grundlage für die Ableitung zielgruppenspezifischer Maßnahmen zur Förderung positiver Verkehrssicherheitskulturen.

*Gefördert durch das Forschungs- und Innovationsprogramm Horizont Europe der Europäischen Union im Rahmen der Förderkennzeichen Nr. 101203314 sowie durch das Schweizer Staatssekretariat für Bildung, Forschung und Innovation (SBFI).

Regeltreu statt prosozial? Erwartungen an (automatisierte) Fahrzeuge in Interaktionen mit Fußgängern
Dr. Daniel Eisele
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Daniel Eisele
Yanbin Wu
Tibor Petzoldt

Soziale Interaktionen im Verkehr werden durch Vorfahrtsregeln strukturiert, die Erwartungen an das Verhalten anderer Verkehrsteilnehmender erzeugen. Gleichzeitig besteht die Möglichkeit zu situativem Entgegenkommen, das von formellen Regeln abweicht. Für automatisierte Fahrzeuge stellt sich damit die Frage, ob sie sich strikt regelkonform (und vorhersehbar) oder flexibel (und sozial entgegenkommend) verhalten sollten. Während diese Frage häufig normativ diskutiert wird, liegen bislang wenige empirische Befunde zu situativen Bewertungen konkreter Fahrmanöver vor.
In einem Onlineexperiment mit 262 deutschen Teilnehmenden wurde untersucht, wie die Einhaltung bzw. Abweichung von Vorfahrtsregeln die Bewertung von Fahrzeugverhalten in Querungssituationen zwischen Fußgängern und Fahrzeugen beeinflusst. Die Teilnehmenden nahmen unterschiedliche Rollen in Videos ein (Fußgänger, Fahrer eines konventionellen Fahrzeugs, Passagier eines automatisierten Fahrzeugs) und beurteilten das Fahrzeugverhalten hinsichtlich Erwartungskonformität, Gefallen und Akzeptabilität. Ergänzend wurden situationsübergreifende normative Einstellungen abgefragt.
Die Ergebnisse zeigten, dass die Einhaltung formeller Vorfahrtsregeln der mit Abstand stärkste Prädiktor aller Bewertungen ist; unabhängig von Fahrzeugtyp und Perspektive. Eine differenzierte Analyse zeigte zudem, dass Regelabweichungen durch das Fahrzeug auffallend negativ bewertet werden, während reaktive Anpassungen an das Verhalten von Fußgängern deutlich milder beurteilt werden. Situativer Druck durch nachfolgenden Verkehr beeinflusste vor allem die nicht jedoch Erwartungen oder Gefallen. Die normativen Einstellungen spiegelten dieses Muster wider.
Insgesamt sprechen die Befunde für ein normzentriertes Verständnis von Interaktionen unter deutschen Verkehrsteilnehmende, bei dem Vorfahrtsregeln Erwartungen fundamental strukturieren und situative Anpassung eine nachgeordnete Rolle spielt.

Der Einfluss visueller eHMI-Konzepte auf das prosoziale Verhalten von Autofahrenden gegenüber autonomen Fahrzeugen
Katrin Hauber
Show details
Authors:
Katrin Hauber
Arnd Engeln

Mit der Integration autonomer Fahrzeuge (AV) in den Straßenverkehr gewinnt die Gestaltung ihrer Interaktion mit menschlichen Verkehrsteilnehmenden an Bedeutung. Als maschinelle Akteure werden sie in Interaktionssituationen, z.B. beim Vorfahrtgewähren, teils weniger kooperativ behandelt. Ein zentraler Lösungsansatz hierfür sind externe Human-Machine-Interfaces (eHMIs), die die Fahrabsichten von AVs explizit kommunizieren können. Die vorliegende Studie untersucht, inwiefern unterschiedliche visuelle eHMIs das prosoziale Verhalten von Autofahrenden gegenüber AVs beeinflussen. In einem videobasierten Online-Experiment (N = 114) werden textbasierte, symbolische und anthropomorphe eHMI-Konzepte sowie eine Kontrollbedingung ohne eHMI in einer typischen Verkehrssituation („Grundstücksausfahrt“) miteinander verglichen. Neben prosozialem Verhalten werden Vertrauen und User Experience erfasst. Es werden konzeptionelle und methodische Implikationen für zukünftige Forschung sowie gestaltungsbezogene Perspektiven für eHMIs im Mischverkehr diskutiert.

Rückwärtige Countdown-Anzeigen zur Abfahrtsankündigung automatisierter Shuttles an Haltestellen – Ein Vergleich von Online- und Feldstudie
Ann-Christin Hensch
Show details
Authors:
Ann-Christin Hensch
Silvio Hess
Matthias Beggiato
Stefan Brandenburg
Josef Krems

Die Integration automatisierter Shuttles in den Straßenverkehr verspricht eine Steigerung der Verkehrseffizienz sowie eine verbesserte Mobilitätszugänglichkeit für verschiedene Personengruppen, zum Beispiel durch den Einsatz von On-Demand Haltestellen. Diese Haltestellenkonzepte erfordern zusätzliche Informationen, mit denen das Shuttle bevorstehende Fahrmanöver, wie dessen Abfahrt, an andere Verkehrsteilnehmende kommuniziert. Derzeit wird eine bevorstehende Abfahrt vorwiegend mit dem Fahrtrichtungsanzeiger angekündigt. Diese Informationen sind derzeit allerdings begrenzt und wenig differenziert hinsichtlich eines konkreten
Abfahrtzeitpunktes. Eine zentrale Herausforderung für sichere und vorhersehbare Interaktionen zwischen automatisierten Shuttles und anderen Verkehrsteilnehmenden liegt daher in der Gestaltung geeigneter Interaktionskonzepte für die Ankündigung solcher Manöver. Ein Vorteil automatisierter Shuttles ist hierbei, dass sie über deutlich mehr und präzisere Informationen einer potentiellen Abfahrt als konventionelle Fahrzeuge verfügen. Um die bevorstehende Abfahrt eines Shuttles frühzeitiger und vorhersehbarer anzukündigen, wurden verschiedene Konzepte rückwärtiger Countdown-Anzeigen (CDA) entwickelt. Diese Konzepte wurden anschließend mittels Online- und Feldstudie evaluiert. Dabei bewerteten die Teilnehmenden drei Interaktionskonzepte (konventionelles Interaktionskonzept bestehend aus Fahrtrichtungsanzeiger und Fahrzeugtrajektorie; zusätzliche CDA und Text „Abfahrt“; zusätzliche CDA und „Pfeil“-Icon) hinsichtlich Verständlichkeit/Vorhersagbarkeit und Interaktionskomfort. Die Ergebnisse zeigen für alle untersuchten Variablen eine klare Präferenz für die untersuchten CDA im Vergleich zum konventionellen Konzept. Insgesamt erwiesen sich rückwärtige CDAs als vielversprechender Ansatz, um bevorstehende Shuttlemanöver anderen Verkehrsteilnehmenden frühzeitiger und
vorhersehbarer anzukündigen. Damit haben CDA das Potential sichere und komfortable
Interaktionen zu unterstützen und die Akzeptanz anderer Verkehrsteilnehmender gegenüber Shuttles zu fördern.

Evaluation von vier Kommunikationskonzepten zur Gestaltung der Interaktion im Mischverkehr mit automatisierten Fahrzeugen
Nuria Brüggemann
Show details
Authors:
Nuria Brüggemann
Katrin Hauber
Arnd Engeln

Das vom Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie geförderte Projekt SALSA verfolgt das Ziel, innovative Kommunikationskonzepte für den Mischverkehr mit automatisierten Fahrzeugen zu entwickeln, um eine sichere und intuitive Interaktion mit unterschiedlichen Verkehrsteilnehmenden zu ermöglichen. In einem nutzerzentrierten Designprozess werden vier Kommunikationsprototypen konzipiert: Avatar, AV-to-X-Kommunikation, ein 360°-Rundumsichtdisplay sowie expressive Fahrdynamik. Die Prototypen werden an spezifische Verkehrsszenarien angepasst und aus den Perspektiven von Fußgänger:innen, Radfahrer:innen sowie Autofahrer:innen betrachtet. Die Darstellung erfolgt in Form von User Narratives mit grafischer Visualisierung der Verkehrssituationen und der jeweiligen Kommunikationskonzepte. Zur Evaluation von User Experience, Akzeptanz und Verbesserungspotenzialen werden teilstrukturierte Interviews (N = 17) sowie ein ergänzender Online-Fragebogen eingesetzt. Die Ergebnisse liefern differenzierte Einblicke in die Wahrnehmung und Bewertung der Kommunikationsansätze und dienen als Grundlage für Gestaltungsempfehlungen zur Kommunikation automatisierter Fahrzeuge im Mischverkehr.

Making sensitive psychological data open: Opportunities and challenges of anonymization and synthetic data
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Carolin Strobl (University of Zurich)
Room: UK
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The Open Science movement has made open research data sharing a widely recognized cornerstone of transparent and reproducible science. In the case of sensitive psychological data, however, open dissemination raises fundamental confidentiality concerns. Anonymization and synthetic data approaches offer a promising way to address the tension between open data and privacy protection. This symposium gives a general introduction to the topic, introduces important concepts and techniques for data anonymization and the generation of synthetic data, and discusses the benefits and limitations of the presented approaches. In addition, it highlights how anonymization and synthetic data can be complemented by organizational and technical safeguards to support the responsible and reliable reuse of psychological research data.

(How) can we share sensitive research data? A conceptual warm-up
Prof. Dr. Carolin Strobl | Switzerland
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Carolin Strobl | Switzerland

This talk provides a short general introduction to the problem of sharing sensitive research data, covering key concepts such as direct and indirect identifiers, disclosure risk, and the trade-off between privacy protection and utility. Besides statistical approaches, technical and organizational approaches for safe data sharing are briefly outlined, including controlled environments and remote execution. The talk sets the stage for the symposium by highlighting anonymization and synthetic data as important means for data sharing, while emphasizing that their usefulness depends on the intended application. In particular, it is discussed that while anonymized or synthetic data may be sufficient for reproducing published analyses, as well as for method benchmarking and teaching purposes, their suitability for future analyses cannot be guaranteed. This is why academic institutions will need to increase their efforts to combine these approaches with organizational safeguards for responsible research data reuse.

Data anonymization as a prerequisite for Open Science: An overview of statistical disclosure control techniques
Roman Müller | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Roman Müller | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Carolin Strobl | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Matthias Templ | Switzerland

The Open Science movement has promoted greater transparency and reproducibility in psychological research by encouraging best practices such as data sharing. However, this shift to open data has also drawn attention to challenges related to participant confidentiality, particularly when sensitive individual-level data is shared. A sound understanding of data anonymization is therefore essential for responsible data sharing. Anonymization practices that focus only on removing direct identifiers (e.g. full names and addresses) are often inadequate, since combinations of seemingly innocuous socio-demographic variables can enable re-identification.
The aim of this presentation is to provide a general introduction to data anonymization and an overview of key statistical disclosure control techniques for psychological research data. Using practical examples, we will give a short “guided tour”, touching upon both classical anonymization methods and more recent approaches based on synthetic data generation, together with their potential and limitations. Because data anonymization inevitably leads to a loss of information, we also examine the trade-off between information loss and data utility. By providing this first introduction and references for further reading, we aim to equip researchers with the knowledge and tools needed to share data responsibly while protecting participant confidentiality.

Synthetic data generation to support open psychological research
Thom Volker | Netherlands
Show details
Author:
Thom Volker | Netherlands

Open data has the potential to accelerate scientific progress tremendously, yet legitimate concerns about participant privacy continue to hinder the open dissemination of psychological research data. Synthetic data offer a promising way to address this tension between open data and privacy protection. By learning key characteristics of an observed data set and using them to generate an artificial surrogate, synthetic data generation can help foster data dissemination while protecting participant privacy.
In this talk, we provide an overview of major approaches to synthetic data generation from an applied perspective. We discuss widely used approaches developed in both the statistical and computer science communities. Traditionally, the statistical community relied on conditional synthesis models, in which a separate model is used for each variable. In contrast, the computer science community focused on non-parametric, deep learning-based models that flexibly learn the joint distribution of the data.
We contrast these approaches through the lens of the privacy-utility trade-off and relate this trade-off to the interpretability of the synthesis models. Model interpretability plays a central role in assessing which information is captured by the synthesis process. This, in turn, informs both what can be learned from the synthetic data and the risk of accidental information leakage. When it is unclear what information is contained in the synthesis model, formal privacy guarantees can be incorporated through differentially private methods. We conclude with the promises and pitfalls of synthetic data and point to software and tutorials that make data synthesis readily accessible to psychological researchers.

Synthetic data as a method for improving the reproducibility of psychological research: An introduction to the data-augmented multiple imputation approach
Prof. Dr. Simon Grund | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Simon Grund | Germany
Prof. Dr. Oliver Lüdtke | Germany
Dr. Alexander Robitzsch | Germany

Open data are often regarded as an important step toward improving the reproducibility of psychological research. However, open data are still rare, and without such data, statistical analyses often remain irreproducible. For this reason, it has been recommended that researchers employ synthetic data, a statistical technique that is based on multiple imputation (MI) and that allows the creation of simulated copies of the data that can be shared even if the original data cannot. In this talk, we provide an introduction to the data-augmented MI (DA-MI) approach to synthetic data, which combines traditional masking techniques with MI and aims to provide an improved balance between the utility and protection provided by the synthetic data. To this end, we first discuss some of the reproducibility-related challenges of synthetic data, before we present the results from a comprehensive case study in which we applied the DA-MI approach to a subsample of the PISA 2018 study. In this context, we also discuss practical challenges that often present themselves in applications of synthetic data such as missing data, multilevel data, and complex sampling designs. We conclude with a discussion of our findings, potential areas of future research, and recommendations for practice.

Synthetic data with LLMs versus parametric models: Limits of data utility
Dr. Anna-Carolina Haensch | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Anna-Carolina Haensch | Germany

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as flexible tools for generating synthetic microdata. This talk provides a systematic comparison between LLM-based approaches and classical parametric and semi-parametric methods for data synthesis. The focus is on utility measures at both the microdata and analysis level, distortions in multivariate relationships, and consequences for statistical inference. Empirical examples illustrate that while LLM-based methods often produce superficially plausible records, they frequently fail to reproduce core statistical structures that are well preserved by established synthesis models. The talk situates these findings within the emerging consensus of the field and argues for substantial caution when considering LLMs for utility-critical synthetic data applications.

Understanding and Addressing Affective Polarization: From Conceptualization and Measurement to Interventions
Chair(s) Dr. Nadine Knab (Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin)
Dr. Lucas Köhler (Humboldt Universität zu Berlin)
Room: FR
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Coupled symposium
Duration: 195 Minutes

Affective polarization – the tendency to evaluate political opponents with negative emotions while liking one’s own group – poses a growing challenge for democratic societies. It is linked to democratic disengagement, avoidance of political discussion, and reduced willingness to compromise. Despite a rapidly expanding literature, key questions remain regarding how affective polarization should be conceptualized and measured best, which underlying emotional and social mechanisms sustain it, and - based on these insights - which interventions should be effective in reducing it – particularly in European multiparty systems.
This coupled symposium integrates two complementary symposia that jointly address these challenges by linking conceptual and methodological foundations with intervention-oriented research. The first symposium focuses on how affective polarization can best be defined and measured. Contributions examine the discrete emotions underlying affective polarization, challenging the assumption that it is primarily driven by hatred and highlighting the role of emotions such as disappointment. Other talks systematically compare traditional measurements like the feeling thermometer with measurement approaches in multiparty systems, assess their validity and temporal stability, and discuss their theoretical and normative implications. Additional contributions investigate key correlates and contexts of affective polarization, including trait empathy across political issues, emotional dynamics in face-to-face political discussions, and the role of media consumption in shaping polarization toward partisan and issue-based political groups.
Building on these foundations, the second symposium turns to interventions aimed at reducing affective polarization and its detrimental consequences. Contributions include large-scale intervention tournaments that systematically compare multiple approaches in real-world political contexts, moral learning paradigms that reshape affective preferences by associating moral behavior with political outgroups, and flexibility mindset-based techniques designed to increase consideration of opposing viewpoints even when belief change is difficult. Complementing these are evidence-based conversational strategies identified through systematic review and meta-analysis, as well as translational approaches that adapt therapeutic mechanisms from clinical psychology – such as reducing cognitive rigidity and emotional reactivity – to weaken outgroup derogation and foster more reflective, less polarized political thinking.
By linking conceptual, methodological, and intervention-focused perspectives, this coupled symposium emphasizes that effective interventions to address the issues related to polarization require theoretically precise definitions, valid and context-sensitive measurements, and interventions based on an empirically informed and theoretically grounded understanding of emotional and communicative mechanisms. Taken together, these works contribute to a better understanding of the psychological underpinnings and consequences of affective polarization and how these can inform interventions to foster societal cohesion and constructive political discourse.

Show details

Measuring affective polarization in multi-party systems is challenging as ingroups and outgroups can be defined in multiple ways: as all but the favorite party, the most- or least-liked party, or as broader divisions such as government versus opposition, left versus right party blocs, or moderate versus extreme parties. While some studies compare subsets of these operationalizations, a systematic empirical comparison across many measures remains absent. This project aims to systematically compare several feeling thermometer approaches to assess vertical affective polarization using six waves of a large-scale longitudinal panel survey in Germany (Nwave ~ 4,000; Ntotal = 12,364). We examine (a) re-test reliability and longitudinal trends, (b) convergent validity across operationalizations, and (c) criterion validity with established correlates of polarization (e.g., satisfaction with democracy, support for political violence, political interest, turnout). Preliminary analyses indicate that least-liked group paradigms, spread-scores, and multiple-outgroup approaches are moderately to strongly associated but largely differ in their temporal stability. In contrast, the division-approaches lead to smaller, sometimes even insignificant associations with other operationalizations, suggesting that they measure unique phenomena. Notably, criterion validity of all approaches is low, questioning the meaningfulness of feeling thermometer affect for societal outcome variables discussed in the literature. We will critically discuss the findings in light of which measures are more or less suitable for different contexts or research questions, including their theoretical implications, such as whether approaches allow for testing social identity processes, and underlying normative assumptions, such as the degree to which dislike toward different (blocs of) parties is assumed to be equally problematic for liberal democracies.

Affective polarization, the tendency of opposing ideological groups to experience negative feelings towards each other, is a growing concern in Western democracies. While often discussed in terms of mutual hatred, there is a lack of a comprehensive exploration of the discrete emotions underlying affective polarization. As an initial attempt to address this gap, this research investigates the unique association between various negative emotions (anger, fear, disgust, contempt, disappointment, and hatred) towards ideological out-group members and AP scores. We argue that, in contrast to the purely negative and destructive nature of hatred, the complex nature of disappointment better captures the dynamics of the relations between ideological out-groups. These relations involve not only intense negative feelings but also positive expectations from outgroup members to contribute to the national common good, as fellow citizens. Our research, conducted among both US (Studies 1-4) and Jewish-Israelis (Study 5), identifies disappointment as the strongest and most consistent emotion associated with AP across studies, ideological groups, and measures of emotions. We discuss the implications of adopting a discrete-emotion perspective for understanding AP, its consequences for societies, and its potential to inform strategies for reducing polarization and enhancing democratic and social stability.

The emotionalization of political debates between opponents is often blamed for fueling affective polarization and hindering constructive discourse. Yet, political discussions do not only occur in the public sphere—they also take place in everyday life, as individuals engage with family, friends, or colleagues to share opinions and emotions about politics. In fact, people who less frequently engage with political opponents have been found to be more affectively polarized. However, experimental evidence on the effects of face-to-face discussions remains mixed. This experiment brings face-to-face political discussions into the laboratory to examine how interpersonal dynamics shape emotional and relational outcomes under controlled conditions.
Participants were randomly paired to discuss a socio-political issue with either like-minded or opposing interaction partners, and engage in pre-discussion cooperation (manipulating their prior relationship) to assess their effects on dyadic cohesion. A particular focus was on participants’ emotional experiences, measured via electromyography (EMG), during the interaction. Using multilevel modelling, we analyze how similarity in opinions and cooperation influence emotional engagement and dyadic cohesion. As emotional mimicry signals affiliative intent of interaction partners, it positively relates to successful cooperation, opinion similarity, and self-reported cohesion. Overall, the present study shows how experiences in face-to-face interactions affect social cohesion despite opposing opinions.

In Study 1 (cross-sectional; N ≈ 1,200), higher trait empathy predicted lower affective polarization on the topic of migration, but showed no association with polarization surrounding climate change. In Study 2 (six-wave longitudinal quota-based panel, balanced for age, gender, education, and political orientation; N ≈ 4,000), we replicated both patterns: individuals higher in empathy became less polarized on migration issues over time, while polarization on climate change remained unaffected. Together, these findings suggest that empathy’s depolarizing potential is not universal but issue-specific — effective where intergroup perceptions are salient and humanized (as in migration), but limited where conflicts center on more abstract dimensions (as in climate change). By showing when and how empathy relates to lower affective polarization, our work highlights its nuanced role in democratic engagement and societal division. These results challenge one-size-fits-all empathy interventions and suggest that polarization rooted in moral or knowledge-based disagreements may not respond to empathic appeals. Efforts to reduce polarization should therefore match psychological mechanisms to the type of issue rather than assuming empathy works the same everywhere.

This study investigates how media use and ideological orientations shape affective polarization, the tendency to favor one’s own group while harboring negative sentiments toward opposing groups. Rather than focusing on single outlets, we analyze the composition, ideological balance, and diversity of individual media diets, accounting for ideological orientation, media format, citizen orientation (e.g., public vs. private), and geographical scope (e.g., local vs. national). Drawing on a nationally representative survey conducted in Germany in 2025 (N=4,036), key outcomes capture affective polarization toward partisan and issue-based groups, focusing on climate and asylum policy. Nearly 17,500 open-ended responses naming respondents’ political information sources were manually coded to capture fine-grained media diet characteristics. Using latent profile analysis, we identify distinct patterns that reflect both the tendency and diversity of media use.

Preliminary findings point to media users being on average more polarized than non-users, particularly those consuming TV and newspapers in print or digital form. Overall, affective polarization appears to increase with the number of media sources. These findings challenge conventional echo-chamber claims, revealing a more nuanced relationship between media diversity and polarization. The study contributes to the literature on affective polarization in multiparty systems and issue-based cleavages, and underscores the pivotal role of media in potentially (de-)polarizing audiences.

Affective polarization and its potential consequences for democratic functioning are a central concern in contemporary democracies, motivating a growing literature on interventions aimed at reducing polarization, anti-democratic attitudes, and support for political violence. The interventions target a diverse set of theoretical mechanisms discussed as potential levers for reducing affective polarization and related democratic consequences, including correcting misperceptions about political opponents, emphasizing common identities, and using pro-democratic elite cues. The interventions are implemented in a randomized survey experiment conducted with a sample of 22,500 Dutch citizens in the Spring of 2026, with quotas ensuring representativeness in terms of age, gender, education, and prior vote choice. By comparing a broad set of interventions within a single design, we aim to identify effective strategies that can be applied to multiparty systems and assess whether patterns observed in the United States generalize to European democracies. Affective polarization, the growing gap between negativity toward political outgroups and positivity toward political ingroups, threatens democracies. German citizens increasingly report avoiding conversations about polarizing topics due to anticipated conflict, social sanctions, or escalation. Psychological research explains such avoidance with mechanisms such as psychological reactance, threat appraisals, or low perceived self-efficacy that crucially shape experiences of affective polarization.

Meta-analytic effect size comparisons will identify strategies with robust, scalable effects on dependent variables related to affective polarization and democratic action.
This work clarifies these relationships and informs the development of psychologically grounded, scalable interventions. It also guides the later operationalization of these interventions in large language model (LLM)-based conversational training applications, which is the core objective of DemocraGPT.

In democratic societies, it is vital to consider different perspectives when deciding upon far-reaching issues such as the implementation of climate policies. However, counterfactual mindset priming increased participants’ self-reported consideration of opposing viewpoints during the manipulation. Consideration of opposing viewpoints, in turn, was related to less belief-consistent argument evaluation subsequently. These findings highlight that increasing the consideration of opposing viewpoints via counterfactual thinking might be a way to overcome polarized debates, but more effective manipulations are needed to have a substantive impact.

Therapy for Peace? On the Potential of Clinical Interventions to Improve Intergroup Relations

Show details
Authors:
Dr. Nadine Knab

Prof. Dr. Klaus Michael Reininger | Germany

A growing body of research shows that affective polarization is sustained by psychological processes such as perceived threat and cognitive rigidity. These mechanisms mirror processes studied and treated in clinical psychology. Yet, the potential of clinical science to inform interventions in intergroup conflict remains systematically underexplored. We aim to bridge clinical and political psychology by proposing a translational framework that maps therapeutic mechanisms onto three domains central to intergroup conflict: (1) reducing outgroup derogation, (2) fostering openness and self-reflection, and (3) reducing stress and emotional reactivity.
Clinical approaches could reduce outgroup derogation by targeting rigid, dichotomous thinking. A central example is the continuum technique, widely used in cognitive therapy to challenge black-and-white beliefs. This method encourages individuals to place people, attitudes, and behaviors along graded dimensions rather than into fixed categories. Applied to intergroup contexts, continuum-based interventions can highlight variability within groups, overlap between groups, and shared human experiences, thereby weakening categorical boundaries that fuel moral absolutism and outgroup devaluation. Similarly, metacognitive training, originally developed for psychosis, helps individuals recognize reasoning biases such as overconfidence and “jumping to conclusions.” When adapted to political contexts, it reduces biased evidence use, ingroup favoritism, and outgroup devaluation, thereby weakening polarization and supporting democratic norms.
We argue that integrating clinical and social psychology through translational research offers mutual benefits, but this goal requires shared language, interdisciplinary collaboration, and careful ethical reflection – but the same processes that restore flexibility and compassion in individuals may also help societies move beyond entrenched polarization.

Affective empathy constitutes an intensively studied psychological construct, yet its valid assessment remains a challenge. In light of the biases of self-report instruments, behavior-based measurement approaches are in demand. In two studies, we pursued the idea that emotional mimicry – the facial mirroring of another’s emotional expressions – could serve as a behavioral indicator of interindividual differences in affective empathy. In Study 1, we presented 61 participants with an initial set of standardized stimulus videos, each depicting a person narrating an emotional experience. We simultaneously recorded participants’ facial expressions on video and then applied automated emotion recognition software to both the participants’ and the stimulus persons’ facial expressions. We then computed synchrony scores between both as a proxy for participants’ emotional mimicry. Results indicated promising evidence for the internal consistency of the single mimicry assessments across different stimuli and emotions. Furthermore, we found a meaningful convergent and discriminant correlation pattern of an aggregated mimicry score with established measures of affective empathy and other constructs, providing initial support for the suitability of this measurement paradigm. Thereafter, we developed 40 new emotional stimulus videos, which were especially tailored to the purpose of the present mimicry analysis. In a multistage selection process, involving automated software and expert ratings, we identified the most valid stimulus videos. In Study 2, we presented this selection to another sample, using a similar methodological approach as in Study 1 and again examined the reliability and validity of the mimicry assessments.

The posts were created and pre-tested in our lab. We asked 273 participants to read and rate a total of 30 emotional SNS posts (15 with positive valence and 15 with negative valence) and four comments related to each post (two negative comments and two positive comments).

The results show that various personality traits, especially extraversion and openness, do indeed influence ratings of emotional SNS posts. Thus, we were able to extend findings from the context of emotional pictures to text-based SNS content. Personality appears to affect the general processing of emotional information. Therefore, future studies investigating emotional stimuli should always take participants’ personality traits into account to avoid systematically biased results.

Executive Functions, Self-Regulation, and Academic Abilities in Early and Middle Childhood
Chair(s) Sophia Grobe
Dr. Jonas Schäfer
Room: NL
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The construct of executive functions (EF) is composed of multiple higher-order cognitive processes serving the control of thought and action in a purposeful, goal-directed manner. In the psychological literature, three core EF are differentiated including the short-term storage and manipulation of information (working memory), the suppression of prepotent responses and distracting information (inhibition), and the ability to flexibly switch attention between tasks or mental sets (cognitive flexibility). Rapid developmental changes of EF in early childhood and continuous improvements across middle childhood have sparked considerable interest in this construct resulting in a vast body of research examining childhood EF and their interplay with other developmental domains, such as self-regulation and academic abilities.
Self-regulation is a closely related construct referring to the ability to control thoughts, behaviors, and emotions according to internal and external goals. While self-regulation has been linked to EF, evidence on the relations between EF and self-regulated learning (SRL) – the regulation of cognition, behavior, and affective-motivational processes in academic learning contexts – is fragmented in childhood samples. Theoretical considerations and empirical studies in older-aged samples suggest that EF may predict SRL and that metacognitive abilities of monitoring and control might mediate this relation. Insights into this mechanism may also offer explanations for links between EF and academic abilities.
Regarding the role of EF for academic abilities such as math and language during early and middle childhood, findings generally indicate positive associations, while several open questions remain. Academic abilities comprise a wide range of skills relevant for school-readiness and -performance, some of which have received little attention. For example, proportional reasoning is considered a central competence in mathematics but has rarely been examined in relation to EF in young children. Another unresolved question concerns the conditions that potentially modulate the relation between EF and academic abilities during childhood. Given that EF are susceptible to environmental influences and that academic development is shaped by learning contexts, children’s home learning environments, particularly in light of rising digital media use, may affect literacy and math skills and modulate the link between EF and these early indicators of academic ability.
This symposium synthesizes recent empirical studies on EF in early and middle childhood. It presents current research on the digital assessment of domain-general EF and their interplay with domain-specific abilities relevant for academic success, including SRL, metacognition, and academic abilities while also considering environmental conditions that may shape these relations. The contributions aim to advance an integrative understanding of how EF support academic development across childhood.
In the first contribution, results on the validity and reliability of a task battery for the tablet-based assessment of EF (TAB-EF) in children at preschool and elementary school age are presented. Latent variable analyses on the underlying structure of the TAB-EF and relations of the latent EF factor with fluid intelligence and science problem-solving indicate the construct validity of the TAB-EF. In addition, analyses of split-half and test-retest reliability yield satisfactory results
Using a latent variable approach, the second contribution examines the interplay of EF, SRL, and procedural metacognition in a sample of preschool and fourth-grade elementary school children. While EF and SRL are significantly correlated in both age groups, procedural metacognition does not mediate this relation in either age group which contrasts findings in older samples and will be discussed.
The third contribution focuses on spatial abilities, including visuo-spatial working memory (VSWM) – a component of EF – and mental rotation (MR), as predictors of preschoolers‘ proportional reasoning. Both VSWM and MR contribute significantly to preschool children’s discrete proportional reasoning, but not continuous proportional reasoning. These findings shed light on the mediating role of working memory for children’s strategy use in number and magnitude processing.
The fourth contribution analyzes the role of home learning environments (HLE) in the relations between EF and early math and language skills. Using a person-centered approach in a sample of preschool children, four HLE profiles are differentiated. Moderation analyses indicate that associations between EF and these early academic abilities differ across profiles. Among other findings, the study suggests that children with low numeracy exposure may rely more on EF to solve math problems, whereas high digital media use combined with little analog input is associated with weaker links between EF and early academic abilities.

Prof. Dr. Miriam Leuchter | RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau
Prof. Dr. Franziska Perels | Saarland University
Prof. Dr. Julia Karbach | RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau

Given the high relevance of executive functions (EF) for various domains, including self-regulation, academic competencies, and well-being, the reliable and valid assessment of EF in children is considered essential. Against this background, we validated a newly developed task battery for the tablet-based assessment of EF (TAB-EF) in a sample of N = 1393 children at preschool and elementary school age (Mage = 7.74 years, SDage= 1.58, rangeage = 4.42 – 12.08 years, % female = 49.61). Children completed the TAB-EF tasks assessing inhibition (Go/No-go Task & AX-CPT), working memory (Backward Corsi Task & Backward Verbal Span Task), and cognitive flexibility (FIST & M-WCST) and measures of reasoning and science-problem-solving. A unitary EF model represented task performance very well (χ2SB (df) = 6.42 (8), p = .600, CFI = 1.00, RMSEA [90 % CI] = 0 [0-.03], SRMR = .01) suggesting construct validity of the TAB-EF. The latent EF factor significantly predicted reasoning (β = .47, p < .001), and, less strongly, science problem-solving (β = .19, p < .001) indicating convergent and divergent validity, respectively. Split-half reliability estimates for the TAB-EF tasks were strong (rs = .79-.96, ps < .001), whereas test-retest reliability estimates were moderate to strong (rs = .54-.79, ps < .001). The results demonstrate satisfactory validity and reliability of the TAB-EF. Moreover, the easy administration and child-friendly design add to the feasibility of the TAB-EF making it particularly useful for the assessment of EF at preschool and elementary school age.

Do Metacognitive Processes Bridge Executive Functions and Self-regulated Learning? Evidence from Preschool and Elementary School Samples
Christina Rocker | Saarland University
Show details
Authors:
Christina Rocker | Saarland University
Dr. Lena Maffert-Grüneisen | Saarland University
Sophia Grobe | RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau
Dr. Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich | Saarland University
Prof. Dr. Julia Karbach | RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau
Prof. Dr. Franziska Perels | Saarland University

Self-regulated learning (SRL) and executive functions (EFs) are considered as crucial prerequisites for successful learning, even in childhood. While SRL comprises context-dependent, goal-oriented learning processes in which learners actively plan, monitor, and regulate their cognition, motivation, and behavior, EFs describe higher-order, context-independent cognitive control processes, such as updating, inhibition, and shifting. Procedural metacognition (i.e., monitoring and control processes) is discussed as a central link between EFs and SRL. Evidence for mediation exists in older samples but is scarce in preschool and elementary school children.
Therefore, this study aims to examine associations among EFs, SRL and procedural metacognition in preschoolers and fourth graders and tests whether procedural metacognition mediates the EF-SRL link. Additionally, age-group differences are analyzed.
EFs were assessed using two tasks per core EF (e.g., Go/No-go for inhibition, flexible item selection task for shifting, and backward word span task for updating), SRL using a strategy knowledge test, and metacognition using a pair association task. Initial latent analyses of preschoolers (n = 227) and fourth graders (n = 210) show that EFs significantly predict SRL (βpreschool = .41; ppreschool = .002; βelementary school = .35; pelementary school = .021). However, the indirect effect via metacognition was not significant in either age group.
The results of the study will be discussed.

Preschoolers’ visuo-spatial working memory is associated with discrete but not with continuous proportional reasoning
Dr. Jonas Schäfer | University of Education Schwäbisch Gmünd
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Jonas Schäfer | University of Education Schwäbisch Gmünd
Prof. Dr. Wenke Möhring | University of Education Schwäbisch Gmünd

Young children’s proportional reasoning is processed differently, depending on whether to-be-matched proportions are visually segmented (discrete) or not (continuous). Previous research suggests that young children typically apply counting strategies when matching discrete visualizations, which often interferes with an accurate detection of proportional relations (natural number bias), suggesting a negative association of counting and task performance. Moreover, the effects of spatial skills relevant for visuo-spatial pattern recognition, such as visuo-spatial working memory (VSWM) and mental rotation (MR), on different types of proportional reasoning have rarely been investigated in young children.
Thus, we tested 37 preschool children (Mage = 4.55 years, SD = 0.81; 35% female) assessing their VSWM, MR, counting abilities, discrete and continuous proportional reasoning abilities. Regression analyses showed that VSWM and MR had significant effects on discrete proportional reasoning (β = .16** and .10*, respectively), but no significant effects on continuous proportional reasoning, after controlling for participants’ age and gender. Counting abilities had significant effects on both discrete (β = .16**) and continuous proportional reasoning (β = .08*).
The findings indicate that VSWM and MR are associated with young children’s proportional reasoning particularly when discrete information is provided, highlighting a nuanced picture: Visual discretization might relieve VSWM resources, that could be allocated to maintenance of relative proportions, and MR might support matching of clearly outlined visuo-spatial patterns. At the same time, counting abilities showed positive effects on both types of proportional reasoning, which contradicts natural number bias theories, stating that children apply counting strategies only in discretized visualizations.

Home learning environment patterns relate to preschoolers’ math and language skills and moderate their links with executive functions
Dr. Susanne Enke | Leipzig University
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Susanne Enke | Leipzig University
Prof. Dr. Catherine Gunzenhauser | Ludwigsburg University of Education
Prof. Dr. Henrik Saalbach | Leipzig University

Executive functions (EF) support children’s engagement with learning opportunities and are sensitive to environmental stimulation. The home learning environment (HLE) constitutes a central context where children acquire domain-specific (e.g., math, language) and domain-general competencies such as EF. With digital media increasingly complementing or replacing family interactions in the HLE, little is known about how different HLE constellations of analog and digital exposure relate to math and language skills and their links with EF. Using a person-centered approach, we build on four previously identified latent HLE classes (including digital media use) and examine (1) differences in early math and language skills between latent classes and (2) whether HLE patterns moderate relations between these skills and EF. Participants were N=369 preschoolers (M_age=55.24 months). Language, math, and EF were directly assessed with standardized tests; parents reported on children’s HLE. Results confirmed differences in domain-specific skills and a significant moderation by HLE. Two profiles with high numeracy-related interactions (i.e., explaining calculations and playing numeracy-related games together) showed the strongest language skills and EF-language associations, suggesting that high-quality verbal, scaffolded interactions jointly foster EF and language. The strongest EF–math association emerged in a profile with low numeracy input, suggesting that, when numeracy routines are infrequent, children may rely more heavily on EF in math-related tasks. A fourth profile characterized by high digital media use showed the lowest language and math skills and the weakest associations. Together, the findings suggest that different HLE constellations may shape how EF supports early math and language learning.
