Innovative Ability Measurement: Psychometric and Technological Approaches
Chair(s) Dr. Timo Gnambs (Leibniz Institut für Bildungsverläufe (LIfBi) )
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Oliver Wilhelm
Room: FI
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Coupled symposium
Duration: 195 Minutes

In these coupled symposia, we aim to highlight novel psychometric and technological developments in ability and achievement research (AAR). Unlike assessment in other fields of psychology, AAR is characterized by three key attributes. First, research adheres to the principle of indifference of the indicator. Second, efforts are often multivariate, and analysis is geared towards the level of latent variables. Third, knowledge develops cumulatively, fueled by more tractable scientific frameworks. The 2 x 4 contributions in these symposia highlight these principles across different fields of AAR. The first symposium focuses on construction principles and the validity of novel measures. Busse et al. study novel measures of object perception that may enlarge the concept of visual processing. Walter and Schroeders report key contributors to item difficulty in novel matrix reasoning measures. Thelen et al. investigate a novel reasoning measure, first used in AI research that emphasizes novel problem solving. Mangold et al. describe a novel validation approach for a vocabulary test by integrating theoretically grounded item features into explanatory item response models. Schroeders and Achaa-Amankwaa will present the results of a new LLM-supported vocabulary measure. Gnambs will discuss the presentations from the first section. The second symposium focuses on testing modes and design features. Kutscher and Gnambs systematically reviewed the impact of remote versus in-person testing. Gnambs et al. compare web-based, video-based, and in-person testing in terms of selection and measurement bias. Köllich et al. experimentally study the psychometric consequences of varying levels of experimental control and instantiation in ability tests. Achaa-Amankwaa et al. place the popular word-puzzle game “Wordle” in a nomological network. Wilhelm will discuss the presentations from the second section of this double symposium.

Beyond Mental Rotation and Paper Folding: Purifying and Extending Common Tests of Visual Abilities
Friederike Busse | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Friederike Busse | Germany
Jasmin Thelen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Oliver Wilhelm | Germany

Established approaches for measuring visual abilities (gv) are plagued by several persistent problems. gv has poor divergent validity with fluid intelligence (gf) - They correlate close to unity with one another, and often their operationalizations are interpreted indiscriminately. Additionally, prototypical gv measures do not nearly exhaust the breadth of visual abilities that are investigated in cognitive neuropsychology for instance. In a series of studies, we want to eradicate these problems by extending the scope of gv and establishing more unequivocal and purified lower order factors of gv. In study 1 we confirmed Gauthier’s factor O (object recognition) and replicated the overly high convergence between prototypical gv and gf measures at a latent level. O was weaker related with gf, relative to gv. In study 2 (ongoing) we want to replicate and extend these findings for a broader portfolio of measurements along more covariates (e.g., speed and visual short-term memory). O is measured broadly with several paradigms and stimulus classes (complex 3D figures, simple 2D shapes, faces). Moreover, gf tasks are experimentally modified to reduce the gv contribution. An overarching model for a much broader gv factor will be established. We discuss overarching strategies for improving construct coverage and discrimination in ability measurement.

Developing BOLT – A Matrix Test Using Boolean Operations to Assess Logical Thinking
Jonas Walter | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jonas Walter | Germany
Prof. Dr. Ulrich Schroeders | Germany

Matrix reasoning tasks are widely used measures of fluid reasoning. Despite variation in construction principles, four difficulty components recur across tests: the number of elements, the number of rules, rule type, and perceptual organization. Among these, rule type is particularly central and can be formally classified into unary, binary, and ternary operations. Accordingly, we introduce BOLT (Boolean Operations and Logical Thinking), a matrix test grounded in Boolean algebra as the formal framework for item generation. Across two online pilot studies (Study 1: N = 473, 45 items; Study 2: N = 430, 42 items) and one operational administration (Study 3: N = 7,150, 39 items), we estimated Rasch item difficulties and examined feature-based explanations of these estimates. Study 1 confirmed that the number of binary rules was the primary driver of difficulty, whereas unary and ternary rules showed no consistent effects. For Studies 2–3, we combined cross-validated LASSO feature selection with linear logistic test models (LLTMs) to quantify contributions of structural features (number of elements, number of rules, rule types) and perceptual-organizational indices that were extracted from stimulus files. Item difficulty could be predicted with sufficient accuracy (LLTM R² = .75 in Study 2; R² = .57 in Study 3). Overall, binary operations and perceptual organization emerged as converging determinants of item difficulty in BOLT items. Future work should replicate and extend the finding that image-derived computer-vision indices make an incremental contribution beyond rule-based predictors and integrate these indices into models of matrix-item difficulty.

Novel Problem Solving After All? Emphasizing Rule Inference in Fluid Intelligence Tasks With the Abstract and Reasoning Corpus
Jasmin Thelen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jasmin Thelen | Germany
Friederike Busse | Germany
Prof. Dr. Oliver Wilhelm | Germany

The Abstract and Reasoning Corpus (ARC-AGI) was developed to assess fluid intelligence (gf) in artificial intelligence systems as well as in humans. Unlike many established measures of gf, which primarily emphasize working memory capacity, ARC-AGI emphasizes divergent aspects of inductive reasoning and rule finding. In Study 1 (N = 100), 20 representative tasks from the original 400-item ARC-AGI evaluation set were examined with regard to their psychometric properties. The item sample covered a sufficient range of difficulty in above average educated young adults. At the latent level, ARC-AGI was moderately correlated with traditional gf and concept formation and weakly with figural originality. Overall, first construct validity evidence of ARC-AGI in humans was promising. In Study 2 (ongoing) we investigate the nomological net of gf tasks focussing on rule finding. Traditional gf, divergent thinking, working memory capacity, visual short-term memory, and object perception serve as covariates. We discuss methodological advantages and potential limitations of the ARC-AGI as an assessment format in specific and gf-tasks focusing on rule finding in general.

Wortschatzerwerb türkisch-deutsch bilingualer Vorschulkinder: Validierung eines Wortschatztests mittels explanatorischer Item-Response-Modelle
Dr. Madlen Mangold | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Madlen Mangold | Germany
Wolfgang Lenhard | Germany
Daniel Schulz | Germany
Julia Schindler | Germany

Der Wortschatzerwerb bilingualer Kinder wird durch eine Vielzahl linguistischer Faktoren bestimmt, die in enger Wechselwirkung mit dem sprachlichen Input und individuellen Voraussetzungen stehen. Um diesen dynamischen Entwicklungsprozess adäquat abzubilden und eine gezielte Förderung zu ermöglichen, müssen diagnostische Instrumente sensitiv gegenüber individueller Variabilität sein und zugleich eine sprachübergreifende Vergleichbarkeit gewährleisten. Die vorliegende Studie validiert ein sprachübergreifend entwickeltes Instrument zur Erfassung des produktiven Wortschatzes im Deutschen. Untersucht werden itembezogene Prädiktoren der Wortproduktion bei türkisch-deutsch bilingualen Vorschulkindern im Vergleich zu deutsch-monolingualen Kindern. Berücksichtigt wurden Itemmerkmale wie Erwerbsalter, Wortfrequenz, lexikalische Kategorie, Wortlänge und lexikalische Komplexität. Zur Sicherstellung der sprachübergreifenden Vergleichbarkeit kam ein literaturbasierter explanatorischer Ein-Parameter-Item-Response-Theorie-Ansatz (1PL IRT) zum Einsatz.
Die Stichprobe umfasste 126 Kinder im Alter von 33 bis 78 Monaten, darunter 51 türkisch-deutsch bilinguale und 75 deutsch-monolinguale Kinder. Der deutsche Wortschatz wurde mithilfe einer neu entwickelten, computerbasierten Bildbenennungsaufgabe mit 32 Items aus unterschiedlichen semantischen Bereichen erfasst. Ein adaptives Testdesign mit einem Routing-Set stellte sicher, dass ein breites Spektrum an Itemschwierigkeiten abgebildet wurde.
Die Ergebnisse bestätigten die intendierte Differenzierung der Itemschwierigkeit. Signifikante Effekte zeigten sich für Erwerbsalter, Wortfrequenz, lexikalische Kategorie und lexikalische Komplexität: Früher erworbene und häufigere Wörter wurden leichter benannt, Substantive zuverlässiger produziert als Verben, und Komposita erwiesen sich als besonders anspruchsvoll. Das Modell erklärte 47 % der Varianz und stützte die Konstruktvalidität des Instruments. Interaktionseffekte zwischen Sprachhintergrund und Itemmerkmalen traten nicht auf, was auf eine strukturell parallele Wortschatzentwicklung bei mono- und bilingualen Kindern hinweist. Methodisch verdeutlicht die Studie das Potenzial explanatorischer IRT-Modelle für die Validierung sprachübergreifend einsetzbarer Wortschatztests im Vorschulalter.

Developing NOVA: A Next-Generation Open Vocabulary Assessment
Ulrich Schroeders | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Ulrich Schroeders | Germany
Priscilla Achaa-Amankwaa | Germany

In psychological assessment, vocabulary tests are commonly used as reliable and efficient indicators of crystallized intelligence, as retrospective proxies for premorbid intelligence, and as measures of language proficiency. However, many of the widely used German vocabulary tests are outdated, proprietary, and lack a clear rationale for item selection. To address these limitations, we developed a new, openly available vocabulary test: the Next-Generation Open Vocabulary Assessment (NOVA). We constructed 110 multiple-choice vocabulary items with support from ChatGPT and administered them to 1,052 German-speaking adults using a multiple-matrix design, along with a declarative knowledge test for validation purposes. Using Ant Colony Optimization, we assembled two parallel 30-item short forms by optimizing reliability as well as item difficulty and discrimination parameters within a three-parameter logistic item response model. The resulting test forms provided unidimensional and reliable measurement, covered a broad ability range, showed no gender differences, and correlated strongly with declarative knowledge. A Shiny app is available to calculate norm-referenced scores based on individual test results. Additional analyses revealed that 61.2% of the variance in item difficulty was explained by word frequency and word length. Prediction accuracy could be further increased to about 80% when PCA-derived dimensions of the word embeddings were used. These findings underscore the potential utility of linguistic features and large language models for guiding future vocabulary test development.

From Lab to Laptop: A Systematic Review of Remote vs. In-Person Cognitive Assessments
Dr. Tanja Kutscher | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Tanja Kutscher | Germany
PD Dr. Timo Gnambs | Germany

Due to the rapid development of digital technologies, self-administered web-based assessments of cognitive abilities are increasingly used as an alternative to traditional in-person testing, particularly in large-scale assessment studies. Remote assessment enables cost-efficient data collection and facilitates the recruitment of large and diverse samples. However, concerns remain regarding selection bias, the standardization of testing conditions, and psychometric data quality.
This systematic review aims to synthesize empirical evidence on the equivalence and psychometric quality of remote assessments of cognitive abilities compared to traditional in-person testing. Specifically, it examines (a) the extent of selection bias in remote assessment studies, (b) the degree to which standardized testing conditions can be ensured in remote settings, and (c) the psychometric quality of remote assessments, including reliability, validity, and test equivalence.
A total of 58 articles published in the last decade were systematically identified from Web of Science, Scopus, and Allen AI Paper Finder using the search terms remote assessment and cognitive ability and their synonyms. The review includes studies comparing remote and in-person assessments, different remote assessment forms, or examining their feasibility and usability (e.g., cheating, distractions, proctoring).
Preliminary findings suggest that remote assessments may provide results comparable to traditional in-person testing. Data quality, however, varied depending on the cognitive ability assessed, participant characteristics, the level of supervision, and technical conditions.
The review will discuss key challenges and provide recommendations for achieving high-quality data in remote cognitive assessments, primarily focusing on large-scale assessment studies.

Mode effects in internet-based cognitive testing: Evidence from an educational large-scale assessment
PD Dr. Timo Gnambs | Germany
Show details
Authors:
PD Dr. Timo Gnambs | Germany
Michael Bergrab | Germany
Prof. Dr. Christian Aßmann | Germany

Cognitive ability assessments typically rely on supervised and highly standardized test settings to ensure comparable conditions for all respondents and minimize the risk of measurement bias. However, in recent years, many psychological and educational studies with voluntary on-site assessments (e.g., in schools or private homes) face declining participation, leading to high non-response rates. This study examined whether switching from on-site to remote testing could provide a cost-efficient alternative without compromising data quality.
As part of an ongoing longitudinal large-scale assessment in Germany, N = 4,298 young adults were randomly assigned to three computer-assisted testing conditions for reading and mathematical competence: (a) unproctored web-based tests, (b) proctored web-based tests via video-conference, and (c) traditional proctored tests in the participants’ homes. The study evaluated the impact of the assessment mode on both selection and measurement bias.
Preliminary results indicated that unproctored, web-based testing had lower response rates compared to video-based or on-site testing. However, systematic selection bias was not observed because response propensity was negligibly associated with participant characteristics. Response rates were similar between the two supervised assessment conditions. Analyses of differential test functioning demonstrated robust measurement models across modes, with only slightly higher rates of missing responses in unproctored, web-based testing, particularly for items with complex response formats and among lower-ability respondents.
Overall, these findings suggest that web-based ability assessments – whether supervised or unsupervised – can provide comparable measurements of cognitive competence and offer a viable, cost-efficient option for future psychological and educational studies.

Bearbeitungsverhalten in verschiedenen Erhebungssettings des NEPS: Offline mit InterviewerIn, Online mit InterviewerIn, Online mit automatischen Popups
Leo Köllich | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Leo Köllich | Germany
Dr. Lena Engelhardt | Germany
Prof. Dr. Frank Goldhammer | Germany

Online Testen, besonders ohne InterviewerIn, könnte ForscherInnen und TeilnehmerInnen viel Ressourcen sparen (z.B. Personal, Zeit und Ausgaben in Zusammenhang mit An- und Abreise, Raum, Ausstattung und Organisation). Dabei gibt es Gestaltungsspielraum hinsichtlich Aufsicht, Adaptivität und Interventionen. Bisher ist jedoch wenig beforscht, wie sich verschiedene Settings auf das Bearbeitungsverhalten auswirken, wenn TeilnehmerInnen keine Konsequenzen erwarten („low-stakes Assessments“), bzw. wie eine möglichst gute Datenqualität erzielt werden kann (Rios & Liu, 2017; Steger et al., 2018; Alahmadi, 2022). Mit einer aktuellen Studie des Nationalen Bildungspanels NEPS (Blossfeld & Roßbach, 2019) wollen wir zur Klärung beitragen. Dabei bearbeiteten 2214 TeilnehmerInnen der Startkohorte 4 (Alter ~ 29) einen Mathe- sowie Lese-Kompetenztest (Zeitlimit jeweils 28 Minuten, variierende Testreihenfolge), aufgeteilt in drei Gruppen: 1) offline Testung mit seitlich nebenan sitzender InterviewerIn („CAPI“), 2) online Videokonferenz-Setting – InterviewerInnenfenster während Aufgabenbearbeitung im Hintergrund, TeilnehmerInnen teilen Bildschirm, Kamera und Audio („CALVI“), und 3) unbeaufsichtigte online Teilnahme mit zusätzlichen Item-Funktionen (Hilfemenü, Popup-Fenster bei Rapid Responding und besonders langsamen Antworten bzw. Inaktivitätsperioden) („CAWI“). Erste Analysen der Mathe-Daten hinsichtlich Rapid Responding (RR) deuten an, dass RR in CALVI über die verschiedenen Items hinweg konsistent am seltensten vorkommt. RR-Quoten von CAWI übersteigen nur später im Testverlauf jene von CAPI. RR-Popups führten selten zu einer Verbesserung der Antwort, haben jedoch scheinbar weitere RRs verhindert (CAWI: mehr Personen mit 1 RR, aber nicht mehr mit mehreren RRs). Abbrüche nach Teststart sind in CAWI geringfügig häufiger. Im Rahmen des Symposiums sollen genauere Ergebnisse zum Bearbeitungsverhalten (Abbrüche, Antwortzeiten, Fensterwechsel, etc.) diskutiert werden, inclusive etwaiger Verknüpfungen von Settingwirkung und Persönlichkeit.

Wordle – A Game-Based Assessment of Verbal Ability?
Priscilla Achaa-Amankwaa | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Priscilla Achaa-Amankwaa | Germany
Jonas Walter | Germany
Prof. Dr. Ulrich Schroeders | Germany

There is a long and successful tradition of incorporating games into cognitive ability assessment, with recent research exploring the potential of online games as engaging and valid measures of cognitive ability. Building on this, we examine the popular word puzzle game Wordle as a possible measure of verbal ability in an adult German-speaking population. In Wordle, players guess a five-letter word within six attempts based on feedback provided for each guess. First, we investigate the dimensionality and reliability of the game using a Generalized Partial Credit Model within an IRT framework, expecting that a unidimensional model fits the data well. Second, we locate Wordle proficiency within a nomological network of cognitive abilities, including vocabulary, declarative knowledge, verbal fluency, and figural reasoning. Drawing on empirical associations between crossword puzzle proficiency and cognitive abilities, we expect correlations of Wordle proficiency with vocabulary, declarative knowledge, and verbal fluency at r = .60 - .70, and with figural reasoning at r = .30 - .40. Third, we examine the associations between Wordle proficiency and demographic variables (age, gender, education), experience-related factors (daily reading time and game experience), as well as strategic approaches to the game, including self-reported strategy use and an entropy-based measure of strategy efficiency derived from the information gain of each guess. We will report the results of this Registered Report (Stage I accepted). Data collection (targeting N = 390) and analysis are scheduled to be completed by March 2026.

Which Instructional Methods Facilitate Transfer? Evidence from a Second-Order Meta-Analysis
Jan Joswig | Trier University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jan Joswig | Trier University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Michael Schneider | Trier University | Germany

Transfer is a central goal of formal education, as learners are expected to apply acquired knowledge to new contexts. Yet facilitating transfer in practice remains challenging and scientific recommendations are not always clear or consistent. This study aims to address this issue by synthesizing existing meta-analyses to estimate the effects of instructional methods on transfer using a second-order meta-analytic approach. Following a standardized literature search in PsycINFO, ERIC, and MetaX, 3537 titles and abstracts were screened, resulting in a full-text review of 803 records. Ultimately, 21 meta-analyses, summarizing 463 primary studies, were included. The analysis examined overall effect sizes, moderating factors, methodological quality, and potential publication bias. Results indicated a small but positive overall effect of instructional methods on transfer (d = 0.30), which was replicated in the subset of randomized controlled studies (d = 0.29), indicating robustness and supporting causal interpretations. Considerable variability across instructional methods was observed, suggesting that not all approaches are equally effective. Both instructional methods that minimized transfer distance (e.g., through spatial or temporal contiguity, d = 0.8) and those focusing on abstraction (e.g., self-explanation, d = 0.59) generally yielded stronger effects than methods lacking these features. Evidence of a small publication bias was found, and several meta-analyses were limited in methodological quality, for instance by not reporting publication bias or data-handling decisions. Overall, transfer can be facilitated by selecting appropriate instructional methods, particularly those that reduce the distance between learning and application contexts or those that promote abstraction.

Meta-Analysis of Interventions on Source Credibility Discernment
Marvin Fendt | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Marvin Fendt | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU) | Germany
Xenia Muth | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU)
Peter Edelsbrunner | Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU)

Critical evaluation of source credibility is essential in today’s digital landscape but often requires explicit instruction. While there are initial efforts to structure the research field, we are not aware of meta-analyses on source credibility interventions.
Our preregistered meta-analysis followed PRISMA guidelines and addresses this gap by examining the effect of interventions to foster source credibility judgement and moderators on participant characteristics and learning environments. We searched for controlled experimental studies on source credibility in Academic Search Complete, ERIC, APA Psycinfo, APA PsycArticles, and OpenDissertations, complemented by snowball search and inquiring corresponding authors for unpublished studies. We included 64 controlled experimental studies to assess the effectiveness of four different intervention approaches (i.e., historical thinking, multiple document literacy, sourcing, and lateral reading) to foster source credibility assessment.
Source credibility assessment interventions were overall effective (g = 0.42, p < .001), with lateral reading showing the largest effects. We found considerable heterogeneity (95% Prediction Interval [−0.33, 1.17]), indicating that expected effect sizes in a random study from among the population of studies reviewed range from small negative to large positive effects. Greater effects were observed with graduated participants compared to other educational backgrounds, as well as in university and school settings, regardless of age and gender composition. Additionally, interventions that used the open Internet demonstrated enhanced effectiveness.
We conclude that (1) lateral reading is particularly suited to the digital information landscape, (2) repeated practice may enhance intervention effectiveness, and (3) ecological validity is highly important for intervention effectiveness.

Developing and Validating an AI Assessor for Teaching Material Quality at Scale
Fiona Wattison | eduki
Show details
Authors:
Fiona Wattison | eduki
Antoine Thuillier | eduki
Paul Ohm | eduki
Dr. Belinda Merkle | eduki
PD Dr. Stefan Janke | University of Mannheim
Lola Garay Abad | eduki

Educational psychology still lacks a scalable way to measure the quality of teaching material, to investigate it as a predictor for learning because existing frameworks typically rely on expert ratings, limiting scalability. To fill this gap, we developed and evaluated an AI-based assessor that rates materials using a LLM aligned with the seven-dimensional quality framework (Garay Abad & Hattie, 2025) including learning goals and structure, differentiation, cognitive demand and depth of learning, collaboration, cultural relevance, time efficiency, and teacher growth features. These criteria were operationalized through iteratively refined structured prompting against expert benchmarks.

To evaluate and improve the AI assessor, we conducted four tests in which criteria were rated as low, medium or high quality. First, agreement with expert ratings reached 81%, exceeding the predefined 80% benchmark. Second, repeated assessments of identical materials showed excellent stability (99.06%; target ≥95%). Third, we examined the validity of the assessor across subject domains, grade levels, and material types based on 2000 materials. Our analyses identified meaningful differences (e.g., higher ratings for Grade 13 vs. Grade 1, Ethics vs. Latin, and lesson plans vs. craft-based materials). Finally, expert validation of top-, middle-, and bottom-rated materials showed near-complete alignment (only one minor deviation).

Overall, results demonstrate that specialized AI assessors can achieve strong expert agreement and high reliability, enabling scalable, theory-based quality evaluation of materials. Future work should further examine potential category biases for subject domains, grade levels, and material types and validate ratings against external outcomes such as classroom effectiveness.

Effects of Probative Pictures and Intellectual Humility on the Correction of Misinformation
Dr. Christoph Mengelkamp | Universität Würzburg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Christoph Mengelkamp | Universität Würzburg | Germany
Marc Möhres | Universität Würzburg

Research indicates that corrective messages are effective in debunking misinformation (e.g., meta-analysis by Chan et al., 2017). However, the role of pictures remains under-researched (Newman & Schwarz, 2024), even though principles like picture superiority, dual coding, truthiness, and processing fluency suggest that pictures could enhance corrections. While recent studies found no effect for non-probative pictures (Whitehead et al., 2025), we hypothesized that probative pictures—those providing evidence—would elicit stronger correction effects than texts alone. Additionally, we investigated whether intellectual humility moderates correction effects, as intellectual humility correlates with a greater willingness to discard misinformation (meta-analysis by Bowes & Fazio, 2024).

In our pre-registered experiment, participants (N = 145) first read misinformation regarding an ice hockey player’s alleged doping. After an attitude assessment and a distraction task, participants received either no correction, a text-only correction, or a text correction accompanied by a probative picture. A final attitude assessment followed. Multilevel modeling revealed that the increase in attitude was significantly stronger in the text plus picture group than in the text-only group. However, this finding should be interpreted with caution due to small, albeit non-significant, baseline differences in attitudes prior to the correction. Notably, intellectual humility significantly enhanced the correction effect. If replicated, these results suggest that probative pictures are a promising debunking intervention, particularly for individuals high in intellectual humility.

How do positive minority-specific identity aspects in LGBTQIA+ parents relate to coparenting? Machine learning-based insights from the RALF study
Betty Geidel | University of Vienna, Austria | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Betty Geidel | University of Vienna, Austria | Austria
Univ.-Prof. Dr. Martina Zemp | University of Vienna, Austria
Dipl.-Ing. Dr.techn. David Steyrl | University of Vienna, Austria
Dr. Magdalena Siegel | University of Vienna, Austria

Following recent socio-legal developments, the number of LGBTQIA+ parent families has likely risen in many countries, including Austria. However, research on the psychological well-being as well as family processes (e.g., coparenting) in these families remains limited, particularly from a resilience-based perspective. Specifically, research examining positive minority-specific identity aspects (e.g., pride, authenticity) remains scarce. This dearth of evidence is compounded by the constraints of traditional linear models in, for instance, modelling intersectional experiences. Consequently, existing research may not yet adequately capture the full complexity of LGBTQIA+ parent family dynamics and the well-being of all family members.
The Rainbow Austrian Longitudinal Family (RALF) study is the first prospective study in Austria to systematically investigate risk and resilience factors in LGBTQIA+ parent families across the individual, couple, and family level. The target sample comprises N = 150 families across diverse family structures.
In the present study, we examine the relationship between coparenting and positive minority-specific identity aspects at the individual (i.e. authenticity, self-awareness), couple (i.e. intimacy) and family (i.e. family pride) level. Questionnaire data from the first data wave (W1; October 2025–February 2026) of the RALF study are analyzed using gradient boosted decision tree models to account for complex, non-linear associations. This machine learning-based analytical approach supports a more nuanced, intersectionality-informed understanding of family processes that may be difficult to capture with traditional statistical methods. Results and implications for research and practice will be discussed.

Gemeinsam von Vielfalt profitieren—aber wie? Neuartige Konzepte und Methoden aus der Teamdiversitätsforschung
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Mona Weiss (Friedrich - Schiller - Universität - Jena)
Room: SI
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Das Motto der diesjährigen DGPs „Haltung. Vielfalt. Zukunft“ unterstreicht die zunehmende gesellschaftliche und psychologische Relevanz von Diversität, also der Unterschiedlichkeit von Menschen in Bezug auf bestimmte Attribute (z.B. Demografie, berufliche Funktion, Hierarchiestufe). Bisherige theoretische Modelle und Messungen von Diversität in Teams sind allerdings häufig konzeptionell und methodisch limitiert. Beispielsweise wird zumeist von stabilen, klar abgegrenzten Teams ausgegangen – fluide Teamkompositionen und multi-funktionale Zusammenarbeit sind aber insbesondere in Hochrisikoorganisationen (z.B. in Krankenhäusern, der Luftfahrt oder der Polizei) der Regelfall und auch in modernen Organisationskontexten findet zunehmend eine Entgrenzung stabiler Teamzusammenarbeit statt (z.B. dynamische Projektteams, virtuelle Teams, Multi-Team-Systeme). Viele Modelle gehen darüber hinaus häufig von unidirektionalen Input-Prozess-Output Mechanismen aus, gemessen über Fragebögen und oftmals retrospektiv, was das Verständnis von unmittelbaren und in „Echtzeit“ ablaufenden Interaktionsprozessen in diversen Teams stark limitiert. Limitiert sind ebenfalls Erkenntnisse zum effektiven Diversitätsmanagement, vor allem, wenn Konflikte bereits stark verschärft sind.
Dieses Symposium setzt an diesen Limitationen an und erweitert bestehende Theorien über die Wirkung von Diversität in Teams. Alle Beiträge bieten innovative konzeptionelle und methodische Zugänge durch Live-Beobachtungen, Laborexperimente, Interaktions- und Sequenzanalysen und netzwerkbasierten Algorithmen in verschiedensten Teamkontexten (z.B. OP-Teams, Escape-Room Teams, Multiple Teammitgliedschaften).
Das Symposium umfasst vier Beiträge (4 x 16 Minuten inkl. Diskussion) sowie eine integrative Abschlussdiskussion (ca. 25 Minuten) moderiert durch Bertolt Meyer mit dem Ziel der Entwicklung einer neuen Forschungsagenda.
Der erste Beitrag von Weiss et al. untersucht das Äußern von Bedenken und Fehlern (Voice) in OP-Teams. Diese Teams zeichnen sich nicht nur durch funktionale Diversität sowie fluide Teamzusammensetzung, sondern gleichzeitig auch durch eine starke statusbezogene Diversität aus (z.B. Ärzt:innen, Pflegekräfte). Dies kann das Ansprechen von Bedenken und den Informationsaustausch hemmen, was zu gravierenden Behandlungsfehlern führen kann. Mithilfe von Live-Beobachtungen von OP-Teams und Sequenzanalysen zeigen Weiss et al., dass Voice die Teamleistung steigern kann, wenn dies im Team eine verstärkte Informationselaboration bewirkt und wenn in diesem Prozess Führungspersonen bestätigendes Feedback geben.
Der zweite Beitrag von Reimer et al. untersucht die Wirkungsweise von informeller Kommunikation auf Teamprozesse und -leistung ebenfalls im Kontext funktional diverser OP-Teamzusammenarbeit. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass informelle Kommunikation hier häufig von Führungspersonen (i.e., Chirurg:innen) ausgeht und weitere informelle Kommunikation im Team triggert. Obwohl informelle Kommunikation keinen direkten Effekt auf die Teamleistung hat, zeigt sich ein informeller „Ansteckungseffekt“, welcher möglicherweise dabei hilft, statusbezogene Barrieren innerhalb des Teams zu reduzieren.
Der dritte Beitrag von Meyer et al. adressiert die wichtige Tatsache, dass Mitarbeitende zunehmend nicht nur Teil eines Teams sind, sondern oftmals gleichzeitig in mehreren, teils dynamisch zusammengesetzten Projektteams (Multiple Team Membership, MTM) arbeiten. Meyer et al. übertragen hierbei das Faultline-Konzept (i.e., hypothetische Trennlinien basierend auf mehreren demografischen Merkmalen, die zu Subgruppenbildung führen können) von der Team- auf die Individualebene. Mithilfe eines neuartigen Algorithmus sagen die Autoren vorher, wie Mitarbeitende in MTM-Umgebungen aus vielen möglichen formalen Netzwerkverbindungen informelle Beziehungen formen und damit einerseits Kohäsion, aber auch Zugang zu vielfältigen Informationen erreichen.
Der vierte und letzte Beitrag von Buengeler et al. befasst sich mit der Frage, wie konstruktive Zusammenarbeit gewährleistet werden kann und welche psychologischen Mechanismen greifen, wenn bereits Subgruppenkonflikte in diversen Teams bestehen. Unter Anwendung des Ablehnung-Respekt-Modells wird die Funktion von Respekt als reaktive Diversitätsmanagementstrategie getestet. Anhand eines randomisiert-kontrollierten Laborexperiments mit neuen und intakten Teams induzierten Buengeler et al. Subgruppen und manipulierten Ablehnung (hoch/niedrig) und anschließend Respekt (hoch/niedrig) und beobachteten die Teams bei standardisierten Teamleistungsaufgaben in einem Live-Escape-Room. Die Ergebnisse dieser präregistrierten Studie werden zum Zeitpunkt der Konferenz berichtet.
Insgesamt liefert dieses Symposium durch innovative konzeptionelle, theoretische und methodische Zugänge wichtige neue Impulse für die Teamdiversitätsforschung und die organisationale Praxis von Vielfalt.

Speaking up und dann? Wie und wann Voice zu verbesserter Informationselaboration in multi-funktionalen OP-Teams führt
Mona Weiss
Show details
Authors:
Mona Weiss
Claudius Reimer
Prof. Dr. Tobias Piegeler

Bisherige Forschung suggeriert, dass Voice (i.e., das Äußern von Vorschlägen und Bedenken) förderlich für die Teamzusammenarbeit sein kann. Allerdings ist bislang nur wenig darüber bekannt, unter welchen Bedingungen dies der Fall ist und welche konkreten Interaktionsprozesse damit verbunden sind. Insbesondere in multi-funktionalen Teams in Hochrisikokontexten (z.B. OP-Teams), welche häufig durch starke Hierarchien zwischen den Funktionsgruppen geprägt sind, ist es sicherheitskritisch zu verstehen, ob und wie das Ansprechen eines Problems tatsächlich zu einem gemeinsamen Umdenken oder einer Neuplanung von Prozessen führt. Ausgehend von einer teamdynamischen Perspektive postulieren wir, dass Voice Informationselaboration auslöst, z.B. in Form von Bestätigungen, der Bereitstellung zusätzlicher Informationen, gemeinsamer Planung sowie weiterem Voice. Wir sagen weiterhin vorher, dass temporal-kontingente Muster aus Voice und Informationselaboration (VIE-Muster) mit einer höheren Teamleistung zusammenhängen und dass dieser Zusammenhang verstärkt wird, wenn Teamleader die Beiträge der Teammitglieder durch Bestätigungen validieren. Wir überprüften unsere Hypothesen durch Live-Beobachtungen von 77 funktional diversen chirurgischen Teams (zusammengesetzt aus anästhesiologischem, pflegerischem und chirurgischem Personal) im Operationssaal und 6.106 kodierten Kommunikationsereignissen. Die Ergebnisse der Lag-Sequenzanalysen bestätigen unsere Hypothesen weitestgehend: Voice löste im Interaktionsprozess überzufällig häufig Bestätigungen, Planung sowie weiteres Voice-Verhalten aus. Allerdings hatten diese VIE-Muster nur dann einen positiven Effekt auf die Teamleistung, wenn leitende Chirurg:innen unterstützendes Führungsverhalten zeigten. Unsere Studie erweitert bestehende Forschung zu den Auswirkungen von Voice in funktional und hierarchisch diversen Teams durch ein verbessertes Verständnis von mikro-level Kommunikationsprozessen während der Zusammenarbeit.

Teamarbeit unterm Messer: Die Wirkung informeller Kommunikation in funktional diversen OP-Teams
Claudius Reimer
Show details
Authors:
Claudius Reimer
Prof. Dr. Tobias Piegeler
Mona Weiss

Eine effektive Kommunikation ist in multi-funktionalen OP-Teams für die Patientensicherheit von zentraler Bedeutung. Während strukturierte, aufgabenbezogene Kommunikation in diesem Kontext gut erforscht ist, wurde der Einfluss von informeller Kommunikation, beispielsweise Humor, bislang wenig im Kontext von Statusdiversität und Multi-Funktionalität untersucht. Basierend auf theoretischen Annahmen zu Macht, Status und psychologischer Sicherheit in Teams postulieren wir, dass informelle Kommunikation vor allem von Führungspersonen ausgeht und positiv mit dem Ansprechen von Problemen (i.e., Voice) sowie weiteren funktionalen und informellen Kommunikations-Outcomes assoziiert ist, da sie das Machtgefälle zwischen den verschiedenen Berufsgruppen reduzieren sollte. Außerdem nehmen wir an, dass partizipatives Führungsverhalten den positiven Zusammenhang zwischen informeller Kommunikation und Voice moderiert, sodass dieser bei höherem partizipativen Führungsverhalten verstärkt wird.
Basierend auf Live-Beobachtungsdaten von N = 77 OP-Teams wurden verbale Interaktionen während der OP-Phase vor Schnitt mithilfe eines validierten Beobachtungssystems kodiert. Die Analysen umfassten Lag-Sequenzanalysen und Regressionen auf Teamebene. Im Einklang mit der ersten Hypothese zeigten die Ergebnisse, dass leitende Chirurgen signifikant häufiger informelle Kommunikationsverhalten zeigten, insbesondere im Vergleich zum Anästhesie-Subteam und der Pflege. Allerdings war informelle Kommunikation nicht mit Voice oder Teamleistung assoziiert, sondern ging primär mit weiterem informellen Kommunikationsverhalten einher. Partizipatives Führungsverhalten zeigte keinen moderierenden Effekt. Die Befunde aus der Studie deuten darauf hin, dass informelle Kommunikation in funktional diversen und stark hierarchisch geprägten OP-Teams von Führungspersonen ausgeht und eher weitere informelle als aufgabenbezogene Kommunikationsprozesse triggert, die sich zwar weniger auf die Leistung auswirken, möglicherweise aber das Teamklima positiv beeinflussen.

Ego-Faultlines: Eine individuelle Multiattribut-Perspektive auf Diversität und Subgruppen in Projektkontexten
Prof. Dr. Bertolt Meyer
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Bertolt Meyer
Prof. Dr. Sherry Thatcher | United States
Prof. Dr. Murat Tarakci | Switzerland

Teamdiversitätsforschung setzt häufig stabile, klar abgegrenzte Teams voraus. In modernen Organisationen arbeiten Beschäftigte jedoch zunehmend gleichzeitig in mehreren, teils dynamisch zusammengesetzten Projektteams (Multiple Team Membership, MTM). Dadurch verändern sich „Teamgrenzen“ und damit auch, wie Vielfalt erlebt, genutzt und sozial strukturiert wird. Wir argumentieren, dass Diversität in solchen Kontexten stärker als individuelles, mehrdimensionales „soziales Umfeld“ (social neighborhood) begriffen werden muss – statt ausschließlich als Eigenschaft eines einzelnen Teams.
Vor diesem Hintergrund übertragen wir das teambezogene Faultline-Konzept auf die Individualebene und führen Ego-Faultlines ein: hypothetische Trennlinien, die eine fokaler Mitarbeitender gemeinsam mit den „ähnlichsten“ Kolleginnen von anderen trennt – basierend auf mehreren Attributen zugleich. Aufbauend auf Homophilie- und Netzwerkperspektiven schlagen wir vor, dass Ego-Faultlines erklären, wie Mitarbeitende in MTM-Umgebungen aus vielen formalen Task-Ties eine handhabbare Menge informeller Beziehungen formen und dadurch gleichzeitig Kohäsion und Zugang zu vielfältiger Information erreichen.
Methodisch entwickeln wir ein Ego-Faultline-Maß samt Algorithmus (inkl. R-Paket) zur Identifikation individueller Ingroup-Strukturen über multi-attributive dyadische Ähnlichkeit. In Studie 1 (N = 1126, 184 Teams) zeigen wir erste Evidenz für die konzeptuelle Abgrenzung gegenüber Team-Faultlines: Ego-basierte Ingroups unterscheiden sich systematisch von team-level Subgroups und sind tendenziell heterogener. Studie 2 (laufend, N = 1189) prüft Hypothesen zur Entstehung informeller Ties (moderiert durch Ego-Faultline-Stärke und gemeinsame Zeit) sowie zu Konsequenzen für Kreativität.

Der umfangreichen Literatur zum proaktiven Management diverser Teams steht vergleichsweise wenig Wissen gegenüber, was den Umgang mit diversen Teams anbelangt, wenn bereits Subgruppen und entsprechende negative Auswirkungen wie der Ablehnung gegenüber der Außengruppe bestehen. Basierend auf Kernannahmen des Ablehnung-Respekt-Modells der Toleranz und des Kategorisierung-Elaborierungs-Modells der Teamdiversität und Teamleistung postulieren wir, dass Respekt es diversen Teams ermöglicht, effektiv mit bestehender Ablehnung im Team umzugehen, wodurch die Teamleistung verbessert wird. Dem Ablehnung-Respekt-Modell folgend beinhaltet diese Form des Respekts die Anerkennung anderer als gleichwertig, indem die gemeinsame Zugehörigkeit zu einer übergeordneten Gruppe wie dem Team herangezogen wird. Anhand eines randomisierten kontrollierten Laborexperiments mit neuen wie intakten Teams induzierten wir Subgruppen und manipulierten zunächst Ablehnung (hoch/niedrig) gegenüber der anderen Subgruppe. Wir manipulierten dann Respekt (hoch/niedrig) und beobachteten die Teams bei standardisierten Teamleistungsaufgaben in einem Live-Escape-Room. Wir werden zum Zeitpunkt der Konferenz über Ergebnisse der präregistrierten Studie berichten können. Die Studie hat wichtige Implikationen für die Forschung zu Teams und Diversität, da sie sich mit reaktiven Diversitätsmanagementstrategien befasst und klärt, ob eine kurze und kosteneffiziente Stimulation von Respekt ermöglichen könnte, negative Subgruppeneffekte zu hemmen und ggf. sogar die Teamleistung zu steigern.

Why Care About Twins in Psychological Research? New Empirical and Methodological Insights From Behavioral Genetics
Chair(s) Dr. Jana Instinske (Bielefeld University)
Room: CZ
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

What drives individual differences and development? How do specific behaviors develop? These form fundamental questions in psychological research that are central within several disciplines, such as developmental, clinical, or personality psychology. Leveraging data from twins and their family members, behavioral genetic approaches can be used to explore how genetic and environmental factors and their interplay account for individual differences. Furthermore, they allow to decipher genetic and environmental pathways underlying cross-construct associations or intergenerational transmission. This symposium covers talks on both methodological considerations and empirical applications of genetically informative research designs.
Drawing on a cross-sequential design, Kandler presents findings on the profile similarity of monozygotic and dizygotic twins in personality trait indicators from childhood to adulthood. Nacke proposes an extension of the Latent State-Trait theory by incorporating genetic, environmental, and idiosyncratic factors, covering formal definitions and an empirical application example. Using longitudinal twin data, Zapko-Willmes examines the genetic and environmental sources of stability and change of values and their associations with a range of life experiences. Based on simulated data, Wezel demonstrates how non-random mating impacts estimates of genetic and environmental variance in classical twin models, emphasizing the benefits of considering information from twins’ parents. Following this, Instinske empirically employs an extended twin family design investigating the genetic and environmental contributions to variance in music engagement and how these contributions shift across different developmental stages. The symposium closes with a general discussion with the audience, aiming to encourage discourse on the possibilities of integrating genetically informative approaches into psychological research questions.

Do Twins’ Personality Profile Similarities Shift Across Adolescence and Young Adulthood? A Cross-Sequential Twin Study
Christian Kandler | Bielefeld University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Christian Kandler | Bielefeld University | Germany
Jana Instinske | Bielefeld University | Germany

Twins’ personality similarity decreases across the lifespan, primarily due to the increasing influence of individualizing environmental factors that may or may not interact with genetic factors. However, some studies have provided evidence of a reverse trend, which was more pronounced in genetically identical monozygotic (MZ) twins than in dizygotic (DZ) twins during the first decades of life, indicating increasing genetic influences as source of the increasing personality similarity of twins. By comparing the personality profile correlations of 1718 MZ and 1940 DZ twin pairs based on data from four birth cohorts of the German twin family panel TwinLife across six survey waves, we tested the hypothesis that positive age effects on twins’ profile correlations are stronger in MZ twins than in DZ twins. The cross-sequential design allowed us to control for cohort and period effects and covered an age range from 10 to 35 years. Controlled for small negative cohort and period effects and age × period effects, we found significant linear age effects on personality profile correlations for both MZ (β=.17, p < .001, 95%CI[.13,.21]) and DZ twins (β=.05, p=.006, 95%CI[.02,.09]). The age effect was stronger for MZ than for DZ twins and this difference was robust across raw and distinctive profile correlations. Explanations for this systematically differently increasing trend of MZ and DZ twins’ similarities (.34-.51 and .23-.28) in their personality profiles with age in adolescence and young adulthood include the cumulative importance of active and evocative gene-environment correlations and interaction effects between genetic and environmental factors shared by twins.

A Theory of States, Traits, Nature, and Nurture
Lennart Nacke | Bielefeld University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lennart Nacke | Bielefeld University | Germany
Jana Instinske | Bielefeld University | Germany
Christian Kandler | Bielefeld University | Germany
Axel Mayer | Bielefeld University | Germany

We present an extension of the revised Latent State-Trait theory (LST-R theory) that posits genetic, environmental, and idiosyncratic developmental irregularities as contributors to the etiology of individual differences in personality traits. In particular, we propose that the latent trait variable as defined in the LST-R theory can be further decomposed into a genetic trait variable, an environmental trait variable, and a developmental noise variable (accounting for the residual trait variance that cannot be explained by either genetic or environmental sources). Moreover, we assume that trait-relevant genetic and environmental influences may covary or interact with each other when shaping individual differences in psychological characteristics. We show that these new etiological variables can be formally defined using already existing concepts of LST-R theory and demonstrate how different biometric Latent State-Trait models can be specified on this basis. Using data from the German Twin Life study, we illustrate the empirical performance of a biometric latent state-trait model with M-1 correlated method factors to show how this model can be used to estimate the genetic and environmental consistency of a short life satisfaction scale. The preliminary results indicate an overall true-score consistency of .727 (averaged across all items and measurement occasions) and a moderate heritability of the trait component of life satisfaction (a2 = .376) with the remaining variance largely due to (non-)shared environmental influences (c2 = .221 and e2= .403).

Value Stability and Life Events: A Genetically Informed Perspective
Alexandra Zapko-Willmes | University of Siegen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Alexandra Zapko-Willmes | University of Siegen | Germany
Christian Kandler | Bielefeld University | Germany

Genetic and environmental effects on individual differences in personal values vary substantially across value dimensions. Value-specific influences of life experiences may partly account for this heterogeneity, both through genotype-environment interplay and through strictly environmental effects. The present study examines the genetic and environmental underpinnings of value stability and change, as well as their bidirectional, quasi-causal associations with a broad range of life events. We further consider the role of life events’ subjective valence and perceived controllability. A total of 660 twin pairs (357 monozygotic, 303 dizygotic; ages 14 to 90; 72–77% female) from the three-wave German Study of Personality Architecture and Dynamics provided data on Schwartz’s 19 value dimensions and 20 categories of life events covering the domains (1) education, occupation, and finance, (2) social life and housing, and (3) health, in addition to experiences of threat, harm, success, and failure. Analyses include latent co-twin control models on cross-sectional and longitudinal value-event associations. The findings will offer a genetically informed account of how life events and event characteristics shape value levels and trajectories, and how personal values, in turn, influence individuals’ exposure to life events.

Differences Between Nuclear Twin Family and Classical Twin Model Parameter Estimates in Assortative Mating Based on Simulated Data
Steven Wezel | University of Basel | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Steven Wezel | University of Basel | Switzerland
Jana Instinske | Bielefeld University | Germany
Markus Janczyk | University of Bremen | Germany
Christian Kandler | Bielefeld University | Germany

The presence of partner correlation, referred to as assortative mating, increases genetic similarity between relatives, leading to a violation of the classical twin model’s assumption of dizygotic twins sharing 50% of additive genetic factors on average. This violation leads to distorted estimates of heritability in the classical twin model. The inclusion of parents of twins in a nuclear twin family design enables to account for these effects. 63 populations with a size of around 500.000 phenotypes each were simulated using GeneEvolve, to examine when and to what extent classical and nuclear twin family models provide different estimates of genetic and environmental sources of variance. The amount of additive genetic variance present, shared environmental effects (sibling-specific and familial) and assortative mating were manipulated. Samples with N = 100, N = 250, and N = 500 of complete twin families were randomly and repeatedly drawn from simulated populations and analyzed with the use of classical and nuclear twin family modeling. Results from over three million models showed the expected underestimation of heritability based on classical twin models in the presence of moderate to strong values for additive genetic variance and assortative mating with reciprocal findings for negative assortative mating. Further implications in the absence of the presence of specific familial effects are discussed under inclusion of meta-analytic results for different phenotypes to support researchers in evaluating model selection for their analyses.

Genetic and Environmental Underpinnings of Music Engagement from Childhood to Young Adulthood: A Multi-Cohort Study of Twins, Siblings, and Parents
Jana Instinske | Bielefeld University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jana Instinske | Bielefeld University | Germany
Hermine H. M. Maes | Virginia Commonwealth University | United States
Daniel E. Gustavson | University of Colorado Boulder | United States

Engagement with music has a range of developmental impacts including on socialization or skill and identity development, especially in childhood and adolescence. So far, however, only a few studies explored how genetic and environmental factors contribute to individual differences in music engagement and how these contributions shift across different developmental stages. Moreover, prior genetically informative studies usually relied on information from twins not considering information from further family members. Given this, the present study leverages data from twins, their parents, and non-twin siblings to (1) examine the genetic and environmental contributions to variance in music engagement, (2) investigate whether these contributions increase across different developmental stages, and (3) decipher the role of intergenerational transmission and gene-environment covariance. Based on data from 9,599 individuals from the German TwinLife study, we differentiated four age cohorts of twins: children (M = 7 years), early adolescents (M = 13 years), late adolescents (M = 19 years), and early adults (M = 21 years). To operationalize music engagement, information on the general engagement and the frequency were considered. The results indicated significant genetic contributions to individual differences in music engagement at all age cohorts, which increased from childhood (8%) to late adolescence (58%), while environmental effects inducing within-family similarity decreased. These trends may reflect influences of active gene-environment covariance during adolescence. Besides discussing the findings in terms of their theoretical implications, we outline how the use of twin family data can provide more specific insights into how music engagement behaviors develop, within and across generations.

New Insights from Measurement and Machine Learning for Applied Psychology
Chair(s) Dr. Philipp Sterner (Technical University of Munich)
Room: DK
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

In this symposium, we present new research on psychological measurement tailored to applied psychologists. In the first talk, David Goretzko calls to abandon rules of thumb for factor retention and provides practical guidance for determining the number of factors in EFA in a more adequate way. Then, Melanie Partsch presents a new machine learning-based method that allows researchers to classify the type and severity of misspecifications in multi-factorial measurement models. She also presents a second ML model for classifying different violations of unidimensionality in one-factorial measurement models. In the third talk, Luz Sanchez Steinhagen contrasts the binary logic of measurement invariance (MI) testing with the continuous bias that non-invariance causes. She highlights how conventional cut-offs for MI testing might miss substantive bias in latent mean comparisons. Tizian Schubeck then picks up this continuous view on MI in the fourth talk. He presents an extensive overview and taxonomy of the specific types of effect size measures for both MI and Differential Item Functioning (DIF) with a focus on how to interpret them. In the fifth talk, Philipp Sterner further extends this view on MI by discussing three different perspectives on MI in a research question-driven framework. Finally, Mareike Ebert wraps up the symposium in the sixth talk in which she offers a network perspective on psychological measurement. She discusses what we measure when we adopt a network lens and explores implications for understanding treatment and change.

Abandon Them Already: Why We Should Not Rely on Overly Simple Heuristics for Factor Retention
Prof. Dr. David Goretzko | Goethe University Frankfurt
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. David Goretzko | Goethe University Frankfurt

Assessing the dimensionality of latent constructs — such as determining the number of factors to retain in exploratory factor analysis (EFA) — is a crucial yet notoriously difficult task, with far-reaching implications for measurement model development, scale construction, and the refinement of substantive theories. Despite its importance, current practice too often relies on overly simple heuristics, such as the eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule or the scree test. These approaches frequently fail to provide valid estimates of latent dimensionality, yet they remain more popular than more accurate, data-driven methods that have been developed in recent years.
In this talk, we review recent advances in factor retention methodology and discuss which approaches should be preferred over these outdated rules of thumb. Drawing on evidence from empirical applications and simulation studies, we provide practical guidance for determining the number of factors in EFA and argue for abandoning factor retention criteria that are inaccurate and potentially misleading.

Machine learning approaches to evaluate and revise one- and multi-factorial latent measurement models
Dr. Melanie Viola Partsch | Utrecht University
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Melanie Viola Partsch | Utrecht University
Prof. Dr. David Goretzko | Goethe University Frankfurt

Evaluating and, if necessary, revising factor-analytic latent measurement models is a challenging task. By now, researchers can select from a toolbox of established and novel methods to evaluate global and local model fit. However, most commonly applied is still the error-prone method of using fixed cutoffs for model fit indices, such as the CFI, RMSEA, and SRMR.
In this talk, we would like to draw researchers’ attention toward novel methods that are more suitable for the majority of empirical use cases, focusing on machine learning (ML) approaches to model fit evaluation. Specifically, we will introduce an ML pipeline for the classification of the type and severity of misspecifications in multi-factorial measurement models and an ML model for classifying different violations of unidimensionality in one-factorial measurement models. The ML pipeline is based on three pre-trained ML models that predict a) if the measurement model is correctly specified or if a latent factor, cross-loadings, factor correlations, or residual correlations have been neglected, b) if any, how many cross-loadings have been neglected, and c) if any, how many residual correlations have been neglected. To evaluate one-factorial measurement models, we trained an ML model to predict if a measurement model is truly unidimensional or if a latent factor or different numbers of residual correlations have been neglected. After giving a short overview of the methods’ rationale, development process, and performance, we make recommendations on how to apply their open-access R implementations and let them guide the revision of a measurement model.

Binary Logic, Continuous Bias: Revisiting Measurement Invariance Testing
Caterina Luz Sanchez Steinhagen | Deutsches Jugendinstitut
Show details
Authors:
Caterina Luz Sanchez Steinhagen | Deutsches Jugendinstitut
Prof. Dr. David Goretzko | Goethe University Frankfurt
Dr. Philipp Sterner | Technical University of Munich

Measurement invariance (MI) is widely treated as a statistical prerequisite for meaningful group comparisons: either a test is invariant, or it is not. In applied research, this binary logic is typically operationalized via cutoff-based decisions on changes in model fit when testing scalar MI. However, this practice of binary decision-making stands in tension with the continuous nature of non-invariance.
In this talk, we argue that viewing MI as a binary property of a test is insufficient for understanding its consequences for scientific inference. Even small degrees of scalar non-invariance can introduce systematic bias into group mean comparisons, while larger violations can substantially distort effect estimates, inflate error rates, and mask true group differences. Importantly, the magnitude of bias depends on the extent of non-invariance and on additional model and data conditions – not on whether a statistical cutoff is exceeded.
Using results from a simulation study on scalar non-invariance, we illustrate how bias in latent mean comparisons increases gradually with the magnitude of intercept differences and demonstrate the inherent inadequacy of binary decisions about (non-)invariance. These findings highlight a conceptual mismatch between current testing practices and the underlying nature of measurement non-invariance.
Based on our findings, we argue that MI should not be treated as a mere technicality, but as a substantive aspect of measurement that – when violated – has direct consequences for the conclusions drawn from questionnaire data. This perspective therefore calls for careful consideration of how constructs and their indicators may function across groups when interpreting group comparisons.

A Guide to Quantifying Measurement Invariance
Tizian Schubeck | Goethe University Frankfurt
Show details
Authors:
Tizian Schubeck | Goethe University Frankfurt
Dr. Melanie Viola Partsch | Utrecht University
Dr. Philipp Sterner | Technical University of Munich
Prof. Dr. David Goretzko | Goethe University Frankfurt

Measurement Invariance (MI) – the property of measures functioning identically across groups or time – is generally approached as a binary decision. Using statistical significance tests, a scale is determined to be either invariant or not. Although very straight-forward, this comes with a crucial caveat – the complete inability to distinguish between a mild and a severe violation of MI. This is particularly problematic, since higher sample sizes alone will increase the likelihood of non-invariance verdicts, even for practically negligible differences. For this reason, effect sizes of MI were developed. By evaluating how much a measure functions differently across groups instead, a much richer and differentiated assessment can be made.
In this talk, we give an extensive overview and taxonomy of the specific types of effect size measures for both MI and its item response theory analogue Differential Item Functioning (DIF) with a focus on how to interpret them. Based on explicit criteria, we provide clear guidelines for choosing appropriate effect sizes given the specific research setting.

Three perspectives on measurement invariance: A research question-driven framework for the comparability of measurements
Dr. Philipp Sterner | Technical University of Munich
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Philipp Sterner | Technical University of Munich
Leonie Hagitte | MSB Medical School Berlin
Prof. Dr. Andreas Brandmaier | MSB Medical School Berlin
Prof. Dr. David Goretzko | Goethe University Frankfurt

Measurement invariance (MI) is often treated as an accept-or-reject decision as a perquisite for comparisons across groups or time. However, MI can also be a substantive phenomenon that informs theory building, construct development, and instrument quality. We propose a research question-driven framework that differentiates three perspectives on MI: (1) MI as a statistical assumption, enabling meaningful cross-group or longitudinal comparisons on the latent level; (2) MI as a substantive phenomenon with impact on theory; (3) MI as a quality criterion during scale construction when relevant groups are unknown or emergent. For each perspective, we map assumptions, recommended models (e.g., multi-group CFA, SEM trees and EFA trees, causal diagrams, alignment, Bayesian approximate MI), and decision criteria (e.g., global tests, local diagnostics, effect sizes, sensitivity analyses). We illustrate the framework with short, discipline-spanning vignettes and provide a reporting checklist that ties conclusions to the targeted research goal rather than to a single accept-or-reject test. The framework provides practical guidance for choosing methods, interpreting non-invariance, and communicating uncertainty. Further, we discuss the importance of approximate MI as an alternative to the perspective of strict MI as an implausible ideal. Ultimately, our goal is to reframe MI from an obstacle into a research design aspect and thus a potential source of theoretical insight and advancement of theory and measurement.

Measurement of Psychopathology – A Psychometric Network Perspective
Mareike Ebert | Goethe University Frankfurt
Show details
Authors:
Mareike Ebert | Goethe University Frankfurt
Prof. Dr. David Goretzko | Goethe University Frankfurt

Psychopathology measurement has long relied on the latent disease model: observable symptoms are assumed to reflect an underlying disease entity that causes them. This conceptualization shapes how we construct scales, interpret scores, and understand how recovery during treatment works. In contrast, the alternative network perspective offers distinct measurement implications: what if psychopathological phenomena are best understood as dynamic networks of symptoms that mutually reinforce one another, rather than as reflections of a latent cause?
This view on psychopathology shifts measurement focus from disorder severity to network structure. Rather than treating symptoms as independent indicators, this approach directs attention to relationships between symptoms and what these look like in disordered states.
In this talk, we will examine what a network-based measurement framework reveals about psychopathology and treatment response. We discuss what we measure when we adopt a network lens and will explore implications for understanding treatment and change. If recovery involves network reorganization rather than simple symptom reduction, what does this mean for how we conceptualize and measure therapeutic improvement? Drawing on empirical examples, we consider how network-based measurement offers distinct insights into treatment mechanisms that traditional latent variable approaches may obscure.

Advances in Mental Health Care: Language-Based AI for Assessment and Clinical Decision Support
Chair(s) Steffen T. Eberhardt (Trier University)
Dr. Antonia Vehlen (Trier University)
Room: BE
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping psychological research and mental health care. Data-informed clinical decision-making has progressed from questionnaire-based feedback toward multimodal approaches that integrate behavioral, physiological, and language-based data. These developments create new opportunities for personalized assessment, monitoring, and treatment planning, while raising questions regarding validity and applicability.

This symposium brings together six contributions from psychotherapy research addressing recent advances in data-informed clinical decision support, with a focus on language-based AI and multimodal models. The opening presentation provides an overview of current approaches, ranging from brief self-report indicators to AI-based multimodal systems that integrate transcripts, ecological momentary assessments, and bio-behavioral markers to identify key dimensions of psychological distress and resources.

Subsequent contributions present empirical studies evaluating locally hosted large language models (LLMs) for the analysis of psychotherapy transcripts. These studies examine AI-supported assessments of patient resources, burdens, and motivational processes, emphasizing approaches that combine session text with self-reported questionnaire data. Further presentations address data-informed treatment strategy selection, illustrating how LLM indicators can support recommendations for motivational versus problem-oriented interventions. Additional contributions extend LLM rating scales to automated routine outcome monitoring and compare AI-derived symptom trajectories with questionnaire-based outcome measures. The symposium concludes with an evaluation of AI-assisted assessments of alliance ruptures and repair processes, traditionally measured through observer coding.

Overall, the symposium demonstrates how language-based AI can complement established psychological assessment methods. By grounding AI applications in theory, psychometric validation, and real-world clinical data, the contributions directly address the congress themes of Mental Health and Digital Transformation and AI.

Theoretical Background: This presentation discusses a data-informed clinical decision system ranging from single-item applications to a multimodal dynamic network model (including biomarkers and Large Language Models) that supports the delivery of personalized feedback to therapists at the beginning and throughout psychological therapy. The presentation will focus on the most advanced element: the development of an AI-based multimodal model that identifies the core elements of psychological distress and resources. This model also enables the quantification and integration of multiple dimensions of distress, such as ecological momentary assessments (including bio-behavioral markers such as physical activity levels, sleep patterns, or physiological signals) and video or audio recordings.

Research Question: How can psychological distress and resources be extracted from digital phenotyping and session transcripts, and then integrated into clinical support tools and adaptive treatment planning for therapists?

Method: A total of approximately 1,400 session transcripts from 287 patients were analyzed using a large local language model to provide therapists with feedback, linking emotional and cognitive parameters to symptom distress levels for each session. Additionally, a sample of 150 patients was assessed four times a day using EMA and a digital wristband. Validation was conducted through the daily empirical assessments, as well as at the session level.

Results: Natural language processing of bio-behavioral, emotional, interpersonal, and cognitive distress is predictive of psychological symptoms assessed via questionnaires. This demonstrates that transcript information is a valuable additional data source. Several case examples illustrate how personalized clinical implications can be derived from individual distress parameters, as well as how this information can be presented to therapists in a graphical format to support clinical decision-making.

Conclusion: New digital assessment methods may provide empirical support for personalized clinical tools, therapy planning, and therapist feedback. However, further validation studies are needed before these methods can be implemented on a large scale.

Introduction: While large language models (LLMs) show considerable promise for standardized, time-efficient assessments in psychotherapy, their validity has only been sparsely investigated. Specifically, the impact of multimodal input on the quality of LLM-based ratings remains unclear.
This study aimed to develop and validate a locally deployed LLM-based rating system for evaluating psychotherapy session transcripts regarding patient resources and burdens. Additionally, the study examined whether integrating patient-reported questionnaire data improves the validity of the model’s ratings.

Methods: Psychotherapy videos of 862 patients were transcribed and segmented. A locally hosted LLM rated various domains (e.g., emotion, cognition, motivation) on a five-point Likert scale. Criterion and construct validity were assessed by correlating LLM ratings with thematically corresponding patient-reported questionnaire measures and with the total, anxiety and depression score of the HSCL-11. Using a multimodal prompting approach, questionnaire data were additionally incorporated as input variables.

Results: Preliminary analyses revealed consistent associations between LLM ratings and the corresponding patient-reported questionnaire measures (r = .20–.40, p < .05). Moreover, higher ratings were significantly correlated with higher HSCL-11 scores (r = .20–.50, p < .05). Substantially stronger correlations emerged when questionnaire data were integrated into the prompt.

Conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs can perform theory-driven and content-valid assessments of individual resources and problem areas. Combining textual session transcripts with psychometric data in a multimodal prompting framework increases performance. This represents a key methodological advantage that enhances the accuracy and clinical relevance of LLM-based ratings for use in both research and clinical settings.

Theoretical Background: Understanding motivational processes in psychotherapy is essential for adjusting interventions to individual patients, because central aspects of motivation such as personality, needs, therapy motivation and self-efficacy influence the important task of defining the right goals for each patient. Recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new possibilities to analyze these constructs directly from psychotherapy transcripts, complementing traditional measurements such as self-reports and observer-based ratings.

Research Question: The aim is the development and evaluation of locally generated LLM-ratings of several important aspects of motivation in psychotherapy.

Method: Based on multiple transcripts of psychotherapy sessions from 862 patients, a locally hosted LLM generated ratings on a five-point Likert scale. Correlations with diverse questionnaires were used to evaluate the criterion und construct validity of each of the four LLM-rating-scales.

Results: Regarding construct validity, preliminary analyses show moderate correlations between motivational LLM-ratings and selected psychometric questionnaires, ranging between r = .10-.30, p < .05. Higher LLM-ratings, which stand for a higher level of burden, were also significantly associated with higher psychological distress (r = .20-.40, p < .05).

Conclusion: LLM-based analysis of psychotherapy transcripts presents an innovative method for capturing motivational constructs such as personality, needs, therapy motivation and self-efficacy in a new way, while evading problems of previous approaches. The application of LLM-supported analyses in psychotherapeutic feedback systems is a promising addition, as the results indicate their validity.

Objective: While psychotherapy treatments are generally effective, there remains a subset of patients who do not respond or experience deterioration. Improvements in outcomes could be achieved by selecting the most appropriate strategy for each individual patient, particularly when guided by empirical data. Additionally to established questionnaires, novel data sources such as audio recordings for text analysis based on large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged. Therefore, our aim was to examine the potential improvement of treatment outcomes through the use of data-informed strategy recommendations, using multimodal data sources (e.g., self-reports, LLMs).

Methods: We analyzed 844 patients from an outpatient clinic, divided into 80% development and 20% holdout samples. Subsequently, the patients were grouped by prevalent treatment strategy (motivation vs. problem-oriented). Elastic net with repeated 10-fold cross-validation identified key predictors for each group. Retrospectively, we assessed whether recommended strategies based on predicted outcomes led to better observed outcomes. The performance of the prediction model was evaluated in the holdout sample.

Results: Preliminary results revealed effect sizes favoring patients receiving the recommended strategy. In addition, results indicated the advantage of integrating multimodal data sources rather than relying solely on self-reports.

Discussion: Implementing data-informed treatment selection offers potential improvements in patient outcomes by helping therapists prioritize strategies early in treatment. Results were obtained using rigorous validation through internal cross-validation and testing in a holdout sample. The prediction model is currently under evaluation in a prospective SMART trial to further assess the generalizability of our preliminary findings.

Aim: Although Routine Outcome Monitoring (ROM) can improve treatment outcomes, its implementation in routine care is often limited by additional workload. Recent findings suggest that large language models (LLMs) can capture latent psychological constructs, raising the question of whether LLM rating scales can measure outcomes, enable automated ROM, and generate progress trajectories comparable to questionnaire-based monitoring.

Method: We analyzed 1,630 transcribed sessions from 358 patients treated at a university outpatient clinic. An LLM-based outcome scale was developed from a pool of 200 items and evaluated using internal consistency, confirmatory factor analysis, and external validity indices (HSCL-11, PHQ-9, OQ-30). Treatment effects and longitudinal trajectories were examined in a subsample of patients with multiple consecutive sessions.

Results: The LLM scale demonstrated high internal consistency (ω = .94) and excellent model fit (CFI = .998, TLI = .997, RMSEA = .042, SRMR = .010). It showed meaningful correlations with validation measures (e.g., HSCL-11, r = .50) and a treatment effect comparable to questionnaire-based outcomes. Longitudinal analyses indicated that LLM-derived trajectories captured general distress over time, although sudden gains and losses were not consistently detected, and higher distress levels tended to be slightly underestimated.

Discussion: These findings suggest that LLM rating scales can capture psychotherapy outcomes with good psychometric quality and may support automated ROM. However, further refinement is needed to improve sensitivity to abrupt changes and reduce bias at higher severity levels.
