This study explores the feasibility of using large language models (LLMs) to approximate human 3RS ratings from psychotherapy transcript segments.

Using the 3RS Manual (Version 2022), we developed a standardized prompt architecture with one item-specific prompt per 3RS item. Initial analyses were conducted on a dataset of psychotherapy segments that received both human and LLM ratings. The model used was OpenAI’s gpt-oss-120b, a 120-billion-parameter, instruction-tuned language model.

Correlations between human and LLM ratings varied across subscales and items and should be considered preliminary. Moderate and significant associations were observed for selected items within the Working Together subscale, including Therapist accepts/validates patient (r = .31) and Patient is engaged in the work (r = .31), as well as for the rupture marker Confrontation: Patient moves against (r = .38) and the repair strategy Patient explores the rupture (r = .26). However, item discrimination was limited for several Working Together and Repair Strategy items, with LLM ratings showing overlap across related items (r ≈ .20–.33).

These findings suggest that LLMs can capture relational and rupture-related processes reliably, while finer-grained differentiation remains challenging. Ongoing work focuses on enlarging the dataset, refining prompts, and integrating multimodal information to improve performance. The results highlight both the promise and current limitations of LLM-assisted 3RS coding.

Parent-Child-Relations over the Lifespan

Topic: Open Area

This double symposium is an initiative of the Family Psychology Interest Group within the DGPs and will bring together scholars from various subdisciplines (e.g., developmental psychology, clinical psychology, (cross-)cultural psychology) as well as practitioners to present their current work related to family psychology. Contributions will cover a range of studies on the topic of parent-child relations over the lifespan.
The first part focuses on families in the context of cultural diversity and societal change. Starting with early childhood, the contributions will address parenting in the context of migration, intergenerational value transmission and the negotiation of cultural identity between young adults and their parents. Further topics include social mobility and intergenerational relations, and adult children’s readiness to provide care for their ageing parents in German families both with and without a migration background.
The second part centers on family psychosocial functioning. Presentations will examine parental stress of mothers who have undergone fertility treatments, cognitive and affective schemata as risk factors for child psychological maltreatment, and extreme social withdrawal among young people. Further, emerging approaches related to digital systemic therapy with families will be presented.
By integrating developmental, cultural and clinical perspectives, this symposium will provide an arena to discuss challenges for contemporary families as well as opportunities for intervention and support in light of cultural, social and technological change.

Luxembourg has undergone rapid societal change and an increase in cultural diversity in recent years, and almost 75% of residents now have a direct or indirect migration background. In the context of migration, families encounter specific challenges when it comes to the renegotiation of values and norms regarding parent-child-relations.
The present study examined how culturally diverse parenting experiences are related to parental stress among parents living in Luxembourg. Specifically, the study investigated whether perceived cultural differences, difficulties integrating parenting values from different cultural contexts, parenting ethnotheories (parenting beliefs) and social support were associated with parental stress.
A sample of N = 56 parents living in Luxembourg (with and without migrant background) filled out an online questionnaire assessing parental stress, perceived cultural differences, difficulties integrating parenting values across cultural contexts, and satisfaction with perceived social support in various domains.
Results showed that higher perceived cultural differences and greater difficulties integrating parenting values were each associated with higher parental stress. Higher satisfaction with support from friends/personal networks was associated with lower parental stress, whereas perceived support from family, school/childcare institutions, and public/community services showed no significant associations with parental stress.
The findings suggest that parental stress in multicultural contexts is primarily shaped by parents’ subjective experiences of cultural differences and difficulties integrating parenting values rather than by migration status background alone. Results will be discussed with regard to different family cultures, and implications for family interventions to support well-being will be highlighted.

Acculturation is a complex, multidimensional process that involves individuals’ orientation toward both their ethnic culture and the resident cultural context. It comprises changes in practices and behaviors, values and norms, as well as identity and identification. Acculturation differs substantially between first- and second-generation immigrants: whereas the first generation is socialized in the culture of origin, the second generation grows up in the country of residence and develops cultural orientations during a period of high developmental plasticity.
The present study examines the sense of belonging and cultural identifications of first- and second-generation members of three families (N = 9) who left Kosovo following the ethnic conflict of the 1990s and resettled in multicultural Luxembourg. Drawing on the multicultural identity integration framework, we analyzed how family members organized their cultural identities and how parents imagined their daughters’ sense of belonging.
Participants completed semi-structured interviews and two visual tasks: an adapted figure-completion exercise (Bradad, 2014) and an adapted version of the Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale (Aron et al., 1992).
The findings of this study shed light on the complexity of acculturation and belonging among first- and second‑generation migrants in Luxembourg, a context characterized by cultural diversity and high levels of multilingualism. Across all three families, we observed a clear tendency toward compartmentalization of cultural identities, feeling a sense of belonging to both. An important intergenerational discrepancy emerged. Although parents viewed their daughters as strongly oriented towards Luxembourgish society, the daughters themselves expressed a more balanced sense of belonging to both cultures. This mismatch highlights how parental expectations and interpretations do not always align with the lived experiences of second‑generation youth. These findings will be further contextualized and discussed.

Time to conceive and number of fertility treatment cycles were not significantly related to state or trait anxiety.
Conclusion: Neither the time to conceive nor the number of fertility treatments appears to increase the stress and anxiety experienced by future mothers – rather the opposite tends to be the case. Thus, the study builds on previous limited research by recording the duration of the desire to have children and reproductive medical treatments more detailed.

Why do parents psychologically maltreat their children? An examination of cognitive and affective schemata as risk factors for child psychological maltreatment
Lara Schwarz | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Lara Schwarz | Switzerland
Antonia Schubert | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Ute von Düring | Germany
Jelena Zumbach-Basu | Switzerland

Child psychological maltreatment is a global public health concern and a significant risk factor for adverse mental and physical health outcomes across the lifespan. Although risk factors for child physical abuse and neglect are well established, those underlying psychological maltreatment remain insufficiently understood.
The Social Information Processing Model posits that distortions at various stages of information processing increase the likelihood of dysfunctional or maltreating parenting behavior. While this model has been validated for physical abuse and neglect, the present study is the first to examine its initial stage – pre-existing schemata – in the context of child psychological maltreatment.
Using a longitudinal design, we investigate associations between parental schemata and parenting behavior along the continuum of psychological maltreatment. We hypothesize that greater deficits in cognitive and affective schemata predict higher levels of psychologically maltreating behavior. At T1, N = 1,030 German and Swiss parents of children aged 0–18 years completed an online survey assessing cognitive schemata (attitudes, attributions, locus of control, expectations) and affective schemata (empathy, self-esteem, anger, hostility, anxious and depressed affect). At T2, N = 491 parents completed a follow-up questionnaire assessing their parenting behavior, including functional, dysfunctional behavior and behavior within the spectrum of psychological maltreatment. Path model analysis is employed to provide a comprehensive framework of mechanisms underlying child psychological maltreatment.
The findings have the potential to inform and refine risk assessment practices for identifying parents at risk for child psychological maltreatment.

Extremer sozialer Rückzug junger Menschen – wenn das Nest sich nicht leert
Prof. Dr. Katja Weidtmann | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Katja Weidtmann | Germany

Die Jugend und das junge Erwachsenenalter prägen u.a. eine zunehmende familiäre Ablösung und Peer-Orientierung, erste Liebesbeziehungen, Schulabschlüsse, Eintritt in den tertiären Bildungsbereich und Beruf bis zum Auszug. Eltern erwartet mit dem empty nest ein Lebensabschnitt, in dem das Paarsystem sowie individuelle persönliche und berufliche Ambitionen wieder mehr Bedeutung gewinnen können. Doch was passiert familienpsychologisch, wenn junge Menschen das Nest nicht verlassen, sich stattdessen zuhause extrem zurückziehen? Ein Extremer sozialer Rückzug (ESR) wird über eine Dauer von mindestens 6 Monaten ohne Teilhabe an Schule, Ausbildung oder Beruf definiert, die Versorgung Betroffener erfolgt meist durch ihre Familien. Je nach Schweregrad gibt es Unterschiede bezüglich Mobilität und (digitaler) sozialer Interaktionen. ESR beginnt meist im Jugendalter, als ursächlich gelten individuelle, entwicklungspsychologische, familiäre und gesellschaftliche Faktoren. Psychische Störungen können eine Rolle spielen bzw. im Verlauf des oft jahr(zehnt)elangen ESR entstehen. In betroffenen Familien besteht hoher Leidensdruck, das Risiko physischer und psychischer Erkrankungen steigt. ESR wird seit den 1990ern v.a. in Japan als „Hikikomori“ beschrieben und beforscht, entsprechende Unterstützungssysteme sind dort am weitesten entwickelt. In den letzten Jahren erschienen auch in westlichen Ländern mehr Arbeiten zum ESR, hohe Dunkelziffern und ein Anstieg werden vermutet. Zu Erleben und Unterstützung betroffener Familien gibt es kaum Befunde. Präsentiert werden Ergebnisse aus Elterninterviews mit für Deutschland erstmals vertieften Einblicken in Beginn und Entwicklung des ESR, Familienalltag, elterliches Erleben, Belastungen und Bewältigungsstrategien, Erfahrungen mit privatem Umfeld und dem Hilfesystem. Angesichts frappierender Versorgungslücken erfolgen Implikationen für eine bessere Unterstützung betroffener Familien.

When the verbal communication isn’t helpful enough: using metaphors in online systemic family therapy
Marie Jeanne Schon | Institut Luxembourgeois de Pensée Systémique et de Thérapie Familiale (ILPS) | Luxembourg
Show details
Author:
Marie Jeanne Schon | Institut Luxembourgeois de Pensée Systémique et de Thérapie Familiale (ILPS) | Luxembourg

This contribution is about digital systemic therapy with families before and overall, since the covid 19 pandemic. The necessary adjustments to the online setting were and are still a challenge for all partners involved: patient(s) and therapist. Some systemic tools used for many years are possible to apply in the online setting in systemic individual and family therapy, while others only apply face-to-face. My work as a family therapist in private practice with metaphoric tools refers mostly to the concept of ‘floating objects’ developed in France by Philippe Caillé and Yveline Rey as well as to the work of Luigi Onnis on metaphors considered as a bridge between mind and body language. After general considerations regarding the systemic online setting, the use of metaphors in face-to-face and their adaptation to online setting, I will focus the online work I developed with DIXIT cards and illustrate my point by clinical examples.

Research for Planetary Health and Transformative Change
Psychological Underpinnings of the Climate Crisis
Chair(s) Dorothea Metzen
Room: PL
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Coupled symposium
Duration: 195 Minutes

The climate crisis is not only an environmental and political challenge but an increasingly salient psychological stressor shaping emotions, motivation, and behavior. These coupled symposia present the work the research initiative Research4Change (Research for Planetary Health and Transformative Change). We bring together empirical and theoretical studies that examine how individuals regulate and respond to climate emotions, and how these responses may either sustain engagement or contribute to exhaustion, delayism, and disengagement.

The first session focuses on the emotional burden of the climate crisis. Contributions investigate activist burnout among climate activists, climate emotions and institutional responsibility among university students, and arousal and emotion regulation processes in adolescents facing climate threats. Further work explores solastalgia in relation to eco-emotions and pro-environmental behaviour, as well as state–trait dynamics of climate emotions within a place-based climate change education intervention. Together, these studies highlight how climate emotions are shaped by climate action, educational context and place-attachment and how they can motivate action and at the same time reduce well-being.

The second session turns to behavioural, social, and discursive dynamics. A meta-analysis examines gender differences in pro-environmental behaviour, while studies on the effectiveness illusion and discourses of climate delay show how misperceptions and maladaptive coping mechanisms may inhibit meaningful climate action. Further we present a novel framework covering transformative discourses and empirically explore distinctions between open and closed forms of utopian thinking as psychological resources for imagining climate futures.

Across both sessions, the symposium aims to advance an integrative understanding of the climate crisis as a psychological phenomenon, highlighting leverage points for education, institutions, and interventions that support well-being and transformative climate action.

Bearing the Weight of Change: Understanding Activist Exhaustion in Environmental Activists
Paula Blumenschein
Show details
Authors:
Paula Blumenschein
Dorothea Metzen
Prof. Dr. Stephan Heinzel
Karen Hamann

Collective action in the environmental domain is essential for socio-ecological change, yet it may also challenge individuals‘ mental health. Previous research described activist burnout as prolonged exhaustion undermining sustained engagement. In two quantitative studies, we examined mental health in the context of environmental activism among German-speaking individuals. In the first study, we compared participants actively involved in collective climate action (n =217) with those not engaged (n = 747). Engaged individuals reported higher symptoms of depression and anxiety and showed stronger emotional reactions to climate change. We extended this work in a second study focusing on predictors of activist exhaustion among environmental activists (N = 254). We included both personal psychological variables (engagement hours, climate isolation, climate anger, activist obligation, self-efficacy, social identification) and perceived group characteristics (culture of selflessness, group conflicts, social support). Regression analyses showed that activist obligation, perceived culture of selflessness, and relationship conflicts within the group were associated with greater activist exhaustion. Conversely, self-efficacy, social identification, and perceived social support within the group were associated with lower activist exhaustion. Together, our findings emphasize that sustaining long-term pro-environmental engagement requires attention not only to personal resilience, but also to supportive group dynamics within environmental groups. Targeted interventions derived from this research should be tested longitudinally to mitigate activist exhaustion and promote sustained engagement over time.

Climate emotions among university students in Germany and how universities should address the climate crisis – a cross-sectional study
Katherina Heinrichs
Show details
Authors:
Katherina Heinrichs
Prof. Dr. Stephan Heinzel
Dorothea Metzen
Christiane Stock

This study aims at investigating a) how strong climate anger and climate sorrow are among university students, b) to what extent the climate crisis is currently addressed or should be addressed by the university, and c) if the climate emotions are associated with this conviction.
An online survey was conducted at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, including items assessing climate anger and climate sorrow, as well as how the climate crisis is already an issue at university and how strong the call for action is. Descriptive analyses were complemented by a multiple linear regression model to investigate a possible association.
Mean scores for climate anger and climate sorrow among students (n=427) were 4.3 and 3.9, respectively (range: 1-5). A considerable percentage of students stated that the climate crisis was (rather) not important to lecturers (36%) or stakeholders (47%) and that it played a (rather) little role on campus (45%) or in the curriculum (53%) at the moment. The majority (63%) reported that they did not feel well prepared for their future profession regarding the consequences of the climate crisis. Almost three-quarters saw a mediocre/very strong call for action that the university should address the climate crisis. Climate sorrow was associated with this conviction (β=.204; p=.011).
The results show strong climate emotions among university students. Climate sorrow is associated with the students‘ conviction that the climate crisis should be addressed by the university. Pursuing this call for action could help to prepare future professionals to deal with the consequences of the climate crisis.

Climate Change as a Psychological Stressor: Investigating Arousal and Emotion Regulation in Adolescents
Nora Spirkl
Show details
Authors:
Nora Spirkl
Veronika Engert
Edwin Lim
Julia Asbrand

Background: Climate change poses a growing threat to psychological well-being. Over half of young people worldwide report climate-related worries, which may contribute to an increasing mental health burden in this age group. While psychosocial stressors such as social stress have been studied extensively, mechanisms underlying climate stress remain poorly understood. Emotion regulation appears to play a central role in coping with such stressors.
Objective: This study investigates subjective arousal and emotion regulation during a climate stress induction compared to social stress in children and adolescents. We hypothesize that both stressors elicit subjective arousal, with lower reactivity to climate stress (H1) and greater overall reactivity in participants with elevated mental health symptoms (H2). We assume that emotion regulation strategies vary depending on the stressor type (H3) and mental health status (H4).
Method: In a laboratory experiment, participants aged 12–17 reporting elevated or low levels of mental health symptoms (measured via PHQ-9 and GAD-7) are randomly assigned to a climate stress condition (video-based) or a psychosocial stress condition (TSST-C), followed by a 30-minute recovery. Subjective arousal (STAI-6) is measured repeatedly and analyzed using mixed linear models. Emotion regulation (ERQ-State) is assessed post-stress and after recovery using repeated-measures MANOVA.
Status and Outlook: Data collection (target N = 50) is ongoing. Our findings will inform the development of targeted prevention measures to help young people find healthy ways to cope with climate change, with emotion regulation being examined as a potential mechanism of change.

Solastalgia in relation to eco-emotions and pro-environmental behaviour
Katharina van Bronswijk
Show details
Authors:
Katharina van Bronswijk
Alexandra Frisch
Prof. Dr. Stephan Heinzel

Background: Environmental news can evoke negative affect like eco-anxiety, eco-anger or eco-grief. Solastalgia (Albrecht, 2005) describes a grief reaction to the perceived change of an environment people are attached to. In international studies, various eco-emotions are correlated (Hickmann et al., 2021). It is therefore important to shed light on the individual effects of each emotion on well-being, coping as well as (pro-)environmental behaviour.
Objective: The presented study measured solastalgia, other eco-emotions, well-being as well as pro-environmental behaviour. This presentation will focus on the motivating function of solastalgia as a form of environmental grief.
Method: We examined the factor structure of the German translation of Brief Solastalgia scale (BSS-D), psychometric quality criteria and associations with constructs from climate psychology in a representative sample of 530 adults from Germany. To test correlations with the other measures Pearson product–moment correlations were conducted.
Results: Solastalgia showed significant but moderate positive correlations with climate-anxiety, climate-sorrow, climate-anger, climate-guilt, as well as measures of (reduced) mental well-being, depression and anxiety. Solastalgia also correlated positively with 4 aspects of pro-environmental behaviour.
Discussion: Our results are in line with other studies finding that participants experience several climate emotions at the same time (Marczak et al., 2023). Since People showing climate-related engagement also reported solastalgia, including a measure of solastalgia into models predicting pro-environmental behaviours and attitudes might be a valuable contribution to find out more about the motivating effects of different eco-emotions.

State–Trait Dynamics of Climate Emotions in a Place-Based Climate Change Education Intervention
Justus Schöller
Show details
Authors:
Justus Schöller
Matthias Ziegler
Anna Beniermann
Annette Upmeier zu Belzen

Climate change education lies at the intersection of environmental psychology and science education, as it translates psychological insights on emotion, motivation, and behavior into educational contexts aimed at fostering constructive engagement with climate change. Beyond cognitive understanding, the interplay of emotions such as hope, worry, interest, and perceived agency constitutes central psychological mechanisms that can either facilitate or hinder adaptive climate engagement. Drawing on Person–Situation Interaction Theory and developmental models of personality and emotion, this study examines how stable climate-related emotional dispositions (traits) interact with situational experiences (states) during a place-based climate change education intervention.
The study employs a quantitative, longitudinal design with children and adolescents aged 10–15 years (n = 700). Climate-related traits, age and personality dimensions of the Big5 were assessed prior to participation, while corresponding climate states and situation perception were repeatedly measured across multiple phases of the intervention.
Analyses combine latent profile approaches with multilevel models (i.e. random intercept cross lagged panel models) to investigate (a) how trait dispositions cluster into distinct profiles and (b) how these profiles shape emotional responses to situational affordances within the intervention. This analytic strategy allows for disentangling between-person differences in emotional dispositions from within-person emotional dynamics across situational contexts. Initial analyses based on the current sample (n = 313) suggest emerging associations between trait-level emotional dispositions and aggregated state-level patterns.
By integrating trait and state perspectives, this contribution advances environmental psychological research on climate emotions and highlights how educational contexts can be designed to support emotionally adaptive pathways toward climate engagement and psychological well-being.

Gender differences in pro-environmental behavior: A meta-analysis of large datasets
Corinna Gemmecke
Show details
Authors:
Corinna Gemmecke
Jens Mazei
Joachim Hüffmeier

Individual changes toward pro-environmental behavior (hereafter: PEB) play a crucial role in addressing environmental crises. Research on gender differences in PEB typically assumes that women engage in more PEB than men, as being concerned about the environment is more strongly associated with women’s (vs. men’s) gender role. However, empirical findings do not consistently support this assumption.
Hence, our goal is to deepen the understanding of gender differences in PEB and examine moderators to help explain why gender differences emerge only inconsistently. Based on extant theory, we predict that the gender connotation and social desirability of specific PEBs moderate gender differences in PEB. We conducted a preregistered meta-analysis of N = 29 large-scale datasets, collected between 2020 and 2025, each assessing at least one specific behavior with environmental impact (PEB items; e.g., plant-based versus meat-based diets). From these 29 datasets, we extracted N = 596 PEB items. In two additional surveys (N = 207 participants), we assessed the gender connotation and social desirability of each of these 596 PEBs.
By the time of the conference, we will have estimated the average gender difference in PEB and tested for moderation by perceived gender connotation and social desirability. Our findings will expand the knowledge on gender differences in PEB and, if we observe related (and moderated) differences, contribute to the development of gender-sensitive interventions to promote PEB.

The Effectiveness Illusion: Public Perceptions of Climate Protection Behaviours in Germany
Julius Grund
Show details
Author:
Julius Grund

Background: One of the aims of the Sustainable Development Goals is to enable all people by 2030 to co-create a sustainable future (United Nations, 2015). An important component of this is effectiveness knowledge, defined as knowledge about the environmental impact of different behaviours (Kaiser & Fuhrer, 2003). Empirical evidence demonstrates deficits in individuals’ ability to accurately assess the mitigation potential of actions (Johnson et al., 2024).
Objective: The study assesses the level of knowledge regarding the effectiveness of climate change–related actions in Germany. Special attention is given to socio-demographic factors as well as to levels of climate change awareness and behaviour associated with this knowledge. The study also explores the learning contexts and opportunities that may have strengthened effectiveness knowledge.
Method: The data is based on a representative survey (n = 3,029). Drawing on existing estimates of the climate-related impact of various actions (Hampton & Whitmarsh, 2023; Ivanova et al., 2020), participants were asked to rate how much different behaviours contribute to reducing the carbon footprint. In addition, climate change awareness (Chryst et al., 2018), sustainable behaviour (based on Hampton & Whitmarsh, 2023), points of contact with sustainability (e.g., friends, social media), educational level, income, and wealth were assessed.
Status and Outlook: Descriptive analyses reveal significant gaps in effectiveness knowledge among the German population. The effectiveness of low-impact behaviours is systematically and substantially overestimated, while the effectiveness of high-impact behaviours is underestimated. More in-depth analyses are presented in the contribution, and implications for climate education and communication are discussed.

Discourses of climate delay as maladaptive coping mechanisms for climate emotions
Prof. Dr. Stephan Heinzel
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Stephan Heinzel
Paula Blumenschein
Dorothea Metzen

Background: Climate change evokes a wide range of emotional responses that influence mental health and pro-environmental behavior. Previous research has primarily focused on climate anxiety, neglecting other relevant emotions such as guilt, anger, or sorrow. In this context, the belief in discourses of climate delay (DOCD, discourses that acknowledge climate change but aim to postpone mitigation efforts) may serve as a maladaptive coping mechanism.
Methods: The present study validates the German version of the Inventory of Climate Emotions (ICE) and investigates the relationship between climate emotions, discourses of climate delay (DOCD), and climate action in a representative German sample (N = 966).
Results: Confirmatory factor analysis supported the eight-factor structure (CFI = .95, RMSEA = .041, SRMR = .057). Across participants, climate anger, anxiety, and sorrow were most prevalent. DOCD were negatively correlated with most climate emotions except contempt and powerlessness and with collective climate action. Moderation analyses revealed that DOCD significantly weakened associations between several emotions (anxiety, enthusiasm, guilt, isolation) and climate action (B’s (DOCD) = –.22 to –.49; all p’s for interaction < .01), suggesting their function as maladaptive coping strategies that reduce emotional distress but impair behavioral engagement.
Discussion: These findings highlight the dual role of climate emotions in motivating action while potentially triggering defensive cognitive patterns that undermine it. Future longitudinal studies should clarify causal directions and develop interventions to foster adaptive emotion regulation without diminishing commitment to environmental protection.

From Delay to Transformation – A Framework for Discourses of Transformation
Dorothea Metzen
Show details
Authors:
Dorothea Metzen
Paula Blumenschein
Heiko Mikolajczak
Felix Peter
Prof. Dr. Stephan Heinzel

Human-induced climate change poses an existential threat, yet effective climate protection measures are still lacking worldwide. A key explanation for this discrepancy lies in the Discourses of Climate Delay (DOCD): discourses that acknowledge the reality and urgency of climate change but delay effective action by shifting responsibility, proposing ineffective solutions, or portraying transformation as impossible. While previous research has successfully identified the mechanisms and actors involved in these discourses, merely refuting the DOCD may not enough to diminish their influence. Refutation neither broadens the scope of imagined social futures nor increases the perceived achievability of a socially and ecologically just transformation.
Based on the multilevel perspective, we argue that social change requires discursive change: only when alternative visions of the future become visible and conceivable can niche ideas challenge the existing regime in a "window of opportunity." In this article, we present a framework for Discourses of Transformation (DOT) – discourses that are already being practiced on a small scale and within movements, and which describe socially and ecologically just futures as necessary, desirable, and possible.
The framework encompasses three areas of discourse: (1) Climate justice (human–human relationships (outgroup), including ecofeminism, decolonial perspectives, intergenerational justice, and redistribution narratives such as "Feed the world, tax the rich"; (2) Economy (human-human relationships (ingroup)), including post-growth approaches and narratives oriented toward the common good; and (3) Human-nature relationship, such as nature-technology symbiosis, ecological embeddedness, arcology, and animal rights.

Blueprint or Compass? An Attempt to Empirically Distinguish between Open and Closed Utopian Thinking.
Heiko Mikolajczak

Jasmin Katzer

Dorothea Metzen
Prof. Dr. Stephan Heinzel

Background: Utopian thinking, the imagination of a better society, is a powerful psychological driver for societal change. However, social theorists characterize it as a double-edged sword: it can inspire inclusive, democratic movements or fuel ideologically exclusionary, destructive social projects. While open utopian thinking contains a collaborative and dynamic process of collectively imagining a better society, closed utopian thinking entails a rigid and final blueprint of the ideal society. This crucial theoretical distinction, however, lacks an empirical foundation in psychology.
Objective: This research project aims to gather initial evidence for establishing and investigating the distinction between open and closed utopian thinking. We will examine how seven established psychological constructs (social dominance orientation, right-wing authoritarianism, openness, social identity complexity, intellectual humility, loneliness, essentialism) moderate the relationship between a general tendency for utopian thinking and different forms of societal engagement. Specifically, we will test whether these variables moderate whether utopian thinking translates into bridge building or exclusive ingroup mobilization.
Method: A cross-sectional online study is planned, involving a German convenience sample. Participants will complete established and validated scales to measure utopian thinking, the seven proposed moderator variables, and the willingness to engage in bridge-building and ingroup mobilization. We will run simple and joint moderated regression models to test incremental predictive power.
Outlook: The findings will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of how people differentially interpret utopian thinking and when it translates into bridge-building and ingroup-mobilization.

Educational Migration as Psychological Transition: A Mixed-Methods Study of Secular Iranian Women’s Emotional and Identity Experiences in Türkiye
Dr. Metin Çınaroğlu | Istanbul Nisantasi Universitesi | Turkey
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Eda Yılmazer | Beykoz University | Turkey
Dr. Metin Çınaroğlu | Istanbul Nisantasi Universitesi | Turkey

This mixed-methods study investigated the psychological motivations, emotional distress patterns, and identity negotiation processes among secular Iranian female students pursuing higher education in Türkiye. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and Identity Process Theory, the research conceptualized educational migration not merely as academic advancement, but as a psychologically driven response to sustained sociopolitical constraints and gender-based restrictions in Iran. The study employed a convergent mixed-methods design. Quantitative data were collected from a diverse sample of 489 secular Iranian female students across 13 Turkish universities using validated measures, including the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scales, Academic Motivation Scale, and Acculturative Stress Scale for International Students. A purposive subsample of 45 participants engaged in semi-structured in-depth interviews to explore personal narratives regarding identity development, coping mechanisms, and future aspirations. Quantitative results revealed considerable psychological variability, with high levels of anxiety (21% moderate, 12% severe), stress, and depressive symptoms. Notably, 68% of participants reported prior restriction of personal freedom in Iran. However, participants exhibited strong intrinsic motivation, viewing education as a vehicle for psychological liberation. Qualitative findings highlighted that students often view Türkiye as a "transitional space" or transit zone for future migration to the West. Coping strategies included compartmentalization, academic engagement, and "identity editing" to navigate ideological transitions. The findings suggest that educational migration for secular Iranian women acts as a form of psychological emancipation and identity reconstruction. The study underscores that emotional distress in this population often predates relocation, necessitating tailored institutional and clinical support that addresses pre-migration sociopolitical stressors alongside cultural adjustment.

Effects of a cross-domain knowledge integration task on pre-service teachers’ cognitive load
Dr. Inka Hähnlein | Martin-Luther Universität Halle-Wittenberg, Halle, Germany | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Inka Hähnlein | Martin-Luther Universität Halle-Wittenberg, Halle, Germany | Germany

Integrating pedagogical knowledge (PK), pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), and content knowledge (CK) is essential for pre-service teachers’ professional competence (Voss, Kunter, & Baumert, 2011) and predicts later expertise (Graichen, Wegner, & Nückles, 2019; König, 2010; Lehmann, 2020). Multiple document comprehension (MDC) is cognitively demanding because forming integrated mental models requires processing multiple interacting elements in working memory (Britt & Rouet, 2012; Sweller, 2010; Sweller, Ayres, & Kalyuga, 2011).
This study examined whether a cross-domain integration task induces higher cognitive load and perceived difficulty than a summary task. Pre-service teachers (N = 54) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (integration and transfer) or a control group (summary). All read four domain-specific texts on teaching competence and then completed their assigned writing task. After reading and again after writing, participants reported cognitive load (Klepsch, Schmitz, & Seufert, 2017) and task difficulty; motivation was assessed using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (Deci & Ryan).
Multivariate analyses (Hotelling’s T²) revealed significant task-type effects (T² = 0.39, F(4,49) = 4.16, p < .01, η²p = .28). The integration task elicited higher extraneous cognitive load (d = 0.75) and germane load (d = 0.61) than the summary task. Intrinsic load differences were marginal, and perceived difficulty did not differ significantly.
These findings show that cross-domain integration imposes substantial cognitive demands, consistent with MDC theory, while subjective difficulty appears insensitive to these increases. Results underscore the need for instructional scaffolding to support knowledge integration without overwhelming working memory.

Interventionen zur Förderung freizeitlicher Making-Aktivitäten: Die Rolle von Autonomie und Nutzen
Sophie Uhing | Friedrich - Alexander - Universität Erlangen - Nürnberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Sophie Uhing | Friedrich - Alexander - Universität Erlangen - Nürnberg | Germany
Prof. Stephan Kröner | Friedrich - Alexander - Universität Erlangen - Nürnberg | Germany

Making-Aktivitäten, z.B. 3D-Druck, könnten dem Nachlassen von MINT-Interesse und -Aktivitäten bei Jugendlichen entgegenwirken. Im Projekt EnvironMINT wurde untersucht, wie deren Making-Intention erhöht werden kann. Nach der Theorie des geplanten (TPB; Ajzen 1991) erklären Norm- und Kontroll- sowie insbesondere Verhaltensüberzeugungen die Intention.

Eine Fokusgruppendiskussion (N=61 Jugendliche) zu Making-Aktivitäten ließ erwarten, dass Verhaltensüberzeugungen gefördert werden durch eine Kombination aus positiver Wahrnehmung sowohl der Konsequenzen (insbes. Nutzen) als auch des Prozesses (insbes. Autonomie) von Making-Aktivitäten. Bevor dies in zwei Experimenten untersucht werden konnte, wurden TPB-Überzeugungsskalen entwickelt (N=29 Jugendliche) und pilotiert (N=398).

In einer 2x2-faktoriellen Videovignettenstudie mit den Faktoren Nutzen und Autonomie betrachteten N=223 Jugendliche Werbevideos eines Makingworkshops. Eine Latent-Change-Score-Analyse ergab, dass bei bloßen Vignetten die Darstellung von Nutzen (β=.31; p=.01), nicht aber von Autonomie (β=-.10; p=.41) die Verhaltensüberzeugungen beeinflusste. Making-Intentionen wurden nicht beeinflusst.

In zwei Feldexperimenten (N=89 Jugendliche) sollten Effekte der Autonomie in einem tatsächlichen Workshop untersucht werden: In Experiment 1 wurden zwei Varianten eines Makingworkshops mit niedriger (KG) vs. hoher (EG) Autonomie als Schulworkshop mit randomisierten Gruppen durchgeführt. In Experiment 2 erfolgte eine Replikation im Rahmen von Sommerferienworkshops. Regressionsanalysen ergaben nur in Experiment 2 Effekte der Autonomie auf die Verhaltensüberzeugungen (βFerien=.50, p=.02; βSchule=.28, p=.23) und Intention (βFerien=.58, p=.03; βSchule=-.00, p=1.00).

Effekte des Settings (Schule vs. Ferienworkshop) werden diskutiert. Insgesamt deutet sich an, dass das Aufzeigen des Nutzens primär für die Gewinnung der Jugendlichen relevant ist, die Verdeutlichung von Autonomie dagegen eher für die Motivierung in den Workshops.

Ajzen, Icek (1991): The theory of planned behavior. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 50(2).

Adaptive Regulation in Action: How Motivation, Ability, and Flexible Goal Adjustment Shape Performance Across Contexts
Chair(s) Dr. Cathleen Kappes (University of Hildesheim)
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Bernhard Leipold (Universität der Bundeswehr München)
Room: IT
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The four studies collectively advance our understanding of goal pursuit and performance by highlighting the dynamic, context-sensitive, and individualized nature of motivation. Loidl and Leipold (1) contribute by demonstrating that flexible goal adjustment—particularly reorientation and goal detachment—is an adaptive process linked to lower stress and better well-being over time. Their longitudinal findings underscore that goal regulation is multidimensional and dynamic, with distinct facets (e.g., reappraisal vs. detachment) playing different roles in psychological adjustment. Brinkmann et al. (2) employ psychophysiological measures and reveal how individual differences in implicit motives (achievement, affiliation, power) shape effort and disengagement, showing that motivation is not uniform but contingent on both personal dispositions and task context. Kappes et al. (3) extend this by showing that when a fundamental goal—like belonging—is blocked, individuals adapt by devaluing the goal’s importance, which paradoxically restores agency and well-being. This devaluation, evidenced by reduced own-group favoritism and lower affective distress, demonstrates goal adjustment as a protective mechanism. Finally, Roth et al. (4) challenge the long-standing linear interaction model of ability and motivation, showing that motivation’s primary role is to sustain engagement in moderately difficult tasks, not to boost performance universally. Their findings position disengagement as a critical regulatory mechanism, with motivation being most impactful where effort is needed to persist, not where ability alone suffices. Veronika Brandstätter will serve as discussant, offering insightful reflections and critical perspectives on these studies that display goal pursuit and goal adjustment as adaptive, context-sensitive processes shaped by individual differences, goal attainability, and the use of disengagement.

Facets of flexible goal adjustment: Longitudinal associations and protective function
Barbara Loidl | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Barbara Loidl | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany
Prof. Bernhard Leipold | Universität der Bundeswehr München | Germany

Processes of flexible goal adjustment (accommodative coping) are central to successful adaptation under stress, yet their dynamic relations over time remain insufficiently understood.
This research examines longitudinal associations between facets of flexible goal adjustment (e.g., positive reappraisal, downward comparison, reorientation, goal detachment), goal pursuit, and subjective stress from two longitudinal studies with three (study 1: N = 839; Mage = 52,68) and four (study 2: N = 105; Mage = 21,88) measurement points.
Results showed that flexible goal adjustment was associated with lower levels of subjective stress. Reorientation was associated with goal detachment, whereas processes of cognitive reappraisal (e.g., acceptance, lowering of aspirations) were associated with goal pursuit.
Overall, the findings suggest that goal detachment and reorientation are closely linked components of adaptive regulation and highlight the importance of modeling goal regulation as a dynamic, multidimensional process.

Individual differences in implicit motives shape effort and disengagement in goal pursuit
Dr. Kerstin Brinkmann | University of Geneva | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Kerstin Brinkmann | University of Geneva | Switzerland
Silvio Laloli | University of Geneva | Switzerland
Dr. Florence Mazares | Université Gustave Eiffel | France
Dr. Michael Richter | Liverpool John Moores University | United Kingdom

When pursuing a goal, people mobilize physical or mental resources (i.e. effort) to carry out instrumental behavior and reach their goal. According to the resource conservation principle, effort intensity is determined by the difficulty of the task and the importance of success. Disengagement occurs when the task is too difficult, or when the necessary effort is not justified by success importance. Both of these parameters can vary according to individual dispositions. Implicit motives are dispositional differences in the strength of the needs for achievement, affiliation and power. These motives can impact success importance depending on whether the task context or the task itself contains incentives that promise motive satisfaction and thus increase success importance. In the present studies, implicit motives are assessed using the Picture Story Exercise, a projective measure of motive strength, before participants engage in a task involving motive-relevant incentives or disincentives. Mental effort (i.e. engagement) during the task is operationalized by cardiovascular reactivity from baseline to task. The results of Study 1 demonstrate that task engagement or disengagement is determined by the strength of the achievement motive and the difficulty of the task. Study 2 shows that affiliation motive strength interacts with whether participants work alone or together to elicit task engagement or disengagement. The findings of Study 3 reveal that power-relevant incentives moderate the impact of the power motive on task engagement or disengagement. These studies demonstrate how contextual or task-inherent incentives influence mental effort during goal pursuit depending on individual differences in implicit motive strength.

When belonging fails: Devaluation of unattainable goals and its role in restoring agency and well-being
Dr. Cathleen Kappes | University of Hildesheim | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Cathleen Kappes | University of Hildesheim | Germany
Anthony Carrel | University of Geneva | Switzerland
Dr. Kerstin Brinkmann | University of Geneva | Switzerland

Adjusting goals is a key process for managing unattainable goals. When individuals let go of a goal that cannot be achieved and shift their focus to a new one, they can restore their sense of agency and enhance their well-being. In two studies (pre-study: N = 41; main study: N = 82), the goal of belonging to a specific group was activated. Participants played a virtual cyberball game twice with their group members. After an initial inclusion phase, half of the participants were excluded during the second round—effectively blocking their belonging goal. Subsequently, they completed a memory task, where correct answers earned rewards in the form of icons representing either in-group or out-group members.
We hypothesized and found that ostracized compared to included participants reported lower perceived goal importance and attainability of the belonging goal, along with a reversed own-group favoritism, lower need satisfaction, and increased negative affect. Correlations between these variables suggest the regulatory role of adjustments in goal importance in response to a blocked goal. Additionally, we expected that included participants would exert greater mental effort when seeing in-group icons, as reflected in higher cardiovascular activity during the task—consistent with a stronger motivation to achieve in-group rewards. Furthermore, increased skin conductance responses were observed during the task when participants viewing in-group icons made errors, suggesting heightened emotional arousal or effortful processing.
Overall, these findings indicate that when the goal to belong is blocked, individuals devalue this goal’s importance associated with reduced own-group favoritism and restored well-being.

Ability and motivation as performance predictors: Competing theories resolved through task disengagement
Prof. Veronika Job | University of Vienna | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Veronika Job | University of Vienna | Austria
Dr. Leopold Roth | University of Vienna | Austria
Christopher Mlynski | University of Vienna | Austria
Krishna Savani | Hong Kong Polytechnic University | Hong Kong, China

Understanding differences in task performance has been a focal goal of theory and applied psychology for decades. For the longest time, a linear interaction between ability and motivation has been proposed as the gold standard (theory of job performance, optimal at high ability and high motivation). Yet, empirical evidence for this assumption is scarce, and was meta-analytically questioned. Hence, we used model comparison to yield the usefulness of the multiplicative relationship between ability and motivation. Across two online studies (N = 372) we experimentally manipulated performance based incentives and increased task difficulty over time to manipulate ability.
Both experiments showed that the proposed linear interaction of ability and motivation is sub-optimal to predict task performance. In Study 1, a non-linear additive model without interaction term outperformed the traditional model. When adding the possibility to disengage from the main task in Study 2, the non-linear multiplicative model was superior against all alternative models.
This finding highlights that the role of motivation in performance is to prolong task engagement. Contrary to earlier theories, motivation was not meaningfully associated with performance in tasks that were either very easy or very difficult, for which ability is more predictive. Rather, motivation helps participants to uphold their engagement in areas of intermediate demands. While these findings require further data, they deliver a more realistic picture of motivation and engagement in task performance. Further, they contain implications for hiring and motivation practices in the workplace.

Situative Bewertung der Teamresilienzkapazität bei verschiedenen Widrigkeitstypen: Simulation einer integrierten Notrufleitstelle
Philipp R. Stirnberg | Universität Trier | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Philipp R. Stirnberg | Universität Trier | Germany
Prof. Dr. Thomas Ellwart | Universität Trier

Wenn Teams anhaltenden oder multiplen internalen und externalen Widrigkeiten ausgesetzt sind, ist die situative Bewertung der Teamkapazität von Bedeutung (Situational Team Capacity, STC). STC ist die situative ungeteilte oder geteilte Teamüberzeugung, dass genügend Teamkapazität vorhanden ist, um gegenwärtige anhaltende oder multiple Widrigkeiten zu überwinden. Bisher fokussierte die Teamresilienzforschung generalisierte Kapazitätsüberzeugungen hinsichtlich singulärer antizipierter Widrigkeiten, ohne die situativen Auswirkungen von auftretenden Widrigkeiten im Längsschnitt zu betrachten. Ziel der Studie ist es, den möglichen situativen negativen Einfluss von Widrigkeitstypen auf STC in multipler Abfolge zu prüfen (H1). Zudem wird geprüft, ob Präferenzen der Teamorientierung im Team und Teamprozesse während Widrigkeiten die Beziehung abschwächend moderieren (H2, H3).
Derzeit haben 112 Teammitglieder (81% Psychologiestudierende, 74 % weiblich, M = 22 Jahre) in 56 Zweierteams an der Studie teilgenommen. In einer simulierten integrierten Leitstelle von Feuerwehr und Rettungsdienst bearbeiteten Zweierteams Notrufe mit agentenbasierter Unterstützung mittlerer Autonomie. Vor der Simulation wurde die Teamorientierung der Teammitglieder mittels der Subfacetten Dominanz und Zugehörigkeit nach Driskrell et al. (2010) erhoben. Nach einer belastungsarmen Einsatzphase durchliefen die Teams drei randomisierte Einsatzphasen mit manipulierten Widrigkeitstypen (internal = Ausfall Agent; external = Zunahme Notrufe; kombiniert). Während der Einsatzphasen wurden Teamprozesse (aktional; interpersonal) mittels Teamkommunikation aufgezeichnet (quantitative Inhaltsanalyse folgt). STC wurde mittels Single-Item am Ende der Einsatzphasen gemessen.
Vorläufige Ergebnisse zeigen, dass STC durch internale (b = -1.11) und kombinierte (b = -2.16) Widrigkeiten abnimmt, nicht jedoch durch externale Widrigkeiten. Ein Trend ist erkennbar, dass hohe Teamorientierung (geringe Dominanz im Team) den negativen Einfluss internaler Widrigkeiten reduziert und STC stärkt (b = -1.41t).

Arbeitsbezogenes Fear of Missing Out in Sozialen Berufen: Skalenentwicklung und Zusammenhänge zum Wohlbefinden
Linda-Elisabeth Reimann | University of Münster | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Linda-Elisabeth Reimann | University of Münster | Germany
Catharina Hüsers | University of Münster | Germany
Christin Langanke | University of Münster | Germany
Prof. Carmen Binnewies | University of Münster | Germany

Theoretischer Hintergrund: Workplace Fear of Missing Out (wFoMO) beschreibt die Angst, wichtige arbeitsbezogene Informationen oder soziale Chancen zu verpassen, wenn man nicht erreichbar oder anwesend ist. Bisherige Forschung untersuchte wFoMO vor allem in flexiblen oder digitalen Arbeitskontexten. In sozialen Berufen (z.B. Pflege, Betreuung oder Bildung) ist dies jedoch kaum möglich, während gleichzeitig hohe Interdependenz und ständiger Informationsaustausch bestehen.
Ausgehend von der Selbstdeterminationstheorie (SDT) und der Conservation of Resources Theory (COR) verstehen wir wFoMO als Mechanismus, der von nicht-erfüllten psychologischen Bedürfnissen ausgelöst wird und Ressourcen erschöpft. Personen mit hoher Ausprägung investieren kognitive und emotionale Ressourcen in berufliche Erreichbarkeit und Aufmerksamkeitsbindung. Diese dauerhafte Ressourcenbeanspruchung verringert Regeneration und kann das Wohlbefinden beeinträchtigen.
Methode: In dieser Studie wurde eine wFoMO-Skala für soziale Berufe entwickelt und in einer zweiwelligen Längsschnittstudie (Abstand: eine Arbeitswoche) validiert.
Ergebnisse: Faktorenanalysen bestätigten eine dreidimensionale Struktur (performance-driven, duty-driven und relatedness-driven wFoMO). Die Skala zeigte gute Reliabilität (α = .74–.87) und Konstruktvalidität.
Regressionsanalysen ergaben, dass relatedness-driven wFoMO negative autoregressive Effekte auf positiven Affekt und psychologisches Abschalten zeigte, während duty-driven wFoMO mit Müdigkeit assoziiert war. Zudem moderierte Resilienz den Zusammenhang zwischen duty-driven wFoMO und Müdigkeit: Personen mit geringer Resilienz und hoher wFoMO-Ausprägung zeigten stärkere Erschöpfung über die Zeit.
Fazit: Die Ergebnisse verdeutlichen, dass wFoMO auch in sozialen Berufen ein relevanter, ressourcenzehrender Prozess ist, der langfristig das psychische Wohlbefinden beeinträchtigen kann.

Neurodivergence in the Work Context: A Conceptual Model, Systematic Review, and Future Research Agenda
Saskia Rauh | Universität Leipzig | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Saskia Rauh | Universität Leipzig | Germany
Prof. Dr. Hannes Zacher | Wilhelm Wundt Institute of Psychology

Neurodiversity is increasingly gaining attention in the work context, as neurodivergent individuals, such as people with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, or sensory processing sensitivity, constitute a substantial proportion of the working population. Estimates suggest that 15-30% of the general population can be considered neurodivergent. This presentation introduces, first, a conceptual framework that adapts existing theoretical approaches and further develops them for the organizational context, and second, the results of a systematic review of the existing research on neurodivergence at work. The analysis reveals significant conceptual and methodological gaps, particularly regarding theoretical models, operationalized constructs, and the consideration of contextual factors. In addition, initial findings from a longitudinal study are presented that examine person-environment fit with respect to neurodivergence from an integrative perspective. Both individual characteristics and work-related environmental factors are considered to capture fit, well-being, and behavior of neurodivergent employees in a differentiated manner. The aim of this research is to establish a scientifically grounded basis for the design of neurodiversity-friendly work environments and thereby to sustainably promote the participation of neurodivergent individuals.

Mental gesund führen im KI-Zeitalter: Ressourcenorientierte Führung in der digitalen Transformation
Prof. Dr. Magdalena Bathen-Gabriel | IU Internationale Hochschule | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Magdalena Bathen-Gabriel | IU Internationale Hochschule | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stefanie André | IU Internationale Hochschule

Hintergrund
Die Einführung von Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) verändert Arbeitsprozesse, Rollenanforderungen und Entscheidungsstrukturen insbesondere in wissensintensiven Branchen wie der Versicherungswirtschaft grundlegend. Neben Effizienzgewinnen entstehen neue psychosoziale Belastungen, etwa durch Technostress, Rollenunsicherheit oder veränderte Verantwortungszuschreibungen (Soulamai et al., 2024). Vor dem Hintergrund der WHO-Leitlinien zur psychischen Gesundheit am Arbeitsplatz wird Führung als zentraler Schutz- und Risikofaktor betrachtet (WHO, 2022). Theoretisch stützt sich die Studie auf Antonovskys Salutogenese-Konzept (Antonovsky, 1979) sowie das Job-Demands-Resources-Modell (Bakker & Demerouti, 2007). Es wird hypothesengeleitet angenommen, dass der KI-Einsatz spezifische arbeitsbezogene Anforderungen erhöht, zugleich jedoch durch geeignete Führungsressourcen potenziell gesundheitsförderlich gestaltet werden kann.
Methoden
Im Forschungsprojekt KIM (KI und mentale Gesundheit) wurde ein Mixed-Methods-Design gewählt. In einer qualitativen Vorstudie wurden Führungskräften aus der Versicherungsbranche interviewt und aus den Ergebnissen Hypothesen abgeleitet. Diese wurden im zweiten Teil der Studie mittels standardisiertem Fragebogen zu Technologieeinsatz, Arbeitsanforderungen, Work-Life-Balance, Führungsrolle, Arbeitsplatzsicherheit und mentaler Gesundheit überprüft (N=86 Führungskräfte).
Ergebnisse
Erste quantitative Ergebnisse weisen auf differenzierte Belastungsprofile im Kontext von KI hin. Insbesondere berichten Führungskräfte über erhöhten Technostress, Work-Life-Konflikte sowie Unsicherheiten hinsichtlich zukünftiger Kompetenzanforderungen. Gleichzeitig wird deutlich, dass transparente Kommunikation, Partizipation und unterstützendes Führungshandeln als zentrale Ressourcen wahrgenommen werden.
Schlussfolgerung
Die Ergebnisse verdeutlichen, dass der Einsatz von KI nicht nur technologische, sondern auch psychosoziale Transformationsprozesse auslöst. Führungskräfte nehmen hierbei eine Schlüsselrolle in der gesundheitsgerechten Gestaltung des digitalen Wandels ein. Präventive Maßnahmen, partizipative Implementierungsstrategien sowie die Integration KI-spezifischer Belastungsindikatoren in Gefährdungsbeurteilungen (§ 5 ArbSchG) erscheinen zentral, um mentale Gesundheit im Kontext digitaler Transformation nachhaltig zu fördern.

Künstliche Intelligenz als Ressource oder Stressor? Eine qualitative Analyse zu den Auswirkungen von künstlicher Intelligenz im Gesundheitswesen
Lara Ausborn | MSH Medical School Hamburg - University of Applied Sciences and Medical University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lara Ausborn | MSH Medical School Hamburg - University of Applied Sciences and Medical University | Germany
Dr. Maren Kersten | BGW Berufsgenossenschaft für Gesundheitsdienst und Wohlfahrtspflege | Germany
Dr. Sabine Gregersen | BGW Berufsgenossenschaft für Gesundheitsdienst und Wohlfahrtspflege | Germany
Melissa Maria Estrella | MSH Medical School Hamburg - University of Applied Sciences and Medical University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Sylvie Vincent-Höper | MSH Medical School Hamburg - University of Applied Sciences and Medical University | Germany

Der Gesundheitssektor steht angesichts hoher Arbeitsbelastungen und des Fachkräftemangels vor erheblichen Herausforderungen. Zeitgleich nimmt der Einsatz von künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) im Gesundheitswesen zu und wird als potenzielle Entlastung diskutiert. Neben möglichen positiven Effekten birgt KI jedoch gleichzeitig technologische, ethische sowie arbeitsorganisatorische Risiken. Bislang liegen nur wenige empirische Erkenntnisse dazu vor, unter welchen Bedingungen KI aus Sicht der Beschäftigten als Ressource oder Stressor wahrgenommen wird und welche Auswirkungen sich daraus für die psychische Gesundheit ergeben.

Ziel der Studie ist es, förderliche und hinderliche personen- und bedingungsbezogene Einflussfaktoren bei der Implementierung und Nutzung von KI zu identifizieren und deren Wirkmechanismen in Bezug auf die psychische Gesundheit der Beschäftigten zu explorieren. Zwischen April 2025 und Januar 2026 wurden 31 leitfadengestützte Interviews mit Ärzt:innen und beratenden Fachpersonen aus dem Gesundheitswesen geführt und mittels qualitativer Inhaltsanalyse nach Mayring ausgewertet. Die Analyse erfolgte deduktiv-induktiv und basierte auf einem integrativen Rahmenmodell, das arbeitspsychologische und human-centered-AI-Ansätze verbindet.

Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass bedingungsbezogene Einflussfaktoren häufiger genannt wurden als personenbezogene. Förderliche Bedingungen umfassen eine gute Usability sowie ein AI supportive climate, das u.a. durch Schulungen, Partizipation und Aufklärung gekennzeichnet ist. Hinderliche Faktoren beziehen sich auf rechtliche und ethische Hürden, Schwierigkeiten beim Transfer in den Arbeitsalltag sowie Zeit- und Kostenaufwand. KI wird überwiegend als entlastend erlebt, insbesondere durch die Reduktion administrativer Tätigkeiten und Zeitdruck sowie durch Entscheidungsunterstützung. Belastungen ergeben sich vor allem durch erhöhte kognitive Anforderungen und begrenzte technische Verlässlichkeit. Insgesamt zeigen sich tendenziell positive Effekte auf die psychische Gesundheit, sofern KI menschengerecht gestaltet und durch organisationale Rahmenbedingungen unterstützt wird.

Wenn Technologie zur Bezugsperson wird: Psychologische Mechanismen der KI-Nutzung in emotional belastenden Situationen
Dr. Lea-Christin Wickord | Universität Koblenz | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Lea-Christin Wickord | Universität Koblenz | Germany

Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) wird zunehmend als potenzielle Quelle emotionaler Unterstützung wahrgenommen. Theoretische Ansätze zur kompensatorischen Mediennutzung, Anthropomorphisierung sowie zur sozialen Präsenz legen nahe, dass insbesondere Einsamkeit, Vertrauen in KI und wahrgenommene Empathie zentrale Determinanten sozialer Zuschreibungen gegenüber KI-Systemen darstellen. Während Einsamkeit mit einer verstärkten Tendenz zur Anthropomorphisierung nicht-menschlicher Entitäten einhergeht, könnten Vertrauen und empathische Wahrnehmung die konkrete Wahl von KI als Unterstützungsquelle beeinflussen. Ziel des Projekts war es, diese Mechanismen integrativ zu untersuchen.

Hierzu wurden zwei quantitative Online-Studien durchgeführt. Studie 1 (N = 97; MAlter = 24,07 Jahre, SD = 7,72) erfasste Einsamkeit (UCLA Loneliness Scale), Anthropomorphisierung (Godspeed), soziale Präsenz (RSPS), KI-Kompetenz (AI Literacy Scale) sowie KI-Nutzungsmotive (AIMS). Studie 2 (N = 81; MAlter = 23,83 Jahre, SD = 6,43) untersuchte anhand von fünf randomisierten Fallvignetten die Wahl einer Unterstützungsquelle (KI vs. Mensch). Zusätzlich wurden Vertrauen in KI (TIAS), wahrgenommene Empathie (PETS) und Selbstoffenbarungstendenz (RSDS) erhoben.

In der ersten Studie zeigte sich, dass Einsamkeit positiv mit Anthropomorphisierung, KI-Kompetenz und den unterschiedlichen Nutzungsmotiven, jedoch nicht mit sozialer Präsenz korrelierte. In Studie 2 variierte die Wahl der Unterstützungsquelle je nach Szenario. Zusätzlich zeigte sich, dass Vertrauen und wahrgenommene Empathie die Wahrscheinlichkeit sich einer KI zuzuwenden, mediieren.

Die Befunde sprechen dafür, dass KI weniger als vollwertiger sozialer Ersatz fungiert, sondern vielmehr als projektiver sozialer Bezugspunkt. Einsamkeit begünstigt anthropomorphe Zuschreibungen, während Vertrauen und Empathiewahrnehmung zentrale Prädiktoren der konkreten Zuwendung zu KI darstellen. KI erscheint somit als ergänzende Ressource zur emotionalen Regulation in belastenden Situationen.

„Hey ChatGPT, ich werde online gemobbt, was kann ich tun?“ – Können KI-Chatbots Jugendlichen helfen, mit vorurteilsbasiertem Cybermobbing umzugehen?
Prof. Dr. Anja Schultze-Krumbholz | Technische Universität Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Anja Schultze-Krumbholz | Technische Universität Berlin | Germany
Dr. Sohni Zahid-Siddiqui | Bergische Universität Wuppertal | Germany

Vorurteilsbezogenes Cyberbullying ist eine Form aggressiven Online-Verhaltens, bei der wiederholt und absichtlich Handlungen gegen ein Opfer durchgeführt werden, die dieses aufgrund seiner tatsächlichen oder wahrgenommenen identitätsbezogenen Merkmale verletzen (Hinduja & Patchin, 2022). Trotz der hohen Zahl an Kindern und Jugendlichen mit Migrationshintergrund (Eurostat, 2024), mit Behinderungen (European Council, 2024) und aus der LGBTQ+-Community in europäischen Ländern (Statista, 2016) ist die Forschung zu vorurteilsbasiertem Cybermobbing nach wie vor sehr begrenzt (Schultze-Krumbholz, 2024), obwohl diese Gruppen eine erhöhte Vulnerabilität für Viktimisierung aufweisen. Bestehende Anti-Bullying-Programme gehen weitgehend nicht auf diese Gruppen ein (Siddiqui & Casale, 2025). Jugendliche aus diesen Gruppen müssen sich möglicherweise anderweitig Unterstützung suchen. Die vorliegende Studie evaluiert daher mit Hilfe eines Delphi-Designs KI-generierte Ideen aus frei zugänglichen Foren zum Umgang mit vorurteilsbasiertem Cybermobbing. Systematisch entwickelte Prompts zu drei Kategorien vorurteilsbasierten Cyberbullyings wurden in die gängigsten kostenlosen Chatbots (ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Meta AI und Perplexity) eingegeben, um Interventionsstrategien und Handlungsideen zu generieren. In einer ersten Runde beurteilten 9 Expert*innen (7 weiblich, 35-51 Jahre alt) aus Forschung, Beratungs- und Bildungskontexten die Handlungsvorschläge. Die Antworten der Chatbots wurden überwiegend als hilfreich und unterstützend wahrgenommen. Die Expert*innen machten insgesamt mehr Handlungsvorschläge als die KI. Obwohl sie zunächst mit allen Vorschlägen übereinstimmten, wiesen sie im Folgenden auf deutliche Schwächen der Empfehlungen hin: z.B. fragwürdige und widersprüchliche Vorschläge, Stereotypisierung von Bullies sowie die Illusion von perfekten Lösungen. Mit einer abschließenden Runde werden auf Konsens der Expert*innen basierende Handlungsempfehlungen gesammelt und mit den Antworten der Chatbots verglichen. Die Eignung KI-basierter Selbsthilfe für Jugendliche wird diskutiert.
