Moderatoreffekte von Servant Leadership und implizitem Leistungsmotiv auf tagesspezifische Einflüsse von Positivem Affekt auf Work Engagement
Janine Esser | Bergische Universität Wuppertal | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Janine Esser | Bergische Universität Wuppertal | Germany
Dr. Elvira Radaca | Bergische Universität Wuppertal
Prof. Dr. Stefan Diestel | Bergische Universität Wuppertal

Während gemeinhin bekannt ist, dass tägliches Work Engagement sich durch affektive Prozesse, Dispositionen und Führung vorhersagen lässt, fehlen empirische Erkenntnisse über theoretisch naheliegende Wechselwirkungen zwischen diesen Einflussfaktoren. Im Einklang mit der Self-Determination Theorie wird Servant Leadership als ein Führungsstil verstanden, der durch die Erfüllung psychologischer Grundbedürfnisse Work Engagement fördert. In welchem Ausmaß dieser Führungsstil Einfluss nimmt, hängt davon ab, inwiefern Mitarbeitende bereits über eine starke implizite motivationale Tendenz zu Leistungsverhalten verfügen. Das implizite Leistungsmotiv sollte bei Aktivierung im Arbeitsprozess (bspw. durch positiven Affekt) Work Engagement begünstigen. Bei Mitarbeitenden mit geringem Leistungsmotiv sollte hingegen Servant Leadership Work Engagement über Autonomie, Empowerment und eine starke Mitarbeiterorientierung stabilisieren, vor allem bei positiven Arbeitserlebnissen. Vor diesem Hintergrund untersuchen wir, inwiefern Servant Leadership und das implizite Leistungsmotiv in einer 3-fach-Interaktion die positiven tagesspezifischen Zusammenhänge zwischen positivem Affekt und Work Engagement moderieren.
Zur Überprüfung unserer Hypothesen wurde eine zehntägige Tagebuchstudie mit 60 Beschäftigten aus unterschiedlichen beruflichen Kontexten (473 tagesbezogene Messungen) durchgeführt. Parameterschätzungen von Multilevel Modeling zeigen, dass der positive Zusammenhang zwischen positivem Affekt und Absorption durch Servant Leadership und das implizite Leistungsmotiv moderiert wird. Demnach verstärkt das Leistungsmotiv den Zusammenhang nur bei geringem Servant Leadership, während bei hohem Servant Leadership und geringem Leistungsmotiv der Zusammenhang ebenfalls stark war. Die Ergebnisse implizieren, dass ein hohes Leistungsmotiv für Work Engagement nicht zwangsläufig erforderlich sein muss, sofern Führungskräfte motivierend auf ihre Mitarbeitenden einwirken. Demnach sollte Servant Leadership durch Führungskräfteentwicklungsmaßnahmen gezielt ausgebaut werden, damit Personen von einem hohen positiven Affekt bei ihrer Arbeit profitieren.

Innovation ohne Anwesenheitspflicht? Die Rolle von Koordination, Team Empowerment und psychologischer Sicherheit in hybriden Teams
Lisa-Maria Marquardt | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lisa-Maria Marquardt | Germany
Carsten C. Schermuly | SRH Berlin University of applied sciences

Hybrides Arbeiten ist zu einem prägenden Merkmal der Arbeitsorganisation in wissensintensiven Bereichen geworden. Zugleich zeigt sich ein Paradox: Obwohl Interventionen wie erhöhte Büropräsenz oder Return-to-Office-Mandate weit verbreitet sind, bleibt ihre Wirksamkeit für zentrale Ergebnisvariablen auf Mitarbeitenden- und Organisationsebene empirisch unklar. Da Zusammenarbeit unter Hybridbedingungen jedoch nach wie vor team- und interdependenzbasiert ist, verschiebt sich der entscheidende Fokus vom Arbeitsort hin zur Frage, wie Teams ihre Zusammenarbeit über Zeit, Raum, Kommunikationsformen und individuelle Präferenzen koordinieren.
Zur Erfassung dieser Abstimmung wurde jüngst das Verhaltenskonstrukt Coordination of Collaboration in Hybrid Teams (CoCoh) entwickelt. Auf dieser Grundlage adressiert der Beitrag eine offene Erklärungslücke: Warum und wann führt hybride Koordination zu übergeordneten Teamergebnissen, insbesondere zu Teaminnovation? Gestützt auf die Team-Selbstbestimmungstheorie, die betont, wie bedürfnisunterstützende (need-supportive) Teaminteraktionen kollektive Motivationsdynamiken und leistungsrelevante Prozesse formen, konzipieren wir CoCoh als einen motivational bedeutsamen Koordinationsprozess. Dieser fördert Teaminnovation über Team-Empowerment, wobei psychologische Sicherheit als klimabezogene Randbedingung fungiert.
Studie 1 liefert konvergente Evidenz für die Kernzusammenhänge: In einer Zwei-Wellen-Stichprobe sagte CoCoh zu t1 Team Empowerment zu t2 moderat vorher. In einem Team-Datensatz zeigte sich ein starker Zusammenhang zwischen CoCoh und Team Empowerment, sowie zwischen Empowerment und Teaminnovation. Studie 2 testet das vollständige moderierte Mediationsmodell in einer Feldstudie. Der Beitrag erklärt prozessorientiert, wann Hybridarbeit innovationsförderlich wird, und leitet Implikationen für Koordinationspraktiken und Teamklimata ab.

Zwischen professioneller Neutralität und emotionalem Rückzug: Frontstage- und Backstage-Darstellungsregeln im Polizeidienst
Linnea Tönjes | Deutsche Hochschule der Polizei, Münster | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Andrea Fischbach | Deutsche Hochschule der Polizei, Münster
Linnea Tönjes | Deutsche Hochschule der Polizei, Münster | Germany

Im Kontakt mit emotional belasteten Personen (z. B. verstörte Opfer, besorgte Angehörige, ungeduldige Verkehrsteilnehmende, gewaltbereite Demonstrierende) wird von Polizist*innen erwartet, professionelle Neutralität zu zeigen und eigene Emotionen wie Angst, Trauer oder Ärger zu regulieren. Die Einhaltung dieser Darstellungsregeln erfordert Emotionsarbeit. Bisherige Forschung fokussiert überwiegend den „Frontstage“-Kontext polizeilicher Emotionsarbeit. Weniger berücksichtigt wird, dass auch im „Backstage“-Kontext, etwa in der Dienststelle oder im Streifenwagen, in Interaktionen mit Kolleg*innen und Vorgesetzten, organisationsgeprägte Darstellungsregeln existieren können.
Ziel der geplanten Studie ist zu untersuchen, ob sich Darstellungsregeln zwischen Frontstage und Backstage unterscheiden oder kontextübergreifend bestehen und welche gesundheitsrelevanten Konsequenzen sich daraus ergeben. Die Felderhebung ist im Frühjahr 2026 vorgesehen; die Ergebnisse werden zur Tagung vorliegen. Auf Grundlage der Theorie und Forschung zur Emotionsregulation (Gross, 2015) nehmen wir an, dass die Norm zur Unterdrückung insbesondere vulnerabler Emotionen (z. B. Angst, Trauer, Distress) Backstage geringer ausfällt als im Frontstage, jedoch nur unter Bedingungen hoher psychologischer Sicherheit, erlebter authentischer Führung und eines positiven Klimas für Emotionsarbeit. Zudem erwarten wir Geschlechterunterschiede auf Grundlage von Theorien und Forschung zu Genderstereotypen. Im männlichkeitsdominierten Polizeiumfeld sollten Männer stärkere Suppressionsnormen wahrnehmen als Frauen.
In einem zweiten Messzeitpunkt erfassen wir Indikatoren psychischer Gesundheit und arbeitsbezogenen Wohlbefindens (Burnout, Arbeitszufriedenheit). Basierend auf der COR-Theorie erwarten wir, dass Frontstage-Suppressionsnormen insbesondere dann mit negativer Gesundheit zusammenhängen, wenn kein ressourcengenerierender „Backstage-Exit“ besteht, also auch gegenüber Kolleg*innen bzw. Vorgesetzen die Norm vorherrscht, vulnerable Emotionen unterdrücken zu müssen. Die Studie kontextualisiert Darstellungsregeln, differenziert deren gesundheitliche Bedeutung und leitet praxisrelevante Implikationen für unterstützende Strukturen im Umgang mit Emotionen in Polizeiorganisationen ab.

Organisationskultur als Ressource: Fehlermanagementkultur im dynamischen Zusammenspiel von Erholung, Affekt und Vitalität
Dr. Elvira Radaca | Bergische Universität Wuppertal/ Schumpeter School of Business & Economics | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Elvira Radaca | Bergische Universität Wuppertal/ Schumpeter School of Business & Economics | Germany

Zahlreiche Studien belegen, dass Beschäftigte, die sich am Abend erfolgreich von ihrer Arbeit erholen, ein geringeres Ausmaß an negativem Affekt berichten, was wiederum ihr psychologisches Wohlbefinden fördert. Unklar bleibt jedoch, unter welchen organisationalen Rahmenbedingungen dieser Zusammenhang unterstütz wird. Ein zentraler Faktor in diesem Zusammenhang ist die Fehlermanagementkultur, da Fehler im Arbeitskontext als Auslöser negativen Affekts gelten. In Organisationen mit einer konstruktiven Fehlermanagementkultur hingegen werden Fehler als Lerngelegenheiten statt als Bedrohungen interpretiert, wodurch die Intensität von negativen Affekten reduziert werden. Entsprechend wird erwartet, dass die Fehlermanagementkultur den indirekten Zusammenhang zwischen arbeitsbezogener Erholung und subjektiver Vitalität über negativen Affekt moderiert. Zur Prüfung der Hypothesen wurde eine zehntägige Tagebuchstudie mit drei Messzeitpunkten pro Tag durchgeführt. Die Daten von 125 Beschäftigten aus unterschiedlichen beruflichen Kontexten wurden mittels Mehrebenenanalysen ausgewertet. Die Ergebnisse bestätigen einen signifikanten indirekten Effekt von Erholung auf subjektive Vitalität über negativen Affekt. Ebenfalls konnte der moderierte Mediationseffekt bestätigt werden. Damit erweist sich Erholung zwar als notwendige, jedoch nicht allein hinreichende Bedingung für die Entstehung subjektiver Vitalität. Die Ergebnisse verdeutlichen, dass die Fehlermanagementkultur eine organisationale Ressource darstellt, die den positiven Zusammenhang zwischen arbeitsbezogener Erholung und subjektiver Vitalität begünstigt. Als Bestandteil einer lernorientierten Organisationskultur beeinflusst sie systematisch affektive Bewertungs- und Regulationsprozesse, indem sie die Bedrohungsvalenz von Fehlern reduziert und affektive Ressourcenbindung begrenzt. Dadurch wird der Zusammenhang zwischen negativem Affekt und subjektive Vitalität abgeschwächt und die Wirksamkeit arbeitsbezogener Erholung für psychologisches Wohlbefinden verstärkt. Zugleich liefern sie konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte für weiterführende theoretische und praxisrelevante Implikationen. Abschließend werden Limitationen der Studie sowie Empfehlungen für zukünftige Forschungsperspektiven diskutiert.

Beyond Individual-Level Determinants, How Socioeconomic Structures Shape Climate Policy Acceptance Across Countries
Dr. Sascha Kuhn | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Sascha Kuhn | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany
Dr. Bernd Schäfer | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany
Dr. Sonja Grelle | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany
Dr. Kim Doell | University of Konstanz | Germany
Prof. Madalina Vlasceanu | Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability | United States
Prof. Dr. Wilhelm Hofmann | Ruhr University Bochum | Germany

The global climate crisis necessitates transformative policies to address ecological and social challenges. Without public policy acceptance (PPA), policies are generally not adopted. Research on PPA in this context has predominantly focused on individual-level predictors and single-country studies in privileged Euro-American contexts, while leaving the influence of broader socioeconomic structures globally underexplored. The present study adopts a multilevel perspective to investigate how critical structural macro-level variables—such as economic freedom, income inequality, per capita carbon emissions, climate hazards & exposure, trust in government, and democratic governance—shape public support for climate policies. Drawing on a dataset from the International Climate Psychology Collaboration (which included nearly 60,000 individuals across 63 countries), we demonstrate that structural factors significantly influence PPA. Our findings indicate that economic freedom and countries’ per capita emissions negatively predict PPA; thus, we argue that neoliberal economic structures and reliance on fossil fuels foster vested interests undermining support for climate action. Conversely, higher levels of income inequality and climate vulnerability are associated with greater PPA, potentially reflecting heightened awareness of environmental risks. Contrary to expectations, trust in government does not exhibit a consistent relationship with PPA. This study underscores the necessity of critically interrogating power relations within socioeconomic structures that sustain resistance to climate policies. This work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of environmental PPA in a diverse global context, advancing pathways for transformative societal change.

Prof. Dr. Ulf Hahnel | Leuphana Universitaet Lueneburg | Germany

Public support for climate policies depends not only on the content of available information but also on how citizens actively seek, process, or avoid this information. We investigate how active sampling of pro or anti-policy arguments shapes policy acceptance in a preregistered, cross-national experiment conducted in 15 countries (N_total = 4900). Participants evaluated four types of climate food policies (taxes, regulations, subsidies, and labels) after sampling arguments across seven rounds each.

Across countries and policy domains, we find robust evidence for confirmatory information sampling: in multilevel-item response models, we find that more climate concerned, more politically left-leaning and higher initial policy evaluation predicted a higher propensity to select a pro-argument. Information avoidance overall was low and slightly higher in participants indifferent towards the policies. On the other hand, reading arguments influenced policy support. Cross-cultural analyses revealed that in countries with higher per capita carbon emissions, overall policy acceptance was lower. Policy support was more malleable in countries with lower GDP/capita and a lower within sample variance in climate concern, suggesting that attitudinal polarization within a country can lead to more firm policy evaluations. Our data suggests the importance of communication and narratives as well as the political and economic context within these discussions happesn for the acceptance of effective mitigation policies. We discuss scalable interventions to increase acceptance of climate food policies and reduce backlash.

A Buffer against Backlash: How the Desire for Governmental Intervention Moderates the Effect of Regulatory Depth on Climate Policy Acceptance
Dr. Sonja Grelle | Ruhr-Universtität Bochum | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Sonja Grelle | Ruhr-Universtität Bochum | Germany
Prof. Dr. Wilhelm Hofmann | Ruhr-Universtität Bochum | Germany

Systemic climate policies are essential for addressing environmental crises, but often face public resistance due to their intrusiveness. Drawing on the Integrative Public Policy Acceptance (IPAC) framework, we examine how the Desire for Governmental Intervention (DGI) shapes climate policy acceptance as a function of regulatory depth. Across two online studies (NStudy1 = 565, Nobs = 11,300; NStudy2 = 971, Nobs = 11,652), participants evaluated climate policies across multiple environmental domains. As expected, higher regulatory depth reduced policy acceptance, while higher DGI increased it. Crucially, DGI buffered the negative effect of intrusiveness: individuals with a strong DGI were more likely to accept even highly intrusive measures such as taxes or bans. This buffering effect was consistently observed, with the evidence strongest at the between-person level. These findings highlight DGI as a key motivational factor for climate policy acceptance. Strengthening this desire may be crucial for increasing public support for ambitious yet necessary systemic climate interventions.

During election campaigns, politicians strategically manage their public image to signal connection with voters. One common tactic involves the use of food cues to convey ordinariness and cultural alignment, rather than elite status. This preregistered study investigates how food portrayals, compared to contextual cues, affect voters’ likelihood of supporting a political candidate (https://aspredicted.org/xqsc-n395.pdf).
A representative US online-sample (N=1,492) viewed 12 AI-generated images of fictitious political candidates (White/Black*male/female), systematically varied by food cues (expensive meal, fast food, no food) and office context (luxurious, open-plan). The analyses reported here focus on White male candidates. Participants rated their likelihood of voting for each candidate.
Contrary to our hypothesis, candidates portrayed without food were more likely to receive a participant’s vote than candidates shown with fast food (b=-0.33[-0.40,-0.27], p < .001) or expensive meals (b=-0.35[-0.42,-0.29], p < .001). Placement in a luxurious office context also decreased voting likelihood (b=-0.17[-0.23,-0.10], p < .001). No significant interaction emerged between food type and office context (all ps ≥ .06). Additionally, perceived similarity between participant and politician was associated with higher voting likelihood.
Office context appears to function as a more diagnostic cue than food portrayals, with average office environments signaling ingroup membership and cultural alignment. The unexpected negative effect of food portrayals suggests that food cues may introduce ambiguity or norm violations rather than reliably communicating cultural similarity. Given the widespread use of food imagery in political campaigns, further research is needed to clarify conditions, voter segments, and politician types for which this strategy is effective.

Dr. Clara Kühner | Leipzig University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Clara Kühner | Leipzig University | Germany
Dr. Maie Stein | Leipzig University
Dr. Karen R. S. Hamann | Leipzig University

For organizations to successfully transform toward environmental sustainability, it is central that employees complete prescribed work tasks in environmentally sustainable ways (i.e., task-related employee green behavior; EGB). Although environmental efficacy beliefs are considered important predictors of such behavior, the distinct roles of self-efficacy and collective efficacy, as well as their potentially reciprocal relations with task-related EGB are so far not well understood. Drawing on social cognitive theory and social identity theory, we propose that environmental self-efficacy and collective environmental efficacy are positively and reciprocally associated with task-related EGB. To test our hypotheses, we collected 5-wave longitudinal data from 1,562 employees in Germany across one year, with 3-month time lags between measurement waves, and analyzed these data using random intercept cross-lagged panel models. Results showed that increased collective environmental efficacy predicted subsequent increases in task-related EGB, and vice versa, whereas no significant associations were found for environmental self-efficacy. These findings highlight the importance of collective approaches to environmental sustainability transformations within organizations.

Reflecting on Psychological Dynamics of Social Interactions with Virtual Social Agents
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Cornelia Sindermann (Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule - University of Psychology)
Prof. Dr. Maria Wirzberger (University of Stuttgart)
Room: BG
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Virtual, non-human social agents - ranging from chatbots to fully fledged virtual influencers with distinct identities - become increasingly prevalent online. These agents are beginning to participate in societally consequential domains, including professional decision-making, political discourse, and social and environmental activism. Yet, the psychological mechanisms shaping human responses to such agents and their broader societal implications remain insufficiently understood. This symposium shares insights from four distinct empirical contributions on the antecedents and consequences of trust in such agents and the effects of interactions with them across different applied and politically relevant contexts.
The first contribution introduces determinants of trust in chatbots, demonstrating that trust is less driven by anthropomorphic persona cues of chatbots, such as perceived gender or age, than by contextual meaning and users’ pre-existing social biases. The second contribution shifts from trust formation to its consequences, showing that discussions on a polarized issue with a trust-inducing, rather than neutral, chatbot promote openness to opposing views and reduced ideological bias, illustrating that trustworthy chatbot discussion partners can foster moderation. Extending the focus, the third contribution examines virtual influencers and tests how stereotypical versus counter-stereotypical portrayals of disability by virtual and human influencers affect social attitudes, addressing the question of whether simulating marginalized identities can foster social acceptance. The final contribution focuses on virtual versus human “greenfluencers”, investigating credibility judgments and engagement with climate-related content as a function of influencer type, gender congruency, and recipients’ trust in humans and AI, thereby advancing the understanding of non-human agents in activism.

Prof. Dr. Maria Wirzberger | University of Stuttgart | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Tabea Berberena | University of Stuttgart | Germany
Prof. Dr. Maria Wirzberger | University of Stuttgart | Germany

Trust is a key determinant of whether users rely on conversational AI systems, yet trust formation is not only shaped by system performance but also by users’ pre-existing social dispositions. In particular, gender- and age-related biases have been widely discussed as drivers of interpersonal trust, but empirical evidence in an AI context remains limited. We conducted an online experimental study with 288 participants (Mage = 45.34, SD = 17.42; 53.12% male) to examine how chatbot gender, chatbot age, and decision-making context influence self-rated trust and trusting behavior, while accounting for individual differences in gender role stereotypes and ageism. Participants interacted with chatbots varying in perceived gender (male vs. female) and age (young vs. old) across four professional decision scenarios (finance, healthcare, education, and law). Linear mixed-effects models revealed no significant effects of chatbot gender or age on trust or trusting behavior. In contrast, scenario context significantly affected trust ratings, with lower trust in healthcare than in other domains. Although individual biases did not moderate responses to chatbot demographics, gender role stereotypes were negatively associated with trust ratings, whereas ageism was positively associated with trusting behavior. Together, these findings challenge assumptions about persona-based anthropomorphic effects in conversational AI and suggest that trust is shaped more through contextual meaning and users’ predispositions rather than demographic persona cues. Consequently, this study provides boundary conditions for social-cue-based trust models and underscores the need for context-sensitive and bias-aware approaches to designing and evaluating trust in conversational AI design.

Cooling the Heat: How Trust-Inducing Chatbot Interactions Influence Reflection on Counter-Attitudinal Evidence in Polarized Topics
Dr. Christine Finn | Friedrich-Schiller-University Jena | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Christine Finn | Friedrich-Schiller-University Jena | Germany
Julian Kauk | Friedrich-Schiller-University Jena | Germany

Polarized beliefs can reduce openness to factual information, especially when evidence contradicts one’s ideological views. In a 4-week online experiment (N = 89), we examined how interpersonal trust in an AI-based chatbot shapes reflection on and evaluation of counter-attitudinal evidence in a controversial domain. Participants were randomly assigned to interact with a chatbot that behaved either neutrally or in a trust-inducing manner across four online sessions. The first two sessions aimed to establish rapport between participants and the chatbot and to familiarize them with the experimental setting. In the final two sessions, participants discussed climate policy as a current polarized topic and completed a two-step reflection task: first, they constructed arguments opposing their own view; second, they evaluated and reflected on a factual statement that again contradicted their stance. Interactions characterized by trust appeared to foster greater openness and more reflective engagement with counter-attitudinal information than neutral exchanges. Moreover, participants in the trust-inducing condition showed a reduction in ideological bias after the intervention, indicating a lower tendency to evaluate evidence in line with their ideological views. These findings highlight the potential of trustworthy AI interlocutors to promote epistemic openness and more balanced reasoning on politically charged issues.

Virtual Influencers with Disabilities: Examining the Role of Stereotypicality and Identity Appropriation
Jiyeon Yeo | Chemnitz University of Technology | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jiyeon Yeo | Chemnitz University of Technology | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jan-Philipp Stein | Chemnitz University of Technology | Germany

Digitally created social media personas—i.e., virtual influencers (VIs)—are increasingly adopted to represent marginalized identities, including individuals with physical disabilities. While this might be seen as a step towards more inclusivity in the online space, VIs are characterized by an ambiguous form of simulated agency; accordingly, the absence of genuinely lived experiences risks evoking an insincere impression or perceptions of identity appropriation. Likewise, viewer responses might be affected by the stereotypicality of the VI’s portrayal, as stereotypical depictions are likely to elicit stronger reactance. In the present study, we examine these hypothesized relations using a preregistered 2 (influencer type: human vs. VI) × 2 (portrayal: stereotypical vs. counter-stereotypical) between-subjects experiment. Images of real influencers from the disabled community are juxtaposed with corresponding AI-generated VIs, which were self-created to appear highly human-like yet still visibly artificial. Additionally, we manipulate the stereotypicality of the shown content by contrasting dependency-focused depictions of disabled individuals (e.g., receiving care) with portrayals contradicting dominant stereotypes (e.g., active participation). Grounded in Mind Perception Theory and intergroup contact frameworks, we expect that viewing the content of human (vs. virtual) influencers prompts more favorable explicit and implicit attitudes toward people with disabilities (H1), moderated by the stereotypicality of the portrayal (H2). Further, we investigate a potential mediation effect via perceived disability identity-appropriation (RQ1). Taken together, our study strives to elucidate the boundary conditions of artificially created online activism—and to find out whether simulating a marginalized identity fosters social acceptance or inadvertently reinforces intergroup boundaries.

Virtual versus Human Greenfluencers - The Psychological Basis of individuals’ Reactions to Posts on Climate Change and Environmental Protection by Different Greenfluencers
Prof. Dr. Cornelia Sindermann | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule – University of Psychology, Heidelberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nils Burgheim | University of Stuttgart | Germany
Prof. Dr. Cornelia Sindermann | Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule – University of Psychology, Heidelberg | Germany

Virtual influencers - fictional digital social media characters with a large follower base - are becoming increasingly prevalent online. Some are already deployed for political communication about climate change and environmental protection, often referred to as virtual greenfluencers. Yet, it remains unclear how humans react to posts by virtual greenfluencers compared to those by human greenfluencers and what the psychological basis of such reactions is. Guided by the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, research on congruency effects, and theory and research on trust in Artificial Intelligence (AI), this experimental study examines how individuals evaluate and engage with posts attributed to different greenfluencer types: (1) AI-controlled virtual greenfluencers, (2) human-controlled virtual greenfluencers, and (3) human greenfluencers (between-subjects factor). Additionally, the study tests the role of gender congruency between recipients and greenfluencers (within-subjects factor) and its interaction with greenfluencer type. Beyond these greenfluencer characteristics, we assess individual differences in recipients’ trust in humans and AI, focusing on their direct effects and their moderating influence on responses to the different greenfluencer types. Primary outcome variables are perceived credibility of the information in the posts and behavioral intentions to engage with the posts (e.g., liking, commenting, sharing). Data will be collected in February 2026. Analyses will be conducted using multilevel modeling. The findings will provide a systematic assessment of recipients’ responses to virtual and human greenfluencer communication, integrating source attributes with recipient-level psychological dispositions.

Identity, Power, and Resistance in Digital Hate and Activism
Intertwined Processes of Vulnerability and Resilience
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Özen Odag (Touro University Berlin)
Room: RO
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Contemporary digital media environments are central arenas for the construction, contestation, and regulation of social identities. This symposium brings together five complementary papers that examine how identity is shaped through online hate speech, political discourse, and digital activism, combining quantitative and qualitative approaches. Across different platforms (Instagram, Reddit, X) and contexts (everyday discourse, activism discourse), the contributions demonstrate how identity operates simultaneously as a target of hostility and a resource for resistance, and relatedly, how power relations lie at the center of online hate speech definitions.
Specifically, the contributions of this symposium showcase how identity construction online operates in ambivalent ways: On one hand, these mechanisms are central to the marginalization of individuals and groups who are positioned as targets of hateful and exclusionary discourse. On the other hand, the same processes of identity construction also provide spaces in which marginalized voices can articulate resistance and reclaim agency.
The panel thus highlights how digital media function as sites where identity-based exclusion and inclusion are deeply intertwined. Practices that draw symbolic boundaries, assign group membership, and mark difference can simultaneously reproduce hierarchies and enable collective empowerment. By bringing together perspectives on hate, political discourse, and digital activism, the symposium advances a relational understanding of identity dynamics as processes that shape both vulnerability and resilience at the same time. Rather than treating marginalization and empowerment as opposing forces, the panel shows how they emerge from shared communicative and social-psychological mechanisms of identity construction online.
The symposium is particularly relevant to DGPS sections concerned with Media Psychology, Social Psychology, and Political Psychology and comprises several student research papers developed as part of undergraduate media psychology courses at Touro Berlin.

Defining Hate Speech: Identity, Power, and Institutional Authority
no diploma Dominique Esther Rybak
Show details
Authors:
no diploma Dominique Esther Rybak
Maxim Vayman
Sajed Ali Chalhoub
Prof. Dr. Özen Odag | Touro University Berlin | Germany

This paper examines how definitions of hate speech shape the protection and regulation of social identities within digital communication. Drawing on a systematic literature review of legal, psychological, and linguistic approaches to hate speech published between 1992 and 2025, the study investigates how disciplinary frameworks embed assumptions about harm, responsibility, and power. Using theoretical perspectives from Michel Foucault and Steven Lukes, the analysis demonstrates that definitions of hate speech are not neutral but reflect institutional authority, speaker status, and the perceived legitimacy of targeted identities.
Legal definitions tend to prioritize enforceability and intent, often recognizing harm only once it reaches a threshold of incitement or violence. Psychological approaches, by contrast, emphasize the cumulative emotional and identity-related harm experienced by targets, while linguistic and discursive perspectives highlight how everyday language reproduces structural power and exclusion. Across these frameworks, identity emerges as a central site where power is exercised: determining whose experiences count as harm, whose speech is regulated, and which groups receive protection.
The paper argues that current definitional divides obscure the lived identity impacts of hate speech on marginalized users and contribute to gaps between regulation and research. It concludes by calling for interdisciplinary models that better integrate institutional power, discourse, and identity-based harm.

Effects of Subtle and Blatant Antisemitic and Islamophobic Hate on Ingroup and Outgroup Members
Prof. Dr. Özen Odag | Touro University Berlin | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Özen Odag | Touro University Berlin | Germany

This experimental study investigates how different forms of online hate (subtle versus blatant) affect individuals depending on their group identity. Two between-subjects experiments examined the effects of exposure to either antisemitic or islamophobic X- (formerly Twitter-) comments, comparing subtle versus blatant hate expressions and responses of ingroup versus outgroup members. Outcome variables included well-being, self-esteem, and response strategies.
As part of experiment one, N = 67 (non)-Muslim participants were exposed to blatant versus subtle forms of Islamophobic messages; as part of experiment two, N = 81 participants were exposed to blatant versus subtle forms of antisemitic messages. The study displayed different hate speech effects for the different identity-groups under study: while Muslim participants were affected especially by subtle forms of hate (in line with hypothesis), Jewish participants were affected more by blatant forms of hate (countering the hypothesis).
The findings highlight how online hate exploits identity-based vulnerabilities and reinforces existing inequalities in digital spaces. By differentiating between subtle and blatant forms of hate speech, the study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how identity and group membership condition psychological harm. The paper discusses implications for coping interventions and the recognition of less visible forms of identity-based hostility.

Social Identity Dynamics in Reddit Discussions of U.S. Immigration: Outgroup Construction across the Political Spectrum
no diploma Ines Gomez Garcia
Show details
Authors:
no diploma Ines Gomez Garcia
Paul Weller
Deon Chikodzi
Prof. Dr. Özen Odag | Touro University Berlin | Germany

This paper explores how political identities are constructed and contested in anonymous online discussions. Using a comparative discourse analysis informed by Social Identity Theory and the Social Identity Model of Deindividuation Effects, the study examines Reddit discussions on U.S. immigration across conservative, liberal, and non-partisan communities across a total of N = 270 Sub-Reddit speech acts (n = 90 per community).
The analysis reveals that identity is performed through value attributions, ingroup solidarity, and outgroup derogation. Conservative and liberal communities construct clear ingroup–outgroup boundaries, while even the non-partisan community reproduces identity distinctions through norms of neutrality and rationality. Across all contexts, immigrants are repeatedly positioned as salient outgroups, with varying degrees of exclusion or conditional inclusion.
These findings demonstrate how platform affordances and community norms amplify identity-based polarization and normalize exclusionary discourse. The study highlights that identity processes are not limited to overtly partisan spaces but are embedded in seemingly neutral environments as well. The paper contributes to understanding how digital media shape political identities and reinforce social boundaries through everyday online interaction.

Digital Activism, Identity Threat, and Community Defense on Instagram
Helin Sharaf Sharaf | Touro University Berlin | Germany
Maria Yanez
Show details
Authors:
Helin Sharaf Sharaf | Touro University Berlin | Germany
Maria Yanez
Özen Odag | Touro University Berlin | Germany

This qualitative study examines how digital activist communities construct identity and solidarity in response to online hate on Instagram. Using inductive thematic analysis of posts, captions, and comment sections from two high-profile activist accounts the study explores how activists and followers negotiate hate speech, collective support, and empowerment.
To allow for comparative analysis of identity-based attacks and community responses, two activists are purposefully selected, representing diverse yet highly contested areas of activism: Schuyler Bailar, a trans rights activist, and Bisan Owda, a Palestinian rights activist reporting from Gaza.
Findings show that both activists engage in identity construction through vulnerability, personal storytelling, and visible self-presentation, transforming individual experiences into collective symbols. Online hate, including identity-based attacks and delegitimization, often triggers community defense, with followers actively countering hostility and reinforcing shared identity through supportive language and symbolic expressions.
Rather than silencing activists, therefore, online conflict frequently strengthens collective identity and efficacy, leading to increased engagement and empowerment. The study highlights Instagram as a key site where identity is co-constructed through interaction, demonstrating how digital spaces can simultaneously expose individuals to harm and enable collective resilience.

Mapping the Hate Speech Landscape in Croatian Social Media
Prof. Larisa Buhin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Larisa Buhin | Germany
Amelén Scheen | Touro University Berlin | Germany

This pilot study aimed to map the landscape of hate speech in Croatian social media and represents the first systematic attempt to examine its presence in Croatian online news discourse. Hate speech was defined as expressions targeting individuals or groups based on protected characteristics (e.g., gender, ethnicity, religion, migration status) containing derogatory, dehumanizing, or threatening content (Council of Europe, 1997). Several researchers (e.g. Obermaier et al., 2023) have linked hate speech with uncivil speech—communication that violates norms of respectful public discourse (such as insults, vulgarity, or name-calling)—but does not target a protected group (Papacharissi, 2004). Following these definitions, we analysed the potential presence of both hate and uncivil speech.
Six highly engaged Instagram news posts from a top-rated news talk show (December 2025–January 2026) were included in the study. An average of 28 comments per post were collected, yielding a sample of 167 comments submitted to qualitative content analysis. Deductive categories included hate speech and uncivil speech; comments coded as hate speech were further categorized by the specific targeted characteristic. Several inductive categories also emerged, including making false claims and accusing the media of lying.
Hate speech appeared in 21% of comments (n = 35), most commonly antisemitic or anti-immigrant expressions. Uncivil discourse was present in 19% of comments (n = 32). Anti-immigrant hate speech was frequently accompanied by accusations of insufficient patriotism, perceived threats to Croatian national values, and allegations of sexual violence. The study highlights how hateful and uncivil outgroup sentiments are frequently intertwined with national identity construction.

Methods as the Backbone of Psychology
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Andreas Frey (Goethe-Universität Frankfurt am Main)
Room: Room C
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Fachgruppensymposium
Duration: 165 Minutes

The development of modern scientific psychology was guided by the adoption and use of existing methods—such as the scientific experiment—and the development of its own methods to measure and analyze data—such as factor analysis. This symposium brings together a group of current studies that underscore the role of psychological methods as the backbone of modern scientific psychology. In addition to presenting current research findings, the contributions will also showcase that without adequate methods, incorrect conclusions can result and thus artifacts can find their way into the literature. With topics such as (A) Theory Specification (Glöckner & Fiedler), (B) Design of Replication Studies (Sengewald, Hoffmann, Twardawski, Gast, Höhs, Kondzic & Pohl), (C) Bayesian Adaptive Testing (Fink), (D) Extreme Response Styles in Extensive Longitudinal Data Collection (Henninger, Menegola, Vanhasbroeck & Tuerlinckx), (E) Missing Data in Multilevel Designs (Grund, Lüdtke, Robitzsch), (F) Psychometric Modeling of Count Data (Doebler, Frick, Demko & Petersen), and (G) Criterion-Referenced Testing (Hartig, Roczen, Fögele & Mehren), the contributions cover a broad range of psychological research methods.

How to Improve Theory Specification in Psychology
Prof. Dr. Andreas Glöckner | (3) University of Cologne
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Andreas Glöckner | (3) University of Cologne

Many theories in psychology are formulated as verbal narratives. However, there are no commonly accepted standards for how such descriptions should be specified. This lack of standardization can lead to inefficiencies in the scientific process: it may be unclear what a theory predicts in a given situation, whether it applies to that situation at all, which statements constitute the theory, or which version of the theory is currently endorsed. This insufficient specification of theories has been described as part of psychology’s “theory crisis.” Various methodological approaches have been proposed to address this problem. In this talk, we focus on Proposition-Based Theory Specification (PBTS), a methodology that adds structure and testability to verbal narrative theories while keeping technical requirements low. We present results from Many Theorists I, a collaborative project aimed at (a) analyzing and (b) specifying classic theories of social psychology using PBTS. Finally, we discuss how systematic theory specification can facilitate more efficient cumulative knowledge development and derive implications for scientific practice and policy.

Causal Inference in Study Comparisons: Recommendations for Conceptual Replication Studies
Prof. Dr. Marie-Ann Sengewald | Friedrich-Alexander-University Erlangen-Nürnberg | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Marie-Ann Sengewald | Friedrich-Alexander-University Erlangen-Nürnberg | Germany
Mathias Twardawski | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München | Germany
Prof. Dr. Anne Gast | University of Cologne | Germany
Dennis Kondzic | Freie Universität Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Steffi Pohl | Freie Universität Berlin | Germany

Current recommendations for achieving close replications of the results of primary studies focus on the equivalence of the material and analysis method. However, other factors, such as the recruitment strategy and characteristics of participants, or the timing and setting of data collection, can unintentionally vary across studies. Instead of treating these sources of effect heterogeneity as mere disturbances, principles of experimentation and causal inference can be applied to replication research to investigate their impact on study results. Accordingly, we extended causal theory to replication research by defining the effects of study characteristics on study results and by introducing a statistical approach to control for possible confounders. In two prospectively planned series of replication studies, we demonstrated how research designs and analytical methods for explaining effect heterogeneity can be implemented in practice. Our presentation synthesizes these theoretical and empirical insights by presenting a toolbox with practical recommendations for designing, analyzing, and interpreting conceptual replication studies from a causal inference perspective. Specifically, we illustrate how to prevent or correct for threats to causal inference in study comparisons, such as variability of treatment and outcome measures, systematic missing data and non-compliance, as well as selection effects related to person or setting characteristics. We conclude with a discussion of the strengths and limitations of our perspective on replication research for explaining effect heterogeneity.

Bayesian Adaptive Testing as a Flexible Framework for Psychological and Educational Measurement
Dr. Aron Fink | Goethe University Frankfurt | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Aron Fink | Goethe University Frankfurt | Germany

Bayesian adaptive testing (BAT) provides a modern and highly flexible approach to psychological and educational measurement by integrating adaptive item selection and ability estimation within a unified probabilistic framework. In contrast to traditional computerized adaptive testing, which typically treats item parameters derived from calibration studies as fixed values during the operational testing phase, BAT explicitly accounts for the fact that these parameters are only estimates containing calibration error. By treating item and person parameters as random variables rather than fixed values, BAT propagates parameter uncertainty throughout the testing process. This can lead to more accurate ability estimates and more realistic standard errors than conventional CAT approaches. In this talk, I will provide an overview of recent developments in Bayesian adaptive testing that demonstrates why it represents a powerful methodological alternative to traditional computerized and multistage testing. I illustrate how BAT naturally accommodates a wide range of assessment scenarios, including multidimensional ability structures, complex response formats such as the answer-until-correct format, and highly constrained automated test assembly. The Bayesian framework further enables the integration of prior information derived from background variables into the assessment process. To demonstrate the versatility of BAT, I further will present results from a simulation study based on PISA data, showing how BAT can be embedded in large-scale assessments to improve assessment design and measurement precision. Overall, the talk highlights BAT as a methodological backbone for future assessment systems.

Affect dynamics or response bias? Extreme response styles in laboratory and daily-life assessments
Prof. Dr. Mirka Henninger | Institute of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Mirka Henninger | Institute of Psychology, University of Basel | Switzerland

Intensive longitudinal data (ILD), such as experience sampling method (ESM) studies, are widely used to investigate affect dynamics, including intraindividual variability and temporal dependencies (inertia). These parameters are often interpreted as meaningful individual differences. However, because ILD primarily rely on self-report ratings, they may be systematically biased by stable response style tendencies, particularly extreme response style (ERS). In the present research, we examined the association between ERS and affect dynamics through data collected from a controlled, laboratory experiment (N = 1,389) and multiple daily-life ESM (total N = 1,254). Across datasets and methodological approaches, higher ERS was consistently associated with greater intraindividual affect variability, operationalized by the within-person standard deviation. In contrast, ERS was not related to moment-to-moment temporal dependencies (affective inertia). These findings suggest that commonly used indicators of affective variability may partly reflect systematic response behavior rather than exclusively genuine affective fluctuations. Overall, our results underscore the importance of accounting for response styles when modeling and interpreting affect dynamics in ILD research. Ignoring ERS may lead to biased estimates of variability parameters with important implications for psychological assessment and theory development.

Handling missing data in multilevel designs using single-level models: A flexible multiple imputation approach with adjusted group means
Prof. Dr. Simon Grund | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Simon Grund | Germany
Oliver Lüdtke
Dr. Alexander Robitzsch | Germany

Missing data are a common challenge in multilevel analyses, and past research has shown that multiple imputation (MI) can be extremely effective at handling them. However, an important requirement of multilevel MI is that the imputation model must adequately take the multilevel structure into account. This is particularly important in multilevel analyses that involve random slopes or interactions, and many specialized methods have been developed for these applications. However, multilevel MI can be difficult to apply in practice, where the number of variables with missing data is often large, and the multilevel structure is often not very pronounced or not of immediate interest. In these situations, existing methods for multilevel MI can become unstable and often struggle to provide accurate results. In this talk, we present a novel and flexible approach to multilevel MI that combines single-level imputation methods with group means (GM) or adjusted group means (AGM) to accommodate the multilevel structure. We then present the results from different simulation studies, in which we evaluated the performance of these methods in different scenarios, including applications with balanced designs, unbalanced designs, and large numbers of variables. In addition, we also provide a more general discussion of the strengths and weaknesses of flexible approaches to MI when compared with more specialized methods for handling missing data, and we discuss the potential role of these methods in psychological research.

Modelling Behavior Counts with Unsupervised Machine Learning Techniques and Flexible Bayesian Latent Variables Models
Prof. Dr. Philipp Doebler | TU Dortmund University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Philipp Doebler | TU Dortmund University | Germany
Dr. Susanne Frick | TU Dortmund University | Germany

Counts of behaviors are natural indicators in many psychological fields, ranging from the
number of ideas to a prompt in creativity research to reading errors in educational
psychology and externalizing behavior counts in developmental or clinical psychology. In
assessment, traditionally, counts have often been disregarded in favor of coarser
categories, like "never", "once a week", "several times a week", and "daily or more". Using a
coarse response scale or binning original counts comes at the price of losing information, a
notion we make precise mathematically. Models have to reflect phenomena inherent in
count data: Observed count variables, e.g. for substance use, have excess zeroes and are
often highly skewed, questioning homoscedastic Gaussian residuals and linear
relationships of underlying latent variables and observations. Flexible models are needed
for the exploration of counts and subsequent confirmatory latent variable modeling in the
style of (explanatory) item response theory models. This contribution showcases recent
developments in the field of count data models: Manifold learning models, a class of
exploratory unsupervised machine learning methods, can represent multivariate count
data in low-dimensional latent spaces without strong assumptions. Complementarily,
confirmatory parametric models are prefered for statistical inference and modelling: In a
Bayesian framework we demonstrate the usefulness of count distributions for excess
zeroes and splines for covariate effects. Bayesian models enable a rigorous psychometric
approach, including methodology for test fairness like differential item functioning. An
exemplary application to a broad assessment of externalizing behavior indicates the
potential utility of the methodology.

Criterion-referenced testing (CRT) is integral for psychological assessment, determining whether individuals have reached a predetermined standard in a construct to be measured. In achievement testing, CRT focuses on mastery of specific contents, making it particularly valuable e.g. for system monitoring, adapting instruction, and aptitude testing. An indispensable method for the implementation of CRT is the comparison of individuals and items on a joint scale by means of item response theory (IRT). Various specific methods for IRT-based standard setting in educational testing make use of estimated item parameters and test-takers ability distributions. The presentation demonstrates the application of CRT for standard setting with data from a test for system competence in the context of education for sustainable development (ESD). The test comprises six tasks on various topics (e.g., fashion consumption and overtourism) with 11 to 12 items each. Theory-based item characteristics affecting the assumed demands of the items (e.g. system complexity) were manipulated in item construction. A sample of 1098 students from 14 schools responded to the test, each working on three of the six tasks. Item difficulties from a partial credit model show a good alignment to the ability distribution. More importantly, item difficulties can be predicted by the manipulated item characteristics. Using predicted difficulties for typical configurations of items, thresholds between proficiency levels can be defined to describe the ability scale with reference to the underlying competence model. The study thus illustrates how IRT-based CRT can provide insights into individual abilities, supporting both research and practice in psychological assessment.

Was ist der Kern der Psychologie? Eine Disziplin im Spannungsfeld zwischen Vielfalt und Einheit
Chair(s) Dr. Matthias F.J. Sperl (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Psychologie (DGPs))
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Mario Gollwitzer

Luisa Baumgärtner (Leipzig University)
Dr. Dr. Alexander Nicolai Wendt
Prof. Dr. Silvia Schneider (Ruhr-Universität Bochum)
Room: Workshop 0
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Panel discussion
Duration: 60 Minutes

Was ist der Kern der Psychologie? Diese scheinbar einfache Frage verweist auf grundlegende Spannungen und Potenziale unseres Fachs. Psychologie bewegt sich traditionell zwischen Natur- und Geisteswissenschaften, zwischen Erklärung und Anwendung, zwischen individueller Erfahrung und gesellschaftlicher Einbettung. Gerade diese Vielschichtigkeit macht ihre Stärke aus – wirft jedoch zugleich die Frage nach einem gemeinsamen Kern auf. Im Rahmen des DGPs-Jungmitgliederprojekts „Was ist Psychologie – wirklich?“ bringt diese Paneldiskussion Vertreter:innen unterschiedlicher Teildisziplinen zusammen, um diese Leitfrage aus verschiedenen Perspektiven zu diskutieren: Welche verbindenden Elemente über methodische, theoretische und anwendungsbezogene Unterschiede hinweg gibt es in der Psychologie und welche Differenzen existieren? Gemeinsam mit dem Publikum soll erörtert werden, was Psychologie im Innersten zusammenhält, wie wir als Psycholog:innen die Vielfalt des Faches produktiv nutzen und die Einheit fördern können. Wir laden dazu ein, den Kern der Psychologie nicht als statische Definition, sondern als dynamischen Aushandlungsprozess zu verstehen und diesen gemeinsam weiterzudenken. Psychologie erklärt nicht nur menschliches Erleben und Verhalten, sondern versucht auch, individuelle und gesellschaftliche Handlungsspielräume zu erweitern. In Zeiten diverser Herausforderungen und Krisen kann diese Diskussion damit nicht nur fach- sondern auch gesellschaftspolitische Diskurse informieren und dazu beitragen, unser Fach zukunftsfähig aufzustellen.

(Epi)genomic analyses in mental health and related phenotypes
Chair(s) Dr. Leonard Frach (Institut für Humangenetik, Universitätsklinikum Bonn)
Room: UK
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Mental health and human behaviour are influenced by a complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors. Genetic variation can influence mental health phenotypes through diverse biological mechanisms, including alterations in brain structure or function, epigenetic regulation (e.g., DNA methylation) or gene expression. Importantly, these biological processes have also been shown to be responsive to environmental factors, e.g., (early) life stressors, and may reflect consequences of already developed psychopathology. In this symposium, we present a wide range of research examining the role of (epi)genomics in mental health and related phenotypes. The presentations span genome-wide association studies of borderline personality disorder and functional brain measures, integrative analyses combining genetics, brain structure and negative affect, stress-related epigenetic changes over development and their associations with depression, and multi-omic frameworks that jointly analyse genomic, epigenetic and gene expression data to study somatic comorbidities in individuals with psychiatric disorders. Collectively, the talks provide an overview of genomic approaches to understanding pathways to mental health or disorders, and highlight the biological complexity underlying their aetiology.

Oscillations in neuronal brain activity are fundamental to information processing and have been widely studied as biological markers of human behavior and psychopathology. About a century ago, in 1924, Hans Berger’s discovery of the human EEG marked the inception of a transformative era in neuroscience, leading to crucial advancements in our understanding of brain function and behavioral phenomena. Although research has demonstrated that brain oscillations are highly heritable, our understanding of their molecular genetic architecture is still very limited. Here, we report findings from the largest genome-wide association study (GWAS) of resting-state EEG oscillations to date, combining data from eight cohorts with up to 14,361 participants. We analyzed power in the alpha, beta, delta, theta, and broadband frequency bands at the vertex, as well as alpha power and peak frequency at occipital sites. We observed substantial and highly significant genetic contributions, with SNP-based heritability estimates ranging from 14% to 27% (SE: 3.7%). We discover two genome-wide significant loci: an intergenic region at 13q12.3 (p=6.6e-09), and a known schizophrenia risk locus in FANCA at 16q24.3 (p=1.4E-08), both associated with alpha peak frequency. We identify 32 additional loci by leveraging pleiotropy with psychiatric traits such as schizophrenia and major depression. Using genetic correlations and polygenic score analysis in up to 340,000 UK Biobank individuals we demonstrate widespread associations, including MRI-based phenotypes, psychological traits, neurological disorders, cognitive performance, and socioeconomic variables. In sum, we here corroborate previous findings on the heritability of brain oscillations and provide novel biological insights into the links between brain structure, brain function, and behavior.

Psychosocial stress is a risk factor for aging-related diseases. We observed significant increases in epigenetic age acceleration (PedBE: b = 0.17, p < 0.0001; GrimAge2: b = 0.08, p < 0.0001) and pace of aging (DunedinPACE: b = 0.13, p < 0.0001) across all age groups. Measures related to physical health and parental socioeconomic status but not objective pandemic stressors, were significantly associated with this change. In adolescents, the pace of aging increased with perceived burden (DunedinPACE: b = 0.04, p = 0.01). Together, these findings suggest biological embedding of a societal crisis though multifactorial processes, with adolescence representing a sensitive phase to its psychological burden. Environmental adversity is linked to major depressive disorder (MDD), potentially via sustained low-grade inflammation. However, serum markers such as CRP are highly variable and sensitive to transient states. In contrast, epigenetic signatures of inflammation may provide a more stable trace of how stress becomes biologically embedded and contributes to depression risk over time. In a subsample of the Marburg-Münster Affective Disorders Cohort Study (MACS; N=579; 320 healthy controls, 259 with MDD), we examined whether early adversity (CTQ) and recent stress (LEQ) are associated with CRP-related DNA methylation (CRPm) at baseline. We further tested whether CRPm predicts depressive symptom severity at baseline and at two-year follow-up (n=407). DNA was extracted from whole blood, and CRPm scores were computed using publicly available genome-wide summary statistics. CRPm explained 21.3% of the variance in serum high-sensitivity CRP (hsCRP). CRPm was significantly associated with early adversity (b=0.01, SE=0.003, p=0.017) and recent stress (b=0.01, SE=0.004, p=0.032), after adjusting for age and sex. CRPm predicted depressive symptom severity at baseline (b=0.68, SE=0.27, p=0.013) and at follow-up (b=0.79, SE=0.25, p=0.002). These associations remained after controlling for white blood cell-type composition but were attenuated after adjusting for BMI and smoking. In contrast, hsCRP was not associated with adversity or depressive symptoms. Our findings indicate that a methylation-based index of chronic inflammation is shaped by psychosocial stress through health-related behaviors and predicts depressive symptoms over time. These results support inflammation as a biological pathway linking stress exposure to depression, while underscoring the central role of health-related behaviors in this pathway.

Individuals with affective disorders and schizophrenia often have co-occurring somatic conditions such as cardiovascular or cardiometabolic diseases. While somatic conditions can sometimes be associated with psychopharmaceutic treatment, they are also observed independent of medication use. Whereas some evidence exists supporting genetic overlap between psychiatric and somatic conditions, less is known about shared biological pathways involving other omics layers like DNA methylation (DNAm) and RNA expression. Here we propose a multi omics approach combining genomic, epigenetic and transcriptomic data to predict somatic comorbidities in patients with major psychiatric disorders and control subjects. We use phenotype and omics data from patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), bipolar disorder (BD) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD), as well as from individuals without psychiatric conditions. Data is taken from the FOR2107, funded by the Collaborative Research Centre 393 (TRR393) as part of the German Mental Health Cohort (GEMCO), consisting of up to 827 individuals in total (NMDD = 310, NBD = 87, NSSD = 92, NCON = 308). We examine genomic data using polygenic risk scores (PRS) for cardiovascular disease (CVD) and type-II diabetes (T2D), as well as epigenome-wide DNAm and RNA sequencing data from blood samples. The analytical approach is split into i) an unsupervised learning approach, predicting somatic comorbidities by PRS, DNAm at individual CpG sites and RNA expression, and ii) a risk-score approach combining PRS with methylation scores and RNA expression scores. Detailed results will be presented at the conference. We expect to identify a set of omics measures (including PRS, CpGs and transcripts) that predict somatic comorbidities in patients with psychiatric disorders. Furthermore, we anticipate associations between multiple omics risk scores and somatic conditions in both psychiatric patients and control subjects. Our results will shed light on the biological mechanisms involved in psychiatric and somatic comorbidities, which may serve as biomarkers or treatment candidates in the future. As part of the TRR393, we will further analyse DNAm and RNA expression longitudinally in the GEMCO study to detect biological changes of major psychiatric disorders over time.

Why do People Support a Universal Basic Income? The role of Job Demands, General Health, and Social Preferences
Gina Kriesmann | Freie Universitaet Berlin | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Gina Kriesmann | Freie Universitaet Berlin | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stefan Krumm | Freie Universitaet Berlin
Prof. Dr. Joachim Hüffmeier | Technische Universitaet Dortmund

As debates about Universal Basic Income (UBI) increasingly shape welfare state discussions, understanding the factors that drive support for such policies has become a central research concern. This study explores the influence of job demands, general health, and social preferences on support for UBI. Specifically, we hypothesize – based on the Person–Environment Fit Theory (Van Vianen, 2018), the Conservation of Resources Theory (Hobfoll, 1989), the Job Demands–Resources Model (Bakker & Demerouti, 2007), and Schwartz's Value Theory (Schwartz, 1992) - that individuals exposed to higher job demands show greater UBI support, reflecting a response to a perceived mismatch between work demands and resources. In contrast, better general health should be associated with lower support due to reduced need for economic protection. Moreover, general health is expected to mediate the relationship between job demands and UBI support, consistent with the health impairment process (Bakker & Demerouti, 2007). Beyond these mechanisms, universalism (at the individual level) and altruism (at the country level) are expected to increase UBI support and to moderate the association between health and UBI support by fostering a climate supportive of redistribution. To test these propositions, cross-sectional data from Round 8 of the European Social Survey (European Social Survey European Research Infrastructure, 2023), the Global Preferences Survey (Falk et al., 2018) and Job Exposure Matrices by Kroll (2015) are used. Hierarchical linear modeling is utilized to assess the hypothesized relationships. Results will be presented and contribute to a better understanding of the individual- and country-level antecedents of UBI support.

Presentation Matters: Aggregated Advice in Decision Tasks
Julia L. Bengelsdorf | University of Göttingen  | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Julia L. Bengelsdorf | University of Göttingen  | Germany
Dr. Christian Treffenstädt | University of Göttingen 
Prof. Dr. Stefan Schulz-Hardt | University of Göttingen 

Advice from others is a central resource in judgment and decision making. Research using judge-advisor systems (JAS) has repeatedly shown that, for quantitative judgment tasks, advice from multiple advisors is heeded more strongly when presented in aggregated form (e.g., an average) rather than as a set of individual opinions. However, it remains unclear whether this effect generalizes to decision-making tasks with discrete choice alternatives, and whether aggregated advice from multiple advisors is followed more than advice from a single advisor.

The present experiment addresses these gaps by comparing advice taking across three JAS conditions in a series of single-choice trivia decisions: (a) aggregated advice from multiple advisors (modal response), (b) non-aggregated advice from the same number of advisors (list of responses), and (c) single advice from one advisor.

Results provide strong Bayesian evidence that aggregated advice was used more than non-aggregated advice (BF₁₀ = 12.02, d = 0.40) and more than single advice (BF₁₀ = 8.78, d = 0.38). In contrast, advice taking did not differ between non-aggregated multiple-advisor advice and single-advisor advice (BF₁₀ = 0.14, d ≈ 0).

These findings demonstrate that the aggregation advantage previously observed for quantitative judgments extends to decision-making tasks. Moreover, they suggest that the increased influence of aggregated advice depends on how multiple opinions are presented rather than on the mere presence of multiple advisors. The results show that how advice is presented shapes decision making, emphasizing the practical relevance of advice presentation in applied contexts.

People automatically imitate a wide range of different behaviors. One of the most commonly used measurement methods to assess imitative behavior is the imitation-inhibition task (Brass et al., 2000), which has been initially validated for laboratory settings and recently also for online settings (Westfal, 2025). However, existing imitation-inhibition tasks work only on computer devices. This limits the range of possible research questions. To deal with this issue, we developed a version of the task that works for mobile devices (phones, tablets, etc.) and validated it in two studies. Study 1 (N = 26) demonstrates its effectiveness by finding the typical imitation-inhibition effects (i.e., congruency, facilitation, interference). Each participant did 60 trials, overall amounting to 1560 trials. Study 2 (N = 201) compared the mobile version with the online version for computers and found similarly strong and reliable effects as the online version. Each participant did 150 trials, overall amounting to 22,500 trials. The mobile version of the imitation-inhibition task widens the applicability and accessibility for socio-cognitive research. For example, with the validated version we developed, experience sampling studies are now possible which allows measuring social-cognitive processes in people’s everyday life.

Kognitive und Emotionale Verzerrungen bei Anlageentscheidungen: Entwicklung und Validierung einer deutschsprachigen Skala

Authors:

Die Anzahl der Privatanleger:innen in Deutschland steigt. Privatanleger:innen sind mit einem komplexen, sich stetig wandelnden Finanzmarkt konfrontiert. Sie müssen aus verschiedenen Optionen wählen und Entscheidungen unter Unsicherheit treffen. Die Behavioral Finance beschreibt, dass hierbei kognitive und emotionale Verzerrungen auftreten, die irrationale Anlageentscheidungen begünstigen. Mögliche Folgen sind eine veränderte Risikowahrnehmung, eine schlechtere Portfolioperformance und eine Destabilisierung des Finanzmarktes. Trotz der hohen praktischen Relevanz existiert bislang weder eine einheitliche noch eine deutschsprachige Skala zur Erfassung von Verzerrungen bei Anlageentscheidungen. Im Rahmen eines ausführlichen Literaturreviews wurden Verzerrungen identifiziert, die in internationalen Studien negative Auswirkungen auf Anlageentscheidungen zeigten. Darüber hinaus wurden Verzerrungen erfasst, die bei deutschen Privatanleger:innen im Kontext von Anlageentscheidungen auftreten. Diese wurden in emotionale und kognitive Verzerrungen klassifiziert. Jede Verzerrung wird als eigenständiges Konstrukt konzeptualisiert. Zur Itementwicklung wurden bestehende Items internationaler Skalen adaptiert. Zudem wurden neue Items ergänzt, die auf theoretischen Definitionen basieren oder von ChatGPT generiert wurden. Anschließend erfolgen ein Expertenreview (N = 15), ein Pretest (N = 15) und eine vollumfängliche empirische Datenerhebung (N = 500) mit dem Ziel, Item- und Faktorenanalysen sowie Reliabilitäts- und Validitätsprüfungen durchzuführen. Im September 2026 werden die finalisierte Skala zur Messung von Verzerrungen bei Anlageentscheidungen sowie die Ergebnisse der Validierungsstudie vorgestellt. Die Skala kann in der Finanzberatung eingesetzt werden, um individuelle Verzerrungsmuster zu identifizieren und Beratungsprozesse gezielter zu gestalten. Darüber hinaus kann sie eine Grundlage für die Entwicklung und Evaluation von Interventionen zur Reduktion kognitiver Verzerrungen bilden. Weitere Anwendungsfelder liegen in der Finanzbildung, der Forschung zu Anlegerverhalten sowie in der Produktentwicklung im Finanzdienstleistungssektor.

Social Factors During Real-Life Decision Making: Leveraging Ecological Momentary Assessments and Large Language Models
Aaron Lob | University of Zurich, Switzerland | Switzerland
Show details
Authors:
Aaron Lob | University of Zurich, Switzerland | Switzerland
Prof. Dr. Renato Frey | University of Zurich, Switzerland | Switzerland

Many theories assume that specific social factors (e.g., social norms, accountability) shape people's decisions. This may be particularly true in real-life situations in which people are constantly exposed to others' options and behaviors, yet virtually all empirical studies in the behavioral sciences have investigated decision making in laboratory settings. Consequently, little is known about the actual occurrence of social factors during real-life decision making and how these should ideally be assessed. To answer these questions, we ran a study (N = 176) using ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) in which we asked participants to report choices they made over the course of seven days (resulting in a total of 2,605 collected real-life decisions). During each situation, participants recorded verbal decision protocols (VDPs; i.e., verbalizations of one's thoughts recorded during decision making) and answered a number of questions regarding the occurrence of seven social factors. Results showed that all seven social factors were prevalent during most decisions and varied substantially across these situations. Moreover, large language models (LLMs) were able to automatically infer the social factors during decision making from the VDPs, with median correlations between participants' and model-predicted ratings of r = .45. Importantly, this automatic assessment outperformed time-consuming assessments involving human raters. These findings highlight the relevance of studying previously neglected real-life decisions and the social factors that may shape them. Moreover, they demonstrate how the combination of EMAs and LLMs constitutes a novel and efficient tool to gain insights into decision making specifically, and real-life behavioral phenomena in general.

Language as a Foundation for Mathematical Learning in Multilingual Contexts
Chair(s) Dr. Carrie Georges (University of Luxembourg)
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Christine Schiltz
Room: GR
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

This symposium brings together complementary perspectives on how language experience, linguistic structure, and cognitive dynamics jointly shape numerical and mathematical learning in multilingual contexts from early childhood through adulthood.

First, a person-centered analysis identifies distinct bilingual profiles in primary school that differ in exposure, proficiency, and language switching, and display differential patterns in executive functions as well as mathematics and reading performance, underscoring the multidimensional nature of bilingualism.

Next, research on home exposure to the instruction language shows that spatial language fully mediates the association between exposure at home and counting in kindergarten, indicating that lower numeracy among children with limited exposure reflects reduced access to relevant linguistic resources rather than inherent numerical deficits.

Extending this to third grade, large-scale data demonstrate that mathematical and general language comprehension in the language of instruction significantly predict numerical performance beyond home language profile. Performance gaps between first- and second-language learners are largely mediated by language comprehension, highlighting the central role of instruction language proficiency in numerical skills.

Shifting from language experience to language structure, cross-linguistic comparisons reveal that lower transparency in verbal number systems is associated with stronger number-size effects in base-ten tasks, suggesting that lexical irregularity beyond conceptual understanding contributes to differences in numerical processing.

Finally, experimental evidence shows that switching languages during mathematical learning reduces performance on newly acquired content but attenuates later switching costs, indicating both consolidation challenges and increased linguistic flexibility.

Together, these studies emphasize interacting experiential, linguistic, and cognitive influences on mathematics learning in multilingual education.
