Research on bilingual advantages in executive functions (EF) has yielded mixed findings, moving the field beyond a simple mono- vs. bilingual comparison toward more nuanced characterizations of bilingual experience. Prior work has typically emphasized single mechanisms (e.g., balanced proficiency, exposure, switching), whereas person-centered approaches integrating multiple characteristics to identify bilingual subgroups remain rare. To date, only one study has applied latent profile analysis (LPA), focusing on preschoolers and excluding literacy-related variables. We extend this approach to primary school students and examine whether distinct bilingual profiles differ not only in EF but also in academic achievement, given concerns that reduced proficiency in the language of instruction may hinder school outcomes, potentially offset by EF. Participants were 105 second- and third-grade students in German primary schools regularly exposed to German and another language. Parents reported language history, proficiency and current usage; children completed direct assessments of EF, German vocabulary and grammar, mathematics, and German reading at T1, with reading and mathematics reassessed four months later (T2). LPA identified three profiles: (1) low language proficiency (13%), characterized by later German exposure and lower skills in both languages; (2) German-dominant (41%), with early balanced exposure but German dominance before school entry; and (3) rather balanced bilingual (46%), with higher non-German proficiency and frequent switching. Profiles significantly differed in EF and academic performance: German-dominant children showed stronger working memory and mathematics skills, whereas rather balanced bilinguals showed advantages in set shifting and German reading. Ongoing analyses examine whether EF differentially predicts academic outcomes across profiles.

Spatial Language as a Key Link Between Exposure to the Instruction Language at Home and Early Numeracy
Carrie Georges
Show details
Authors:
Carrie Georges
Eylül Turan
Caroline Hornung
Sonja Ugen
Christine Schiltz

Children with limited exposure to the instruction language at home often show not only weaker proficiency in that language, but also lower mathematical performance. This study examined whether general and spatial language skills in the language of instruction explain the association between exposure to the instruction language at home and counting. Considering that broad language abilities scaffold more specialized linguistic knowledge, we tested parallel and serial mediation models linking exposure to the instruction language at home to counting.
Kindergarten children (n=107) were grouped according to whether they spoke Luxembourgish, the language of instruction, with at least one parent. Regression analyses indicated that exposure to the instruction language at home initially predicted counting, but this effect disappeared after including spatial language skills. Listening comprehension in Luxembourgish did not uniquely predict counting beyond spatial language. Mediation analyses showed that the link between exposure to the instruction language at home and counting was fully mediated by language-related mechanisms, with spatial language emerging as a robust mediator. A serial pathway via Luxembourgish listening comprehension and spatial language appeared when controlling for SES only, but not after accounting for spatial skills, suggesting shared variance between the latter and listening comprehension. No moderation effects were found.
Overall, spatial language appears to be a proximal mechanism linking exposure to the instruction language at home to numeracy, indicating that lower counting skills among children with limited exposure to the instruction language at home reflect reduced access to relevant linguistic resources rather than inherent differences in numerical ability.

The Impact of Test Language Skills on Numerical Performance in Linguistically Diverse Third Graders
Vera Hilger
Show details
Authors:
Vera Hilger
Sonja Ugen
Linda Romanovska
Katharina A. M. Tremmel
Christine Schiltz

Research has consistently shown a close connection between language and mathematics, with language abilities serving as key predictors of mathematical achievement throughout development. Recent studies have also emphasized the central role of content specific, mathematical language. This is particularly relevant in multilingual environments, such as Luxembourg, where most elementary-school students do not speak the language of mathematics instruction at home (German or Luxembourgish), which has been associated with lower academic outcomes. The present study investigated how test language relates to numerical performance in linguistically diverse children, while accounting for their socioeconomic background. We assessed mathematical and general language comprehension in the language of instruction using self-developed measures. Numerical performance was assessed through five tasks: number writing, number naming, ordinal judgement, number comparison and place-value identification. We analyzed data of 551 third-grade children in Luxembourg, whereof 57.50% did not speak the language of instruction at home. Among these second-language learners, 31% spoke French, 30% Portuguese and 39% other languages. Regression analyses revealed that both mathematical and general test language comprehension significantly predicted numerical performance, beyond the effects of home language profile and socioeconomic status. Moreover, children speaking French or Portuguese at home showed significantly lower performances compared to first-language learners. A mediation analysis indicated that these gaps were significantly explained by mathematical and general language comprehension. Our findings underscore the importance of test language proficiency in third-graders’ numerical performance. Fostering general and mathematical language skills may potentially enhance mathematics achievement and reduce gaps between linguistically diverse children in multilingual education contexts.

Verbal Number System Transparency Reduces Number Size Effects in Base-Ten Tasks
Cloé Geuquet
Show details
Authors:
Cloé Geuquet
Nicolas Masson
Bert De Smedt
Mai-Liên Lê
Marie-Pascale Noël

Languages vary according to the degree of transparency to base-ten of their verbal number systems. In many Asian languages, verbal numbers express explicitly their decimal structure (e.g., “78” expressed as “seven-ten-eight”) whereas most Western languages exhibit varying degrees of opacity either through specific lexicons for teens and decades (e.g., “twelve”, “twenty”) or through decade-units order (e.g., “78” expressed as “eight and seventy” in Dutch). It is still debated whether transparency influences the development of base-ten comprehension which has been considered as a function of the powers of ten defining the number, starting with two-digit numbers, followed by three-digit numbers, etc. However, the observation of size effects within two-digit numbers in preschool children challenged this assumption.
Here, we addressed the language transparency debate and investigated whether number size effects are modulated by the transparency of the verbal number system. We tested Vietnamese, Dutch- and French-speaking first graders on a large spectrum of base-ten tasks, controlling for general cognitive ability, arithmetic level, home numeracy and socio-economic status.
Our results revealed that larger numbers led to more errors and less use of elaborate strategies. Crucially, children speaking opaque languages exhibited a stronger size effect than in the Vietnamese group, in which this effect was reduced or even absent.
The modulation of the size effect by language transparency suggests that the irregularity and lexical complexity of opaque languages hinder performance, pointing to a lexical rather than purely conceptual origin of the observed differences.

Language-Dependency in Cumulative Mathematical Learning
Moritz Wußing
Show details
Authors:
Moritz Wußing
Roland H. Grabner
Kevin Baumschlager
Bert De Smedt
Lennart Schalk
Henrik Saalbach

In multilingual education, learners frequently face situations in which knowledge must be accessed in a language different from the one in which it was encoded. Such language switches are reliably associated with additional cognitive costs (“language-switching costs”; Grabner et al., 2012). Theoretically, these costs are based on encoding-specificity accounts (Tulving & Thompson, 1973), emphasizing that knowledge is encoded in a context-sensitive way. Since language is a crucial contextual factor, learning likely yields language-dependent knowledge representations, making retrieval from an incongruent linguistic context more effortful. To date, such language-switching costs have been studied as a linguistic incongruency between language of learning and language of testing. Much less is known about language-switching within ongoing learning processes: what happens when learners must build on prior knowledge that was encoded in another language?
In a preregistered study with 180 university students, participants learned mathematical concepts across two consecutive sessions either entirely in German (L1), entirely in English (L2), or with a language switch between sessions (German→English; English→German). After learning, participants completed two tests: one on content of the second session (subsequent learning) and one on the first session (initial learning). Within each test, there were non-switch items (same language as the corresponding learning-session) and switch items (incongruent language).
Switching languages during learning reduced performance (accuracy) on subsequent-learning content (η_p^2=0.122***) but also attenuated within-test switching costs (η_p^2=0.033**). Notably, analogous patterns emerged for initial-learning content, indicating a retroactive influence of within-learning switching on consolidation (η_p^2=0.026*) and linguistic flexibilization (η_p^2=0.021*) of prior knowledge.

Synergy in Small Group Performance: How Integrative Complexity Enables Groups to Outperform Individuals in a Problem-Solving Task
Christina M. Brunner | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU) München | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Christina M. Brunner | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU) München | Germany
Michael E. Rauch | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU) München | Germany
PD Dr. Katharina G. Kugler | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU) München | Germany
Prof. Dr. Felix C. Brodbeck | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU) München

Although teamwork is highly prevalent in organizations, interacting groups often perform worse than their members would if they worked independently. So, how should groups interact to outperform mean individual group members (weak synergy) or even the best individual group member (strong synergy)? In this study, we focused on group integrative complexity (i.e., the degree to which group members differentiate and integrate different solution strategies) as a possible driver for weak and strong synergy in group performance.
In a 2×2 laboratory experiment, 72 interacting groups of three people and 72 individuals worked on a problem-solving task (letters-to-numbers task). We manipulated high levels of integrative complexity via instructions and a discussion structure (vs. a control condition without instructions/structure). As measures for weak and strong synergy, we compared the performance of interacting groups with the mean and best-member performance of three individuals randomly assigned to non-interacting groups (i.e., nominal groups).
Supporting our hypotheses, we found that interacting groups on average achieved weak synergy, but only achieved strong synergy at high levels of integrative complexity. Mediation analyses revealed a significant indirect effect of the integrative complexity manipulation on weak and strong synergy via observed integrative complexity of the group discussion. Exploratory analyses indicated that the positive effects of integrative complexity on weak and strong synergy are further mediated by the use of more complex (i.e., entropy-reducing) solution strategies.
This study thus contributes to a better understanding of the conditions and structure of group interaction that enable groups, on average, to outperform independent individuals.

Giving Non-Human Stakeholders a Seat at the Table: Forum Theatre as an Intervention to Counter Anthropocentric Managerial Decision-Making
Emily Waltermann | WHU - Otto Beisheim School of Management | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Emily Waltermann | WHU - Otto Beisheim School of Management | Germany
Jun.-Prof. Dr. Anna-Karina Schmitz | WHU - Otto Beisheim School of Management

Most managerial decision-making is informed by anthropocentric logics that systematically prioritize human prosperity while considering nature insofar as it serves organizational interests. Consequently, non-human stakeholders like ecosystems, animals, and living organisms are rarely treated as entities with intrinsic value that merit protection in their own right. Instead, they are framed as resources, risks, or constraints for decision-makers. Such anthropocentric orientations restrict which stakeholders managers recognize as relevant in decision-making.
Our paper proposes forum theatre as an experiential intervention that counters managerial anthropocentrism by expanding who is recognized as a stakeholder. Grounded in Augusto Boal’s Theatre of the Oppressed, forum theatre stages organizational decisions and invites participants to intervene, assume roles, and experiment with alternative courses of action. By explicitly embodying organizations’ non-human stakeholders, this performative setting enables managers to enact decision-making scenarios in which non-human stakeholders are treated as visible equals. Thereby, forum theatre allows engaging in considerations that acknowledge the intrinsic value of nature beyond human utility. We further propose that giving non-human stakeholders a voice in decision-making processes activates managers’ biospheric values, i.e., concern for the protection of nature independent of instrumental benefits, thereby reducing anthropocentrism.
In the next steps, we will empirically test our propositions to answer our guiding research questions: (1) What is the influence of simulating non-human stakeholder integration through forum theatre on managerial anthropocentrism? (2) How does biospheric value activation mediate this influence? We contribute to academic literature by advancing an intervention-based approach to reduce the gap between organizational sustainability commitments and anthropocentric practices.

Intersectional Advantage: Male Continuing-generation Students are Seen as Most Confident and Competent in Social Interactions
Olena Vitkovska | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Olena Vitkovska | Austria
Prof. Veronika Job | University of Vienna | Austria
Dr. Christina Bauer | University of Vienna

Prior research suggests that male continuing-generation students think of themselves as more intellectually capable than their peer groups (i.e., female continuing-generation students, male first-generation students, as well as female first-generation students). The present research investigated the correlates of this self-view in interpersonal interactions. Our main assumption was that male continuing-generation students may not just see themselves as more intellectually capable, but they may also act in ways that are perceived as more competent by others. To test this theorizing, we had university students with mixed backgrounds (N = 200) work together on a bogus task (selecting items from a sinking ship) and then respond to questions about their interaction. Interactions were also videotaped and rated by research assistants in terms of students’ displayed behavior.
In line with our assumptions, we find that male continuing-generation students not only view themselves as most intellectually capable (replicating previous findings), but also were also perceived to be more confident and competent by their peers. Further, observer ratings indicated that male continuing-generation students spoke more, and were perceived to have a more confident voice, as well as posture.
Overall, findings suggest one way in which male continuing-generation students as an understudied group may maintain their status.

Revisiting Accountability in Group Decision Making: A Conceptual Replication and Extension
Lukas Dorsch | University of Göttingen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Lukas Dorsch | University of Göttingen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Stefan Schulz-Hardt | University of Göttingen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Jan Häusser | Justus Liebig University Giessen | Germany
Dr. Stella Wanzel

Groups often struggle to make optimal decisions, particularly when critical information is distributed across members. One proposed approach to improving group decisions is process accountability—that is, holding individuals accountable for justifying how they reached their decision. This study provides a conceptual replication of prior work on process accountability in groups and extends it by (1) examining outcome accountability—where individuals are held accountable for decision outcomes—and (2) comparing real groups, in which members interact, to nominal groups composed of non-interacting individuals whose decisions are combined post hoc. In a 2 (process accountability: present vs. absent) × 2 (outcome accountability: present vs. absent) × 2 (group type: real vs. nominal) between-subjects design, 480 participants were assigned to three-person groups. All groups completed a hidden-profile task, which requires integrating uniquely distributed information to identify the best decision alternative. Analyses revealed no effects of process accountability, outcome accountability, or their interaction on solution rates. No interactions with group type emerged. Analyses of information exchange in real groups showed effects of information type: shared information was exchanged and repeated more frequently than unshared information. However, neither accountability type influenced the overall amount or repetition of exchanged information. These findings fail to replicate previously reported benefits of process accountability in group decision making. As both manipulations were demonstrably effective, the absence of effects can’t be readily attributed to methodological shortcomings. The results raise questions about the robustness of accountability effects in group contexts and highlight the need to clarify when they may reliably improve group performance.

Assessment of Genuine Multitasking: Development and Validation of a Non-Compensatory Measure of Coordinated Concurrent Performance
Florian Thaler | SCHUHFRIED GmbH | Austria
Show details
Authors:
Florian Thaler | SCHUHFRIED GmbH | Austria
Alexandros Lazaridis | SCHUHFRIED GmbH | Austria
Isabell Baldauf | SCHUHFRIED GmbH | Austria
Marco Vetter | SCHUHFRIED GmbH, Universität Wien, Universität Salzburg | Austria

As progressive digitalization and new technologies reshape modern work, multitasking is emerging as ubiquitous occupational demand, requiring employees to coordinate multiple information streams. Traditional measures face conceptual and methodological limitations. Multitasking is typically operationalized as performance decrement under dual-task conditions relative to single-tasks, rather than capacity to maintain performance across demands. Measures conflate task switching with genuine coordination and rely on demands with limited ecological validity, restricting applicability to complex real-world multitasking contexts. Additionally, measures are vulnerable to practice and preparation, undermining test security – critical in high-stakes testing. The Multi-Tasking Test (M-TASK) was developed to address these limitations. M-TASK conceptualizes multitasking as coordinated concurrent control under continuous time pressure. Instead of an overly simplified paradigm, candidates perform three concurrent tasks tapping executive functions, processing speed, and visual monitoring, covering a broader, generally applicable multitasking skill. Multitasking is operationalized as absolute performance across concurrent demands, summarized in one score, calculated as harmonic mean of task-specific performances. This non-compensatory integration ensures that neglect of any task substantially reduces the score, capturing coordinated multitasking rather than isolated task proficiency or sequential switching. To enhance test security, M-TASK uses large, automatically generated pools of psychometrically equivalent and randomly administered items. A validation study with a representative German-speaking sample (N = 316) indicates strong psychometric properties. Analyses show excellent reliability (α > .90), and differential correlations supporting convergent (r = .708) and discriminant (r = .282) validity. Detailed insights into AI-assisted test design, validity and fairness analyses will be presented und discussed alongside limitations.

Standardise (Open) Science?
Ways to improve scientific quality through standardisation
Chair(s) Maximilian Frank (Ludwig-Maximilans-Universität München (LMU))
Chair(s) Dr. Lisa Spitzer (Leibniz-Institut für Psychologie (ZPID))
Room: CZ
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The replication crisis in psychology and beyond led to an increased awareness of the importance of methodological rigor and openness. To advance these research qualities, various practices, often summarised under the umbrella term “Open Science”, were introduced. As many of these efforts were developed bottom-up, this led to a wide range of different ideas, tools, templates, and recommendations from and for the scientific community.

On the one hand, this wide range of approaches enables a high level of flexibility in specific research situations. On the other hand, it can also introduce uncertainty as to which tool to use or which recommendation to follow, contributing to a high level of heterogeneity in research quality. To mitigate these problems, stand-alone recommendations can be synthesised into broader consensus standards, providing a consistent framework for researchers, journals, institutions, and funders.

The symposium brings together contributions from psychology and other neighboring disciplines, each representing a different phase of the standardisation process. From the consensus-based development of a new standard to the application of an already existing standard to a new field and the empirical testing of the effectiveness of standardisation, the symposium offers a holistic understanding of the topic. Together, these contributions provide a comprehensive and critical view of how standardisation can support - not constrain - scientific progress.

Developing community-driven, consensus-based best practice guidelines for psychology
Dr. Lisa Spitzer | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID)
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Lisa Spitzer | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID)
Dr. Katarina Blask | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID)
Dr. Flavio Azevedo | Utrecht University

In 2015, the Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Committee introduced the TOP Guidelines, which can be used by journals to indicate their level of commitment to Open Science practices (i.e., they can select a lower or higher level of commitment, informing their submission policies). While originally developed for psychology, the guidelines were adapted across disciplines despite being only partially compatible. To mitigate this problem and make the guidelines more broadly accessible, a new version has recently been released.

This update, however, brings a key change to the highest level of the guidelines, associated with the highest level of commitment to the respective Open Science practice. While previously requiring concrete, verifiable actions, the current version is more abstract, relying on adherence to “best practices”. Since these are not clearly defined or established across or even within disciplines like psychology, this shift compromises the implementation of the guidelines.

Therefore, the Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID) and Framework for Open and Reproducible Research Training (FORRT) initiated the development of community-driven, consensus-based best practice guidelines for psychology. By bringing together researchers from different psychological sub-disciplines, open science experts, and the infrastructure community, we develop modular guidelines that can help implement the TOP Guidelines in psychology. We will illustrate our approach using the example of preregistration, as one of the practices covered by the guidelines.

By providing a standardised framework for best practices in psychology, we hope to eliminate uncertainty in the application of the TOP Guidelines and promote the adoption of Open Science.

Giving CRediT Fairly: Standardising Authorship Awarding Practices for Student Contributions
Maximilian Frank | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
Show details
Authors:
Maximilian Frank | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
Raphael Merz | Eindhoven University of Technology
Bennet Strahmann | Ruhr-Universität Bochum

Transparent and fair authorship attribution is a cornerstone of scientific integrity and aligns with the goal of Open Science reforms. Yet, early scientific contributions by students often go unrecognized, in part due to a lack of clear, standardised guidance and different perceptions of their roles. Meanwhile students actively contribute to the scientific process, whether as research assistants or through their bachelor’s or master’s theses.

A nationwide survey by the Open Science working group of the German Psychology Students’ Council Conference (PsyFaKo) found that 86% of psychology students and 38% of researchers were unaware of established authorship guidelines. Both students and early-career researchers reported widespread perceptions of unfair authorship practices. To address this gap in formal recognition, the Faculty of Psychology at Ruhr University Bochum developed and implemented a faculty-wide, mandatory authorship framework through a participatory process involving students, faculty staff, and professors. The framework combines (a) curriculum-integrated modules on authorship norms and the CRediT taxonomy, (b) a decision-support tool (“authorship traffic light”) that maps CRediT roles to authorship expectations, and (c) a standardised supervision agreement that prompts early discussions and documents anticipated contributions.

We choose this use case to illustrate success factors for standardisation processes: translating perceived dissatisfaction with the status quo into a consensus-based, institutionally developed framework that reduces uncertainty and variability in awarding authorship and fostering cooperation between stakeholder groups at universities. As a model for standardisation, this reform demonstrates how transparent authorship practices can be integrated into higher education and scaled across institutions.

Toward standardization of ecologically sustainable open science practices in biological psychology
Prof. Dr. Sebastian Ocklenburg
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Sebastian Ocklenburg
Dr. Lara Puhlmann | Technische Universität Dresden
Dr. Alina Koppold | Universität Bielefeld
Dr. Gordon Feld | Zentralinstitut für Seelische Gesundheit
Dr. Helena Hartmann | Universitätsklinikum Essen

How can psychological data be acquired, stored, and shared effectively, while considering both the principles of the open science movement and ecological sustainability? In this talk, two projects focused on the interplay of open science and ecological sustainability will be highlighted, with a specific focus on standardization. In the face of the climate crisis, reducing anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions is an important goal. At the same time, advancing psychological knowledge is crucial for mental wellbeing, but can incur a negative impact on the environment. Biopsychological methods are particularly resource-intensive.

Thus, there is a tension between scientific research, open science principles, and ecologically sustainable scientific stewardship. We discuss how sustainable open science practices can be implemented in biopsychological research at each step of the research cycle following the ARIADNE framework. Specifically, we suggest to (1) re-place new data with open data whenever possible, (2) re-fine methods to make them more sustainable, and (3) re-duce carbon emission of testing by precisely determining sample sizes and research protocols beforehand.

Furthermore, the talk will highlight the development of a catalogue of criteria for the standardized assessment of ecological sustainability aspects in psychological publications. More and more funders ask researchers to include research ecological sustainability statements in their proposals. However, what is currently missing from the literature is a standardized evaluation scale to rate the sustainability of publications for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and other use cases. Therefore, we will present findings about the development of a scale to rate the ecological sustainability of psychological papers.

Sharing data openly conveys great potential for science, as it facilitates reproducibility and sustainability. In the field of psychoneuroendocrinology (PNE), which investigates links between hormones, behavior and health, sharing data openly is currently not common practice. This may be partly because preparing hormonal data for publication can be time-consuming and challenging, as the correct interpretation relies on contextual factors and technical details of the data acquisition. At the moment, no standard format in PNE has been established, complicating data sharing and reuse.

The Task Force Neuroendocrinology Open Data Exchange Standard (NODES) aims to develop a community-driven standard data structure for PNE as well as supportive infrastructure, like web applications that help in restructuring and validating datasets and meta-data prior to publication. NODES intends to clearly define which information is necessary to correctly interpret PNE data while at the same time addressing related practical considerations like accessibility and compatibility. In the first step, a Delphi study was conducted to reach an expert consensus regarding important open questions concerning the development of a standard data structure. In a second step, the Task Force currently develops and validates standard templates and creates supportive infrastructure.

The contribution will introduce the NODES Task Force, present the results of the Delphi study as well as the status of the template and infrastructure development and give an outlook on future milestones and plans. We will thereby showcase how standardization can be fostered in a community-driven manner, and highlight challenges and opportunities that may arise along the way.

Barriers to Standardised FAIR Data Sharing
Dr. André Bittermann | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID)
Show details
Authors:
Dr. André Bittermann | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID)
Dr. Anna Löhlein | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID)
Dr. Christian Omieczynski | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID)
Dr. Tim Lauer | Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID)
Prof. Dr. Mario Gollwitzer | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
Prof. Dr. Kai Sassenberg | Universität Trier

How can data be shared in the most effective way to ensure its reusability? To address this, the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) were introduced in 2016. They were meant to provide guidance, not to dictate specific criteria for FAIRness assessment. This flexibility comes at the cost of a potential wide range of different implementations of FAIRness.

To shed light on the status quo and the potential barriers to FAIR data sharing, we report empirical results of a large-scale examination of 11,384 datasets in psychology. FAIRness was assessed using the automated F-UJI tool, which is based on the FAIRsFAIR Data Object Assessment Metrics—a standardised implementation of the FAIR principles. Although data sharing increased between 2013 and 2024, FAIRness remained stable with reusability scores stagnating at a low to medium level. The chosen data repository turned out to be a major factor for data FAIRness. The most prevalent platform, OSF, performed significantly worse than PsychArchives, Zenodo, and Figshare. GitHub scored lowest, partially due to the lack of persistent identifiers. Comparing the scores of the automated F-UJI assessment with human ratings of FAIRness revealed moderate agreement for findability and poor agreement for interoperability and reusability. Notably, no agreement was found for accessibility.

Our results imply that technical issues of repositories and differing interpretations of FAIRness challenge standardised FAIR data sharing. In light of these barriers, we propose a triangulated approach involving repositories, authors, and journals.

Blurring boundaries through digital media use – A qualitative investigation of high school students’ challenges and needs regarding boundary management in a digital world
Dr. Svenja Schumacher | Osnabrueck University | Germany
Aliessa Mentrup | Osnabrueck University | Germany
Viktoria Hoerning | Osnabrueck University | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Svenja Schumacher | Osnabrueck University | Germany
Aliessa Mentrup | Osnabrueck University | Germany
Viktoria Hoerning | Osnabrueck University | Germany
Prof. Dr. Karsten Mueller | Osnabrueck University | Germany

Media convergence increasingly blurs contextual and role-related boundaries creating challenges in navigating these boundaries in the context of digital media use. Boundary management refers to integrating or segmenting different life domains and represents a crucial yet underexplored facet in the context of digital competencies. Reflectively navigating life domains in a digital setting is a crucial skill for people of all ages and needs to be trained from a young age.

In preparation of developing such a training, this study aimed to identify high school students’ challenges, needs, and preferences regarding digital media use, boundary management, and training design. In a qualitative approach, 59 students (year 5-12) from two secondary schools took part in focus groups. Digital media use, critical incidents, and students’ requirements for a training program were analyzed using a qualitative content analysis approach.

Results indicated that digital media affect students’ everyday lives across school, leisure, and social contexts. Students reported blurred boundaries between life domains, digital distractions, and negative effects on concentration and academic performance. The identified needs include enhanced self-control, improved goal-setting skills, and greater knowledge about reflective digital media use. Furthermore, students require external support (e.g., guidance, technical tools) and emphasized a preference for practical, interactive training focusing on self-regulation strategies.

As fostering boundary management skills is crucial to successfully navigating a blurred and digital world, the findings emphasize digital boundary management as a relevant skill for students in secondary school and provide valuable insights for the development of a needs-oriented digital training program for adolescents.

Wie anthropomorphe KI Flow fördert: Vertrauen als Mediator

Flow, ein Zustand völliger Vertiefung und des optimalen Erlebens, ist ein wesentlicher Aspekt für intrinsisch motiviertes und sinnerfülltes Arbeiten. Die Forschung zum Flow-Erleben in KI-gestützten Arbeitsumgebungen ist jedoch bislang limitiert. Wenn Mensch und KI-System als kollaboratives Team konzipiert wird, wird das Vertrauen in die KI zur grundlegenden Voraussetzung für das Erreichen von (Team-)Flow. Vorausgehende Forschung deutet darauf hin, dass dieses Vertrauen durch die anthropomorphe Gestaltung des Systems gesteigert werden kann, was potenziell zu einem verbesserten Flow-Erleben führt. Um diesen möglichen vermittelnden Zusammenhang zu untersuchen, wurde eine Laborstudie mit einem einfaktoriellen Within-Subject-Design durchgeführt, in dem der Grad der anthropomorphen Gestaltung eines KI-Systems (niedrig vs. hoch) variiert wurde. Die Manipulation des Anthropomorphismus umfasste vier Attribute: Name, Aussehen, Stimme und Kommunikationsstil. An der Studie nahmen insgesamt 60 Versuchspersonen teil. Sie führten eine komplexe Steuerungs- und Kontrollaufgabe aus, bei der sie von zwei unterschiedlich gestalteten KI-Assistenzsystemen unterstützt wurden. Es wurden die Hypothesen aufgestellt, dass ein höherer wahrgenommener Anthropomorphismus die wahrgenommene Vertrauenswürdigkeit steigert, was sich wiederum positiv auf das Flow-Erleben auswirkt. Die Hypothesen wurden mithilfe gemischter linearer Modelle getestet. Zusätzlich wurde der vermittelnde Zusammenhang als Mediation modelliert. Die Ergebnisse der Studie bestätigten alle angenommenen Zusammenhänge. Der Effekt der anthropomorphen Gestaltung des KI-Systems auf das Flow-Erleben während der Kollaboration wird vollständig durch die wahrgenommene Vertrauenswürdigkeit in einer rein indirekten Mediation erklärt. Die Studie liefert somit wichtige empirische Hinweise darauf, dass Vertrauen einen zentralen psychologischen Mechanismus darstellt, über den anthropomorphe Gestaltung das Flow-Erleben in KI-gestützten Arbeitsumgebungen fördern kann.

Less Human than Human? Anthropomorphism and the Perception of Violence in Violent Video Games
Dr. André Melzer | Luxembourg
Show details
Author:
Dr. André Melzer | Luxembourg

Although violent video games (VVG) require morally questionable actions, these games are extremely popular. In order to reduce inhibitions against violent actions and thus stimulate mechanisms of moral disengagement (Bandura, 2002), certain cues embedded in VVG enable players to engage in virtual violence without feeling guilty (Hartmann et al., 2014). The game’s narrative, for example, makes violent actions appear morally justified.

In two studies, we investigated whether the gaming experience differs when the opponents—the victims of violent acts— are less human-like in the first-person shooter Call of Duty: Black Ops III. Does the variation between human and non-human characters moderate the perception of game violence? In Study 1 (N=186), participants watched video clips in which either humans characters or zombies were shot. In Study 2 (N=63), participants played the game in one of these two conditions in the lab.

Higher levels of anthropomorphism (i.e., the individual tendency to humanize entities; Study 1) and affective empathy (both studies) were associated with stronger negative emotions. However, the game conditions did not affect the emotional evaluation in either study. The gaming experience and individual identification as a gamer were more decisive factors, with higher scores being associated with more positive emotions and fewer moral concerns.

Factors related to the player’s personality are known to be important for the emotional and moral evaluation of VVG (e.g., Allen & Anderson, 2021; Wagener & Melzer, 2024, 2025). They appear to be more significant than content-related characteristics, such as whether the opponents are human or non-human.

Soziale Prozesse in der Studierenden-Chatbot-Interaktion

Authors:
Eileen Plagge | Universität Münster | Germany
Prof. Dr. Regina Jucks | Universität Münster | Germany

Generative KI wie ChatGPT und Co sind mehr als moderne Tools. Sie werden zu Interaktionspartnern, denen menschliche Eigenschaften (wie „Warmherzigkeit“, vgl. Asch (1946); oder Vertrauenswürdigkeit) zugeschrieben werden und deren Äußerungen an sozialen Vergleichsmaßstäben evaluiert werden. Welche Merkmale der Chatbot-Äußerungen beeinflussen diese Zuschreibungsprozesse? Gibt es Unterschiede zwischen Studierenden der Hard- vs. Soft-Sciences beim (Ver)Menschlichen generativer KI?
In einem 2 × 2-Experiment (N = 308) bewerteten Studierende die Beschreibung eines Chatbotprototypen. Der Chatbot wurde über kurze Beschreibungen eingeführt, die systematisch variierten hinsichtlich (a) des sprachlichen Framings (anthropomorph vs. technisch) und (b) von Persönlichkeitshinweisen (freundlich vs. unfreundlich). Anschließend bewerteten die Teilnehmenden die wahrgenommene Wärme und die wahrgenommene Menschlichkeit. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass ein anthropomorphes Framing zu einem geringfügigen Anstieg der wahrgenommenen Wärme führt. Deutlich stärker und konsistenter wirken hingegen die Persönlichkeitshinweise – insbesondere die kommunizierte Freundlichkeit –, die sowohl die Wärme- als auch die Menschlichkeitsurteile maßgeblich beeinflussen. Diese Befunde legen nahe, dass sozial bedeutsame Hinweise die Wahrnehmung generativer KI durch Studierende bereits vor einem tatsächlichen Gespräch prägen können. Die Studie unterstreicht damit die Bedeutung von Pre-Use-Framing für menschenzentriertes Design und liefert praktische Implikationen für die Implementierung chatbotbasierter Lernunterstützung in der Hochschulbildung.

Clinician Caution, Public Openness: Diverging Attitudes to AI in Psychotherapy (Germany)
Alfio Ventura | University of Duisburg Essen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Alfio Ventura | University of Duisburg Essen | Germany
Dylan Mercury Cooper | University College London | United Kingdom
Lisa Stahlkopf | Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security | Germany
Lea Maria Schäfer | Charié - Universitätsmedizin Berlin | Germany
Prof. Nils Köbis | Research Center Trustworthy Data Science and Security | Germany

Across societies, demand for psychotherapy exceeds available supply. This prompts growing interest in digital support, including, increasingly, generative-AI-based mental health applications. Successful adoption of AI in psychotherapy will depend on whether such systems meet the expectations and requirements of both practising psychotherapists and potential clients—and on how accurately each group anticipates the other’s views.

We conducted a preregistered, exploratory online survey of 301 ordinary German adults (recruited via Prolific) and 131 German psychotherapists (licensed and in training). We assessed attitudes toward AI in psychotherapy, perceived opportunities and risks, willingness to delegate specific tasks to AI, and preferences for resolving concrete product-development trade-offs (e.g., between usability, transparency, and safety).

Our results show that psychotherapists expected both their colleagues’ and clients’ views to be more sceptical than they actually were, and they themselves placed greater weight on risks than on opportunities. Although the samples broadly agreed on several benefits and concerns, they diverged on whether AI would meaningfully expand access to and availability of psychotherapy, and on the risks of undermining critical thinking and compromising data protection. General German adults were also more open to allowing delegation of a range of therapy-related tasks to AI than psychotherapists were willing to. By contrast, the groups were strikingly similar in the product-development trade-offs, but clear trade-off priorities were rare and did not always align with current product trends.
Overall, the findings highlight where expectations align, where they diverge, and where misperceptions could hinder implementation—informing communication, regulation, and participatory design for successful AI-supported psychotherapy.

Minding Me, Minding You, Minding Our Planet: Mindfulness Across Individual, Social, and Environmental Outcomes
Chair(s) Dr. Cornelia Wieck (Universität Leipzig)
Room: HR
Topic: Psychology of Sustainable Behavior
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

It is broadly acknowledged that mindfulness supports individual well-being, particularly by reducing stress. However, in the face of mounting societal and ecological challenges, mindfulness is increasingly recognized as a broader resource with the potential to shape social interactions and ecological behavior.
The present symposium brings together four empirical contributions that examine how mindfulness relates to outcomes such as stress, prosocial behavior, value-consistent action, and sustainable behavior. By combining correlational and experimental approaches with multi-method assessments, the contributions offer a nuanced and complementary perspective on mindfulness-related effects across levels of analysis.
Kunzmann et al. use a randomized controlled design to disentangle the independent and combined effects of mindfulness practice and exposure to natural environments on perceived stress and nature connectedness. Wieck et al. extend mindfulness research into the social domain by examining trait-level associations and intervention-related changes in prosocial behavior using both self-report and behavioral measures. Karpova et al. address the persistent value–behavior gap by investigating whether mindfulness supports alignment between biospheric values and pro-environmental behavior across correlational and intervention-based designs. Finally, Blanke et al. draw on data from a mindfulness-based program targeting ethical and sustainable behavior in students to examine changes in emotion regulation and coping strategies and their associations with stress and pro-environmental behavior.
Collectively, the studies illustrate the broad potential of mindfulness and emphasize its relevance in addressing contemporary societal and ecological challenges. The findings encourage further investigation into mechanisms, interventions, and practical applications that harness mindfulness to foster adaptive behavior across domains.

**Due to a subsequent conference on September 10–11, 2026, we kindly request that the symposium, if possible, be scheduled between September 7 and 9.**

Prof. Dr. Ute Kunzmann | Leipzig University | Germany
Show details
Authors:

Dr. Elisabeth S. Blanke
Maria Karpova | Leipzig University | Germany
Dr. Torsten Masson | Leipzig University | Germany
Dr. Cornelia Wieck | Leipzig University | Germany

Mindfulness practice and exposure to natural environments are widely assumed to have beneficial effects for individuals, yet their unique and combined contributions remain poorly understood. This randomized controlled trial aimed to disentangle the effects of mindfulness practice and nature exposure on stress and nature connectedness. Participants (N = 199) were randomly assigned to one of two intervention types (mindfulness vs. relaxation control) in one of two environmental contexts (urban park vs. indoor setting). Participants in the mindfulness condition engaged in guided meditation practices led by a certified teacher. Participants in the relaxation control condition spent the same amount of time together in self-chosen low-effort activities and were accompanied by a research assistant. Stress and nature connectedness were assessed before and after the intervention using the Perceived Stress Scale and the Connectedness to Nature Scale. Mindfulness practice was more effective in reducing stress than the relaxation control condition, regardless of whether it was conducted indoors or outdoors. Mindfulness practice also led to greater increases in nature connectedness, independent of environmental context. At the same time, being outdoors increased nature connectedness compared to being indoors, across both intervention types. Contrary to expectations, combining mindfulness practice with outdoor exposure did not yield additional benefits. This absence of an interaction effect may reflect limited statistical power or reduced contrasts between conditions. From a practical perspective, the results indicate that mindfulness and nature can be used as effective, stand-alone interventions for stress reduction and nature connectedness, even in ordinary, everyday contexts.

While mindfulness is well established as a resource for individual well-being, accumulating evidence suggests that it may also foster social outcomes such as prosocial behavior. However, most prior correlational and intervention research has relied on self-reported prosociality, which is shaped by contextual and normative influences and shares method variance with mindfulness. The present study therefore examines trait-level associations and intervention-related changes in mindfulness and prosociality using a multi-method assessment of prosocial behavior. In a randomized controlled trial with N = 199 participants, individuals were assigned to a brief mindfulness intervention or an active control condition and completed the program in one of two environmental contexts (urban park vs. indoor setting). Both groups completed a four-hour program in small groups. The mindfulness group participated in guided meditation exercises, whereas the control group spent the same amount of time in self-directed, low-effort activities typically performed in everyday life. Prosociality was assessed using a self-report questionnaire and an indirect behavioral task; trait prosociality was measured one week prior to the intervention, whereas state prosociality was assessed immediately before and after the program. At the trait level, higher mindfulness is expected to be associated with greater prosociality. At the intervention level, we hypothesize stronger increases in prosociality in the mindfulness group compared to the control group. By integrating trait- and intervention-based analyses and combining self-report with behavioral measures, this study provides a focused test of mindfulness-related prosocial effects beyond subjective evaluations.

While concern for the environment is widespread, it often fails to translate into consistent pro-environmental action, a phenomenon commonly described as the value-behavior gap. Mindfulness may help bridge this gap by supporting self- and emotion regulation, value clarification, and affective processes such as nature connectedness. However, empirical evidence linking mindfulness and alignment between values and behavior remains limited. To help fill this gap, we conducted two studies that examined whether mindfulness serves as a resource for aligning biospheric values with pro-environmental behavior. Study 1 (N = 200) examined cross-sectional associations between trait mindfulness and value-behavior congruence, using self-reports and a behavioral indicator task to assess pro-environmental behavior. Study 2 (N = 81) investigated whether a mindfulness-based intervention emphasizing nature experience and reflection on personal values would increase the congruence between biospheric values and pro-environmental behavior relative to a passive control group. We predicted that higher trait mindfulness would be associated with stronger alignment of biospheric values and pro-environmental behavior, and that intervention participants, but not participants in the control group, would increase in value-behavior congruence from pre- to post-intervention. In additional analyses, we examined whether increases in mindfulness within the intervention group would predict the increase in value-behavior congruence. By focusing on value-behavior congruence rather than isolated behavioral or attitudinal outcomes, this research highlights a potentially overlooked mechanism through which mindfulness may support sustainable, value-consistent action. The findings aim to inform the development of mindfulness-based interventions seeking to support sustainable behavior.

Practicing mindfulness, the attention to and acceptance of present-moment experiences, has been associated with behaviors benefitting planetary health, defined as the interplay between human health and the health of natural systems. In an evaluation study, a mindfulness-based intervention, the Mindful Students Program (MSP), which aims at fostering ethical and sustainable behavior, was shown to reduce individual stress and increase pro-environmental behavior, thereby benefiting individuals and the planet. One mechanism through which individual stress may be reduced and pro-environmental behavior fostered could be increased capacities in dealing with individual and global stressors. We used the data from the evaluation study with 505 students (quasi-experimental pre-post-design; 78% female; 203 in the MSP group, 302 in two control groups) to investigate the effect of the MSP on several emotion regulation and coping strategies, and their relation to stress and pro-environmental behavior. We chose established strategies related to individual stressors, some mostly adaptive strategies (e.g., positive reappraisal), and one mostly maladaptive strategy, rumination. We further explored two strategies in coping with a global stressor, the climate crisis. As expected, participants in the MSP group reported increases in almost all adaptive strategies. Contrary to predictions, there was no change in rumination. There were also no effects on coping with the climate crisis. Strategies varied in their association with stress; associations with pro-environmental behavior were small. The findings show that the MSP can contribute to increase behaviors related to planetary health. Sequential effects in cognitive psychology: Comparing apples with oranges?
Chair(s) Dr. Anne Voormann (Albert-Ludwig-Universität Freiburg)
Room: IT
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Sequential effects are the smallest building blocks of learning and training effects. In cognitive psychology, sequential effects refer to the observation of performance gains in the case of repetitions and performance losses in the case of alternations. They are a very robust phenomenon and occur in a number of paradigms, for example, in two-choice reaction time tasks, in dual-tasking, in interference tasks, and in visual search. Historically, sequential effects have been addressed separately within each experimental paradigm, and were seldomly investigated across paradigms. However, recently researchers started to compare sequential effects across paradigms and to formulate frameworks with mechanisms that generalize over paradigms. In this symposium, we cover research on sequential effects in its whole variety. We start with a structured comparison of theories for sequential effects across a number of paradigms. Additionally, we address experimental manipulations that moderate the size of sequential effects. And finally, we investigate comparisons of specific theoretic frameworks for sequential effects in specific paradigms with experimental approaches. We will end the symposium with a discussion about to what extent findings about sequential effects in one paradigm can be generalized to other paradigms and how joint frameworks can be developed while still taking paradigm specific characteristics into account.

Reviewing theories of sequential effects across paradigms: Commonalities and differences
Anne Voormann
Show details
Authors:
Anne Voormann
David Dignath
Andrea Kiesel
Heinrich R. Liesefeld
Jeff Miller
Irina Monno

Differential impacts of repetition and alternations on task performance have been investigated for a century (see for example, Jersild, 1927). Over the decades, sequential effects in different paradigms had been in the focus of research, starting in the 1960s with sequential effects in two-choice reaction time tasks and in the 1990s with sequential effects in visual search, interference tasks, and task-switching. Although there has been extensive research in recent decades, the concrete mechanisms behind sequential effects still puzzle researchers. Accordingly, many different theories have been proposed. However, on a closer look, theories from multiple paradigms share certain assumptions (e.g., sequential effects result from episodic memory traces or expectations), whereas other assumptions are unique to theories from specific paradigms (e.g., detection of conflict and resulting control adaptations in interference tasks).
The aim of this talk is to systematically compare theories of sequential effects across paradigms. Therefore, we will focus on assumptions that are shared across paradigms, but also highlight differences in the theories of sequential effects across paradigms.

How to establish robust congruence sequence effects for the Stroop task
Andrea Kiesel
Show details
Authors:
Eldad Keha
Felix Cramer
Elisa Straub
Andrea Kiesel

The Stroop task is often used to assess congruence effects – indicated by slower and less correct responses in incongruent compared to neutral or congruent word-color combinations. In recent years, cognitive control was not only addressed by the congruence effect itself, but by its sequential modulation. This congruency sequence effect refers to the observation that the congruence effect is smaller after an incongruent compared to a congruent trial. This sequential modulation enables to assess differences of congruence effects as marker of cognitive control processes, while congruence effects themselves are indicator for cognitive interference and cognitive control processes simultaneously.
Interestingly, sequential modulations of congruence effects were mostly considered for other conflict paradigms, while findings on congruence sequence effect in the Stroop task reveal mixed results. Here, we report three experiments in which we assessed sequential modulations either in a confound-minimized design, ruling out any repetitions of color, word or response in consecutive trials, or in a confound design with partly overlapping stimuli. As a consequence, sequential modulations in the confound design might be confounded by trialwise learning effects.
We observed robust sequential modulations only for the confound-minimized design, while in the confound design, congruence effects were larger after incongruent compared to congruent trials, revealing a reversed congruence sequence effect. Thus, whereas trialwise learning effects increase sequential modulations in other conflict tasks, they impair sequential modulations in the Stroop task. Importantly, however, when applying a confound-minimized design, robust congruence sequence effects can serve as indicator for cognitive control processes.

Sequential modulation of cognitive control in dual-task processing
Patricia Hirsch
Show details
Authors:
Patricia Hirsch
Prof. Dr. Iring Koch
Tilo Strobach

Dual-task performance requires the coordination of two concurrent tasks, which are assumed to be jointly represented as a task-pair set. Several studies showed that performance is worse when switching to a new task-pair than when repeating a task-pair, resulting in task-pair switch costs. These costs are thought to reflect the need to reconfigure the active task-pair set and to overcome proactive interference from the previous task-pair set. Recent findings demonstrated that task-pair switch costs are reduced after a task-pair switch relative to a task-pair repetition, indicating a sequential modulation of these costs. This pattern suggests that task-pair set control is dynamically adjusted based on recent processing demands. The present study examined whether this sequential modulation arises from automatic repetition priming of task-pair sets or from an increase in cognitive control that is triggered by a task-pair switch and persists into the next trial. Participants performed a dual-task experiment in which we manipulated the task-pair sequence in the current trial, the task-pair sequence in the previous trial, and the proportion of task-pair switches within each block (25% vs. 75%). We hypothesized that if the sequential modulation reflects heightened cognitive control after a task-pair switch, the modulation should be more pronounced in low switch-proportion blocks, where proactive control demands are minimal, than in high switch-proportion blocks, where frequent task-pair switches encourage a generally elevated control state reducing the need for an additional control increase after a task-pair switch. The results are discussed with respect to bottom-up vs. top-down models of cognitive control.

When Do Action Effects Modulate S–R Bindings? On the Role of Meaningfulness and Response-Specificity
Dr. Nicolas D. Münster
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Nicolas D. Münster
Christian Frings

Human actions are typically performed to achieve intended goals, with their sensory consequences serving as indicators of successful goal achievement (i.e., action effects). According to theories of action control, features of stimuli (S), responses (R), and effects (E) are integrated into event files. Partial feature repetitions reveal binding and retrieval processes, which are reflected in the influence of a preceding action episode on subsequent performance – commonly referred to as binding effects. While robust bindings between stimuli and responses as well as between responses and their effects are well established, it remains unclear under which conditions action effects can modulate S-R bindings. In the present study, we examined how the meaningfulness and response-specificity of action effects contribute to such S-R modulations. Using a distractor–response binding paradigm, participants responded to target letters flanked by distractors while action effects varying in meaningfulness and response-specificity could occur. The results show that S–R bindings are strengthened by the presence of action effects, but only when these effects are both meaningful and response-specific. These findings suggest that action effects can enhance instrumental S–R bindings, but only when they are used as indicators of goal achievement. The results thus refine our understanding of the functional role of action effects in shaping event-file processing.

Procrastination: How can we prevent it at school and at university? Starting points from four studies
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Carola Grunschel
Prof. Dr. Katrin B. Klingsieck
Room: IE
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

In light of procrastination’s detrimental effects on academic performance and subjective well-being, we will discuss effective approaches to preventing procrastination among high school and university students in the symposium. The interactive discussion with all contributors and the audience is informed by four contributions. The first contribution (Bäulke et al.) on 4,063 high school students shows via latent growth curve modelling that procrastination not only increases throughout the school year but is also negatively associated with a successful transition to the next class level, rendering prevention programs necessary. Showing that the relationship between stress and procrastination in high school students (N = 74) is partially mediated by compulsive internet use, the second contribution (Bobe et al.) suggests that prevention efforts might benefit from considering stress management and mindful media use. The third contribution (Kulp et al.) shifts attention to adolescents’ development. The experience sampling study with 164 first year university students (n = 484 measurements; duration of 4 weeks) shows via random-intercepts linear mixed effects models that the delay component of procrastination increases while students’ conscientiousness and academic self-concept play an important role, suggesting that prevention programs should also attend to students’ self-concept. The fourth contribution zooms in on exam preparation, a high demanding situation in university studies. The adaptive experience sampling study applying hierarchical Bayesian continuous time dynamic modeling (N = 88; n = 2880 measurements; one week before the exam) highlights the role of task ambiguity and daily mood which might hint on didactical aspects in preventing procrastination.

Procrastination—the unnecessary delay of intended tasks despite anticipated negative consequences—is a widespread phenomenon in educational contexts and is considered detrimental to learning processes (Steel, 2007). While numerous studies in higher education have shown negative associations between procrastination, academic performance, well-being, and dropout (e.g., Grunschel et al., 2016), evidence from school settings remains limited. Initial findings suggest that school-related procrastination occurs in a domain-specific manner (e.g., Bäulke et al., 2024). However, little is known about how domain-specific procrastination develops over the school year or relates to educational transitions. The present study examines (1) changes in domain-specific procrastination during the first year of upper secondary education and (2) whether domain-specific procrastination predicts a successful transition to the subsequent grade level. Data from the first three waves of the ongoing longitudinal study TOSCAneo were analyzed, collected at the beginning, midyear, and end of the school year. The sample comprised 4,063 students (54.0% female; 45,9% male, 0,1% diverse, mean age = 16.4 years, SD = 0.89). Domain-specific procrastination was assessed via student questionnaires in German, English, mathematics, chemistry, biology, and physics. Information on grade-level transition (operationalized as promotion to the next grade) was provided by schools. Latent growth curve models were applied. Results showed a significant increase in procrastination across the school year in all subjects. Procrastination in science subjects—most notably mathematics—was negatively associated with a successful transition. These findings underscore the importance of early prevention and intervention efforts targeting procrastination in school contexts.

Show details

The association between procrastination and stress has been shown in various populations and contexts. According to the stress context vulnerability model of procrastination (Sirois, 2023), stress predicts procrastination by depleting an individual's coping resources, thereby reducing their capacity to tolerate negative affect. These negative emotions are then avoided by procrastinating tasks associated with them (mood repair hypothesis; Sirois & Pychyl, 2013). We apply this relatively new model to a population that has been understudied in procrastination research: high school students (N = 74, 62.2% male; M = 18.01, SD = 1.29). Based on empirical findings indicating that compulsive internet use is used to regulate distress (Valkenburg et al., 2017) and can exacerbate problematic procrastination (Nordby et al., 2019), we hypothesize that compulsive internet use (CIUS; Meerkerk et al., 2009; ω = .70) mediates the relationship between stress (PSS-10; Schneider et al., 2020; ω = .81) and procrastination (PPS; Steel, 2010; ω = .88). In the mediation model (explained variance: 36.2%), compulsive internet use significantly and partially mediates the relationship between stress and procrastination (indirect effect: b = .133, 95% CI [0.026, 0.246]; direct effect of stress on procrastination: b = .227, p < .001). The findings support the idea of compulsive internet use, and digital distractions in general, being a key mechanism through which stress translates into procrastination. Given the potential for self-perpetuating cycles of stress, compulsive internet use, and procrastination, there is a need for procrastination interventions that target stress management and mindful media use.

While there are already important findings on the development of delay during the course of studying (e.g., Bäulke et al., 2019), little is known about both behavioral and emotional dynamics directly at the beginning of studies, although this phase is particularly interesting due to its diverse demands and challenges (Bosse & Trautwein, 2014). In summary, it seems worthwhile to consider academic procrastination already in the first weeks of studies to support students’ study behavior right from the start. Future studies should therefore consider a longer period of time and more diverse samples.

Data were analyzed with hierarchical Bayesian continuous time dynamic modeling (Driver & Völkle, 2018), including the control variables and daily mood (three time-dependent predictor variables) on the dependent variables task-ambiguity and procrastination behavior. The significant results were: High valence predicted stronger autoregression effects in perceived task-ambiguity (Mposterior = 0.067, 95% CI [0.037, 0.099]) and procrastination behavior (Mposterior = 0.487, 95% CI [0.296, 0.688]. Perceived task ambiguity was associated with a risk of procrastination behavior (Mposterior = 0.785, 95% CI [0.162, 1.443], and vice versa (Mposterior = 0.219, 95% CI [0.153, 0.286]. Openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, emotional stability, rumination, trait procrastination, and age predicted these relationships (Mposterior = 0.137–-3.563, 95% CI [0.013, 0.267]–[-5.072, -2.002]). The findings support and extend previous research by providing a more comprehensive understanding of students' moods, task perceptions, and procrastination in the context of upcoming examinations.

Perceived Organizational Support als Schlüsselvariable transformationaler Führung: Eine meta-analytische Strukturgleichungsmodellierung
Laurent Metje | Universität Bremen | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Laurent Metje | Universität Bremen | Germany
Prof. Dr. Vera Hagemann | Universität Bremen

Transformationale Führung (TL) und Perceived Organizational Support (POS) wurden in den vergangenen Jahrzehnten im Zusammenhang mit Mitarbeiterengagement sowie organisationaler Bindung untersucht. Trotz der Vielzahl an Primärstudien zu ausgewählten Zusammenhängen, fehlt eine umfassende Zusammenführung, die Interaktionen der Konstrukte berücksichtigt.
Für die Meta-Analyse wurde eine systematische Literaturrecherche in wissenschaftlichen Datenbanken (Web of Science, EBSCOhost, Scopus, PsycINFO, PubMed) durchgeführt. Nach zweistufigem Screening (Titel/Abstract und Volltext) wurden 623 peer-reviewte quantitative Primärstudien eingeschlossen, die statistische Effektparameter (Korrelationen oder standardisierte Regressionskoeffizienten) berichteten. Es wurde eine meta-analytische Strukturgleichungsmodellierung (Two-Stage Structural Equation Modeling; TSSEM) eingesetzt, die auf Random-Effects-Meta-Analysen der Korrelationsmatrizen basiert, um die simultanen Wirkpfade zwischen TL, POS, Engagement und organisationaler Bindung zu testen. Moderatoranalysen sowie Verfahren zur Prüfung potenziellen Publikationsbias ergänzten die Analysen.
Die Ergebnisse zeigen signifikant positive Zusammenhänge zwischen TL, POS, Engagement und Bindung. TSSEM verdeutlicht, dass TL-Effekte auf Engagement und Bindung indirekt über POS vermittelt werden: TL – POS (β = .48), POS – Engagement (β = .36) und POS – Bindung (β = .44). Die indirekten Effekte über POS sind bedeutsam (Engagement: β = .17; Bindung: β = .21), während direkte TL-Effekte bestehen bleiben (Engagement: β = .29; Bindung: β = .26), jedoch abgeschwächt werden; insgesamt werden 37 % (Engagement) bzw. 45 % (Bindung) der Gesamteffekte durch POS vermittelt.
Die Befunde präzisieren bestehende Führungstheorien, indem sie POS als Wirkmechanismus transformationaler Führung ausweisen. Zugleich legen sie nahe, dass die Wirksamkeit transformationalen Führungsverhaltens davon abhängt, inwieweit dieses von Mitarbeitenden als Ausdruck organisationaler Wertschätzung und Unterstützung wahrgenommen wird, und bieten damit Anhaltspunkte für Führungskräfteentwicklung sowie organisationale Interventionen.

„War das wirklich der richtige Schritt für mich?“ − Eine explorative Studie über das Bereuen der Übernahme einer Führungsrolle
Konstanze Arnoldussen | Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Konstanze Arnoldussen | Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) | Germany
Emily Kratsch | Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU)
Sabine Hommelhoff | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (LMU)

Die Übernahme von Führungsverantwortung gilt als wichtiger Karriereschritt. Führungskräfte müssen weitreichende Entscheidungen treffen; sie sollten andere inspirieren und weiterentwickeln sowie Ratgeber und Vorbild sein. Es kann jedoch passieren, dass Führungskräfte mit ihrer Rolle hadern und ihre Entscheidung, Führungskraft geworden zu sein, in Frage stellen. Dies kann womöglich Ressourcen binden, die dann für Führungsaufgaben nicht mehr zur Verfügung stehen. Vor diesem Hintergrund explorieren wir das Phänomen des managerial regret -- das heißt, das Bereuen der Entscheidung, eine Führungsposition übernommen zu haben. Ziel ist es, zu verstehen, wie solche Gefühle des Bereuens entstehen, wie sie von Führungskräften erlebt und beschrieben werden und wie andere Personen darauf reagieren.
Unsere Untersuchung basiert auf einer präregistrierten Natural-Language-Processing-Analyse von Reddit-Posts aus den Subreddits r/managers und r/leadership von Oktober 2023 bis Dezember 2025, in denen Führungskräfte explizit mit ihrer Entscheidung hadern, je Führungskraft geworden zu sein. Analysiert werden sowohl die ursprünglichen Beiträge der Führungskräfte als auch die Reaktionen anderer Reddit-Mitglieder in Form von Kommentaren, wobei der Fokus hierbei auf empfohlenen Coping-Strategien und sozialer Unterstützung liegt.
Die Posts und Kommentare werden bis zur Konferenz mithilfe einer thematischen Analyse nach Braun und Clarke (2006, 2021) ausgewertet. Die Ergebnisse sollen Einblicke in die Entstehung und Ausprägung von managerial regret sowie in die sozialen Reaktionen darauf liefern und damit einen bislang kaum erforschten Aspekt von Führungsverhalten beleuchten. Die Studie trägt zum besseren Verständnis emotionaler Herausforderungen von Führungskräften bei und beleuchtet mögliche Auswirkungen von managerial regret auf die Führungskräfte selbst, ihre Mitarbeitenden und Organisationen.

Kreuzchen vs. Linie – eine Pilotstudie zur Übereinstimmung von Fragebögen und gezeichneten Verläufen zur Erfassung von Beanspruchung im Tagesverlauf
Dr. Dominik Dilba | TU Chemnitz | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Dominik Dilba | TU Chemnitz | Germany
Prof. Dr. Bertolt Meyer | TU Chemnitz | Germany

Das Interesse an zeitlichen Dynamiken arbeits- und organisationspsychologischer Phänomene wächst seit Jahren (z.B. zunehmend mehr Tage- und Wochenbuchstudien zur Erfassung von kurzfristiger Variation und zeitlichen Verläufen von Beanspruchung oder Wohlbefinden). Typischerweise erfordern diese Fragestellungen aufwändige Studiendesigns, mit vielen wiederholten Messungen und den typischen daraus folgenden Herausforderungen (z.B. hohe Rekrutierungskosten oder Dropouts).

In einer Serie von Pilotstudien haben wir Studienteilnehmende stattdessen zeiteffizient einen zeitlichen Verlauf für interessierende Variablen wie z.B. Fatigue *zeichnen* lassen. Dadurch konnten wir pseudo-longitudinale Informationen sammeln, etwa Beanspruchungskurven nach hypothetischen Stressoren oder retrospektive tägliche Verläufe von Fatigue. Es zeigte sich u.a., dass Parameter gezeichneter Beanspruchungskurven (z.B. unmittelbare Reaktion auf Stressoren, Dauer und Vollständigkeit der Erholung) mit Fragebögen für Resilienz, Erschöpfung oder Schlafqualität korrelierten.

Die aktuelle Pilotstudie soll nun die Überlappung von gezeichneten Verläufen mit regulären Fragebögen direkt überprüfen: Studienteilnehmende werden an einem einzelnen Tag zwischen 8.00 und 17.30 Uhr alle 30 Minuten kontaktiert und beschreiben ihr aktuelles Level an Fatigue (Tagebuch). Am Abend werden dann tägliche Aktivitäten abgefragt (Day Reconstruction) und ein retrospektiver Verlauf für Fatigue in einer App gezeichnet.

Bisher haben kurz nach Studienbeginn bereits 84 Studierende unserer Universität den Auftaktfragebogen beantwortet und sich für die Teilnahme an der Hauptstudie im Januar 2026 bereiterklärt. In unserem Beitrag werden wir die Überlappung beider Messmethoden prüfen und Präferenzen der Teilnehmenden explorieren (hinsichtlich subjektiver Passung der entstandenen Verläufe zum erlebten Tag, zeitlichem Aufwand, Eingriff in alltägliche Abläufe etc.).

Die Chancen und Herausforderungen beider Methoden sowie mögliche Anwendungsfälle für Verlaufszeichnungen zur Erfassung psychologischer Konstrukte werden diskutiert.

Planning and Performance at Work: A Meta-Analysis
Dr. Nina Trenz Komann | Institut für Psychologie, Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany
Show details
Author:
Dr. Nina Trenz Komann | Institut für Psychologie, Technische Universität Darmstadt | Germany

Planning is an essential tool for structuring work activities and can benefit goal achievement and performance at work. Yet, studies examining the effects of employees’ planning at work report mixed findings, with some studies reporting null effects on performance. This meta-analysis sought to synthesize the results of field studies on the relationship between employees’ planning and performance and to explain the heterogeneity in findings by considering content-related (i.e., differences in planning strategies), contextual (i.e., differences in autonomy, cultural time orientation), and methodological (i.e., study design, source of performance measure) moderators. We used a multilevel mixed-model approach on 64 effect sizes from 5,994 employees across 30 studies and found a positive overall relationship between employees’ planning and performance (r = .29, SE = .03, p < .001, 95%CI [0.228, 0.352]). The effectiveness of planning varied across planning strategies, but contrary to expectations, anchored planning (i.e., scheduling of goals and activities into specific time slots) showed larger effects than contingency planning (i.e., flexible planning with alternative plans for changes in external circumstances). As expected, the effectiveness of planning varied with autonomy (larger effects in targeted samples of occupations with high autonomy vs. general samples), across cultural time orientations (larger effects in polychronic vs. monochronic cultures), and across study designs. These results suggest that employees in work environments with high self-regulatory demands can particularly benefit from planning. Future research on planning needs to consider differences in planning strategies and the professional and cultural contexts in which they are applied.
