The Dynamics of Daily Functioning in Aging: Insights From Intensive Longitudinal Approaches
Co-chair(s) Dr. Urmimala Ghose (Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin)
Prof. Dr. Denis Gerstorf (Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin)
Room: LU
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Understanding daily life in older adulthood requires capturing the dynamic interplay of affect, cognition, and behavior in real time This symposium presents four intensive longitudinal studies examining older adults’ routines, emotion regulation, cognition, and affect dynamics. Heckmann-Umhau et al. examine how changes in older adults' daily routine relate to subjective health across days and years. They conceptualize daily routine as a self-regulatory strategy to stabilize functioning when health fluctuates. Using intensive smartphone-based assessments and continuous-time models, they test bidirectional routine-health links and interindividual differences. Hagenström et al. investigate the cognitive foundations of context-sensitive emotion regulation. Given age-related declines in fluid abilities and stability or even slight increases in crystallised abilities, it is proposed that younger adults might rely more on fluid abilities, while older adults might rely more on crystallised abilities to guide emotion regulation. Schilling et al. use ambulatory assessment data from the currently ongoing VITAL project to separate between-context from within-context short-term intraindividual variability of momentary affective and cognitive responses in old very age. Their results reveal first evidence of the idea that these distinctive variabilities could mirror adaptive flexibility versus maladaptive instability of psychological functioning in old age. Ghose et al. investigate how, over and above levels of cognitive functioning, more than two decades of cognitive trajectories shape older adults’ moment-to-moment emotional experiences – indicated by baseline negative affect, stressor reactivity, and affective variability. This study further explores how momentary control beliefs may buffer vulnerability across multiple timescales in later life. Riediger will synthesize these findings, highlighting insights into lifespan development, aging, and adaptive daily functioning.

Julia Heckmann-Umhau | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Julia Heckmann-Umhau | Germany
Prof. Cornelia Wrzus | Germany
Prof. Dr. Oliver Schilling | Germany
Prof. Dr. Christina Röcke | Switzerland
Minxia Luo | Switzerland

Daily routine tends to become more structured in later life, often co-occurring with poorer health. Such stable, repetitive activity patterns have been interpreted both as a potential marker of health decline and as an adaptive adjustment to diminishing health. However, the temporal ordering and longitudinal dynamics linking routine and health remain poorly understood. Using two measurement bursts from the Mobility, Activity, and Social Interactions Study (MOASIS), we applied continuous-time structural equation models to examine reciprocal within-person dynamics between daily routine and subjective health and to test conscientiousness as a moderator. In each burst, older adults completed two weeks of smartphone-based EMA, with seven time-stamped reports of the momentary activity per day and one end-of-day rating of their subjective health (2018: N = 150, ages 65–91; 2024–2025: N = 120). Daily routine was operationalized via Recurrence Quantification Analysis (RQA), capturing the repetition of similar activities at similar times across days. In the longitudinal subsample assessed in both bursts (N = 76), mean routine increased from 1.50 to 1.95 between bursts (Cohen’s d = 0.41). Greater increases in routine across bursts were associated with declines in subjective health (r = −0.17, p < .05), whereas baseline routine was unrelated to subsequent health change (r = −0.02, p = .87). Within each burst, estimated cross-lagged effects were small and provided no clear evidence for day-to-day reciprocal coupling. Overall, routine–health links were more apparent across years than across days, suggesting that increasing routine may mark longer-term health-related adaptation.

The adaptiveness of emotion regulation strategies is increasingly understood as context-dependent, highlighting the importance of flexible regulation, one aspect of which is context-sensitivity. Such context-sensitivity is assumed to require cognitive resources to accurately assess situational demands and select appropriate regulatory strategies. In this study, we examine how fluid and crystallised cognitive abilities are associated with context-sensitive emotion regulation, operationalised as the within-person covariation between perceived stressor controllability and the use of situation modification. Given age-related declines in fluid abilities and stability or even slight increases in crystallised abilities, we propose that younger adults may rely more on fluid cognitive resources that support online monitoring and moment-to-moment reasoning, whereas older adults may rely more on crystallised, experience-based resources when regulating their emotions. This account is consistent with evidence that context-sensitive emotion regulation is maintained or even improves into at least young-old age. Younger (n = 133) and older (n = 119) adults completed a cognitive test battery assessing fluid (processing speed, reasoning) and crystallised (vocabulary, verbal fluency) abilities. They then took part in a 28-day daily diary study, each evening reporting the perceived controllability of the worst stressor of the day and their respective use of situation modification. Planned multilevel models will estimate each individual’s within-person association between perceived stressor controllability and situation modification as an index of context-sensitivity. We will test whether context-sensitive regulation is more strongly associated with fluid abilities among younger adults, and with crystallised abilities among older adults. Analyses are currently ongoing.

Short-term intra-individual variability (SIIV) of daily-life emotion, cognition, and behavior in very old age has been understood either in terms of adaptive flexibility in responding to varying contextual demands or maladaptive instability of functioning signaling increasing vulnerability of the psychological system. Thus, flexibility may be linked with variability across different situational contexts, whereas instability may cause variability within the same or similar situational contexts. Following this reasoning, we aimed to examine how contextual features prompt SIIV in old people’s daily life. We analyzed ambulatory assessments (6 per day across 7 consecutive days) from an old age sample (VITAL project, following-up participants from the BASE 2 and ILSE studies, N=185; aged 73-92). included. With data collection still ongoing, we used for the first extensive information of momentary contextual characteristics included in the VITAL data to present an approach to disentangle within-context from between-context SIIV of selected momentary outcome variables. To illustrate this approach, we will focus on results obtained for scores of momentary positive and negative affect, and work memory. Between-context variability amounted to 40-50% of SIIV in affect, but < 10% of SIIV in the cognitive test scores, and further analyses suggest tentatively that higher between-context variability in affective reactions is associated with more favorable (between-person) self-reported well-being and health. These findings provide first, yet not conclusive, evidence on the conceptual distinction of maladaptive within-context instability versus adaptive between-context flexibility of psychological functioning in old age.

Affect dynamics in daily life are closely associated with functioning in other domains, including cognition: individuals with lower cognitive capacities often show greater emotional vulnerability in response to stress. Yet, it remains unclear how slow, decades-long changes in cognitive functioning relate to fast-paced affective dynamics in later life. To address this gap, we examined three components of momentary affect dynamics: (a) base level negative affect, or the level of negative emotion experienced during moments without stressors; (b) stressor reactivity, defined as increases in negative affect when a stressor was reported relative to stressor-free moments; and (c) affective systemic noise, referring to moment-to-moment fluctuations in negative affect unrelated to stressors. We also explored whether momentary control beliefs serve as proximal buffers of these dynamics. Our study drew on more than 20 years of repeated cognitive assessments combined with up to 42 ecological momentary assessments (EMA) across seven days. Participants were 155 older adults (ages 65–69 and 85–88; 47–59% women) who contributed over 6,500 momentary reports of negative affect, perceived stressor exposure, and control beliefs. Analyses are currently ongoing. Potential findings from this study promise to inform how affective responses emerge from the interplay of long-term cognitive aging and momentary control beliefs across multiple timescales, contributing to the broader developmental understanding of affect dynamics as people move across old age.

Emotions and Emotion Regulation in Educational Contexts: Insights from Students and Teachers
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Ulrike E. Nett (Universität Augsburg)
Prof. Dr. Stephanie Lichtenfeld
Room: HU
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The school context is inherently emotional for both students and teachers. Theoretical and empirical research consistently demonstrates that the emotional experiences of students and teachers are closely linked to their well-being as well as to learning and work-related outcomes, respectively. Accordingly, effective emotion regulation is of central importance for both teachers and students.
In this regard, theoretical accounts (Gross, 1998; Harley, 2019) and empirical evidence (Rottweiler et al., 2023) suggest that emotion regulation is person-, situation-, and emotion-specific in nature. However, relatively little is known about the corresponding predictors and correlates of effective emotion regulation across these components. Moreover, the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which emotion regulation strategies shape emotional experiences and related outcomes remain insufficiently understood.
The papers presented in this symposium aim to address these gaps by examining emotion regulation from the perspectives of both students (Papers 1 and 2) and teachers (Papers 3 and 4). Paper 1 examines person-specific tendencies in elementary school students’ emotion regulation and their associations with individual characteristics. Paper 2 focuses on the moderating role of attachment security in the relationship between emotion regulation and outcomes such as procrastination and motivation regulation. Paper 3 investigates the interplay between teachers’ discrete emotions, emotional labor, and burnout-related constructs, including emotional exhaustion and depersonalization, highlighting the person- and emotion-specific nature of emotion regulation. Paper 4 explores the situation- and emotion-specificity of teachers’ emotion regulation, including potential interacting effects. A concluding discussion will integrates the findings across all four papers.

Process-Oriented Emotion Regulation in Elementary School – A Person-Centered Approach
Lilian Schnell
Show details
Authors:
Lilian Schnell
Stephanie Lichtenfeld
Arnold Lohaus
Jana-Elisa Rüth

Emotion regulation (ER) is crucial for children’s development and well-being. ER strategies are commonly classified as functional (e.g., reappraisal) or dysfunctional (e.g., suppression). From a process-oriented perspective, strategies can also be categorized according to their temporal position within the emotion-generating process into five families of ER strategies: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change, and response modulation. Depending on their position in this process, individuals may rely on different ER strategies. Person-centered approaches enable the identification of patterns in strategy use, but research on ER profiles in childhood, especially from a process-oriented perspective, is scarce.
The present study aimed to identify ER profiles in primary school children. The sample comprised 362 children (7–11 years) who completed the Process-Oriented Emotion Regulation Measure for Children and Adolescents (POEM-CA), assessing functional and dysfunctional strategies across the five strategy families. Latent profile analysis identified five ER profiles.
Profiles 1 and 2 were characterized by predominantly functional or predominantly dysfunctional strategies. Profile 3 showed moderate use of all strategies. Profile 4 was marked by high use of all strategies except situation selection and modification. Profile 5 primarily used functional situation-related strategies but dysfunctional strategies of attentional deployment and cognitive change. These findings indicate that distinct patterns of ER strategy use are already evident in childhood. Further analyses will examine the role of age and gender as well as differences in well-being between the ER profiles. These analyses could provide initial insights into ER as a potential risk or protective factor for child development.

Student Attachment Style as a Moderator of the Relationship Between Emotion Regulation and Procrastination

Show details
Authors:

Viviane Scherenberg
Katrin Klingsieck

Previous studies show that emotion regulation skills reduce procrastination and have an influence on motivation regulation. The Adaptive Coping with Emotion model developed by Berking and Znoj (2008) posits the adaptive regulation of aversive emotions as a central component of emotional competence. From the perspective of adult attachment theory, self-soothing through the activation of secure attachment representations makes a key contribution to adaptive emotion regulation. Although many studies show that secure attachment, in constrast to anxious or avoident attachment, is a key predictor of the development of emotion regulation skills, there are currently no studies investigating the influence of attachment security on the relationship between emotion regulation and procrastination or motivation regulation.
The present study aims to close this research gap. It has been shown that different attachment patterns are associated with different implicit preferences in emotion regulation. Accordingly, it is expected that attachment style has a moderating influence on the relationship between emotion regulation and other outcomes that are influenced by emotion regulation, in this case procrastination and motivation regulation.
A cross-sectional study based on self-report data (N = 69 students; 65% female, M = 17,9 years; SD = 0,9) indicated that, especially among students with an avoidant attachment style, higher levels of self-soothing were negatively associated with procrastination and difficulties in motivation regulation. Self-soothing appears to be negatively correlated with procrastination in students with an insecure-avoidant attachment style, while it is associated with reduced motivation regulation in students with a secure attachment style. Contrary to our assumptions, anxious attachment does not moderate these relationships. Implications and limitations will be discussed in the presentation.

Teachers’ Emotional Experience as a Core Driver of Burnout: The Role of Discrete Emotions and Emotional Labor
Anne C. Frenzel
Show details
Authors:

Lia Daniels

Teacher emotions and their regulation are central to teachers’ psychological well-being. Specifically, emotional labor (e.g., hiding negative emotions to abide with display rules) predicts teacher burnout. Notably, existing emotional labor research has largely neglected discrete trait emotions as burnout predictors, and to operationalize emotional labor with respect to specific emotions (i.e., faking joy, hiding anger). In the present contribution, we propose that teachers’ discrete trait emotions and their emotion-specific labor strategy use jointly predict teacher burnout.
To test this, teachers from Canada and Germany (N =375, Mage =38.44, 52% male) reported their emotional exhaustion and depersonalization, the frequency and intensity of their teaching-related anger, anxiety, shame, and joy and their emotion-specific labor strategy use (hiding and faking).
Preregistered regression analyses controlling for gender and teaching experience showed that frequent and intense anger (β=.38, p < .001), anxiety (β=.60, p < .001), and shame (β=.28, p < .001) positively and joy (β=-.49, p < .001) negatively predict emotional exhaustion. A similar pattern emerged for depersonalization. Above and beyond those effects, the findings supported that hiding anger (β=.23 , p < .001) and faking joy (β=.12, p=.008) positively predict emotional exhaustion, with comparable effects for depersonalization. Beyond main effects, anger and hiding anger interacted to predict depersonalization (β=.11, p=.015), indicating that hiding anger is more strongly associated with depersonalization among teachers who experience higher levels of anger. Our findings underscore the central role of discrete emotions in teacher burnout and that emotional labor can exacerbate the effects of frequency and intensity of negative emotions.

Teachers’ situation- and emotion-specific emotion regulation
Tanja Bross
Show details
Authors:
Tanja Bross
Ulrike E. Nett

Teachers encounter various situations in their daily work (Frenzel et al, 2015), each eliciting different emotions that require regulation. Although theoretical models (Gross, 1998; Harley, 2019) and empirical studies (Rottweiler et al., 2023) emphasize that emotion regulation is specific to the person, situation, and emotional experience, little is known about how teachers regulate emotions across different professional situations. This study examined (1) whether emotion regulation differs across daily work situations and (2) whether strategy use depends on the experienced emotion in these situations.
165 teachers from elementary (n=86) and middle schools (n=79) participated in a 14-day diary study (Mage=43.31 years, SD=11.12; 83.6% female), overall completing 1,604 daily questionnaires. Work situations were reported openly and coded into six categories: teaching, interaction with colleagues, organization, preparation, interaction with parents, and other situations. For each situation teachers reported emotions (joy, pride, enthusiasm, anger, anxiety, boredom) and emotion regulation strategies (avoidance, taking action, social support, distraction, rumination, reappraisal, suppression, expression).
Results showed that teachers’ strategy use varied by situation and emotion. During teaching and interacting with colleagues, avoidance and distraction were used less frequently than in other situations. In organizational situations, teachers reported less reappraisal and expression but greater use of suppression. During preparation, teachers relied less on social support, rumination, and expression, but used suppression more frequently. When interacting with parents, avoidance and expression were used less, whereas rumination and suppression were used more frequently. Strategy use also differed by the specific emotion experienced. Interaction effects of situation and emotion will further be discussed.

The discussion will synthesize the findings of the four presented papers and situate them within the broader theoretical and empirical landscape of research on emotional experiences and emotion regulation in school contexts. The results will be interpreted with respect to underlying psychological mechanisms, boundary conditions, and the dynamic interplay of person-, situation-, and emotion-specific processes that shape emotion regulation. Building on these insights, the discussion will highlight key theoretical implications for models of emotion regulation in educational settings and outlines directions for future research, including methodological and conceptual avenues, to advance a more nuanced understanding of emotion regulation in educational contexts.

From Experience to Intervention: Exploring Loneliness Across Daily Dynamics and Life Stages
Chair(s) Anne Neuber (University Witten/Herdecke)
Room: PT
Topic: Mental Health
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Loneliness is a pervasive experience with substantial consequences across the life course. Understanding when and how loneliness arises, how it is regulated in everyday life and how it develops over time is crucial for informing prevention and intervention programs. This symposium integrates qualitative and quantitative research to examine loneliness across cultural contexts, lived experience, daily regulatory processes, long-term trajectories, and intervention mechanisms. The symposium starts with a cross-national perspective by examining social and emotional loneliness across 25 countries to contextualize age-related differences in loneliness across cultural settings. The second talk explores how loneliness is experienced by university students, drawing on qualitative research to capture their lived experiences in higher education. The third talk focuses on later life and examines psychological obsolescence, i.e., perceived difficulty keeping up with societal and technological change, as a predictor of loneliness change in older adulthood. The fourth talk shifts the focus to within-person processes, conceptualizing loneliness as part of a functional regulatory cycle linking loneliness states, reaffiliation motivation, and social contact in daily life. Extending this process-oriented perspective, the fifth talk investigates whether patterns of daily loneliness dynamics predict changes in trait loneliness over time. The symposium concludes with a contribution on intervention mechanisms, examining mediators of a cognitive-behavioural internet-based self-help intervention for loneliness. Together, these contributions illustrate loneliness as a dynamic, context-sensitive phenomenon that unfolds throughout life, highlighting the importance of integrating experience-based, mechanistic, and applied perspectives to advance theory, empirical research and intervention.

Social and Emotional Loneliness Around the World: Evidence from 25 Countries
Anne Neuber
Show details
Authors:
Anne Neuber
Susanne Buecker

Previous research shows that social loneliness (i.e., lacking a broader network) and emotional loneliness (i.e., lacking intimate relationships) are only moderately correlated and follow distinct age-related trajectories across adulthood. However, most facet-specific research on loneliness has focused on Western, European contexts, leaving it unclear whether these patterns generalize across cultural settings. This study examines age differences in social and emotional loneliness across 25 countries in Europe, Asia, and South America using data from the Generations and Gender Survey. The analyses draw on largely cross-sectional data with several thousand participants per country spanning the adult life course. Social and emotional loneliness are assessed with comparable measures across countries, allowing the derivation of country-specific norm values for both facets. These norms provide a reference for interpreting absolute and relative levels of loneliness across national contexts. Multilevel models with individuals nested within countries are used to examine age-related differences in social and emotional loneliness and to compare these age patterns across countries. Based on prior research on cultural differences in overall loneliness, we expect higher average levels of both loneliness facets in more collectivistic compared to more individualistic countries. Moreover, we expect age gradients in both loneliness facets to vary across countries, indicating that the life-course timing and magnitude of social and emotional loneliness differ depending on cultural context. By differentiating between social and emotional loneliness, providing country-specific norm values, and covering a wide range of countries, this study advances a more nuanced understanding of how loneliness manifests across cultures and across adulthood.

"I Didn’t Experience It as Studying Together" – An Exploratory Qualitative Study of Loneliness Experienced by University Students
Vanessa Wenig
Show details
Authors:
Vanessa Wenig
Laura Pilz González
Christiane Stock
Katherina Heinrichs

Background: The transition to university is a pivotal stage in emerging adulthood, characterised by personal and social changes. Many students experience loneliness during this time, which can detrimentally affect their well-being and academic development. This study aimed to explore how university students describe and experience loneliness within the context of higher education. It also aimed to understand how loneliness emerges in the university environment from the students' perspective.
Methods: We explored the lived experience of lonely students in Germany by conducting 17 qualitative semi-structured interviews, which we analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.
Results: Loneliness at university was experienced as an absence of everyday companionship and connection with peers, rather than as lacking emotional intimacy. This was primarily related to shared study activities and everyday situations, such as shared mealtimes or group work. Students sought meaningful relationships, though these did not necessarily need to be with fellow students. Social connections were challenged by differing life contexts and institutional barriers. Universities were perceived as prioritising performance over belonging, with few opportunities for connection and little awareness of loneliness. High expectations, shaped by societal narratives and challenges of transition, intensified these experiences, while stigma and shame hindered students from seeking help.
Conclusion: This study calls for universities to actively promote social connection as a key aspect of student well-being, rather than relying on one-size-fits-all interventions. Loneliness among students is not a personal issue, rather, it is influenced by relational, university-related, and societal factors.

A specific challenge of later life relates to the perceived pace of social change (i.e., psychological obsolescence), which may contribute to enhanced feelings of loneliness. Loneliness (assessed with the 6-item De Jong-Gierveld Loneliness Scale) was measured at baseline and follow-up and modeled as a manifest variable. Psychological obsolescence and several covariates were specified as correlates of baseline loneliness and as predictors of change in loneliness. We observed that feelings of obsolescence were significantly associated with baseline loneliness, indicating higher initial levels among individuals with higher values of obsolescence. Beyond baseline levels, psychological obsolescence significantly predicted loneliness at follow-up, suggesting an association with changes in loneliness over time. Loneliness showed substantial temporal stability. Among the covariates, being socially isolated and not living in a partnership were associated with higher levels of subsequent loneliness, indicating a risk factor over time. Findings suggest that in old age the experience of obsolescence is particularly associated with increasing loneliness over time, above and beyond other established risk factors.

A Functional Perspective on the Within-Person Dynamics of Loneliness and Reaffiliation
Christoph Heine
Show details
Authors:
Christoph Heine
Susanne Buecker
Michael Dufner

Functional theories conceptualize loneliness states as an adaptive signal that motivates individuals to reconnect with others. Chronic (i.e., high trait) loneliness is thought to involve impairments in this regulatory process. We examined this conceptualization in a 30-day daily diary study (N = 442; n = 10,194 diary entries). Using linear multilevel models, we tested this regulatory cycle as three within-person contingencies linking loneliness, reaffiliation motivation, and actual social contact. Results supported this idea of a functional cycle: Within individuals, (1) higher loneliness states predicted a stronger desire for reaffiliation, (2) a stronger desire for reaffiliation predicted more social contact on the next day, and, closing the cycle, (3) greater social contact predicted lower loneliness states. Results further indicated that the regulatory cycle was impaired among individuals high in trait loneliness, as trait loneliness moderated two of these paths. Specifically, for trait-lonely people, (2) the positive association between reaffiliation motivation and subsequent social contact was weaker and (3) the negative association between social contact and loneliness states was stronger. These findings suggest that chronic loneliness may be rooted in difficulties to translate the desire for social contact into action, combined with a heightened sensitivity to reduced social contact.

Loneliness describes an unpleasant feeling that people experience if their social relationships and contacts do not meet their social needs. This feeling can be experienced as a momentary state or as a relatively stable trait over a longer time period. Recent research suggests that for some individuals, trait loneliness increases and subsequently persists at high levels. To prevent this adverse development and its negative consequences it is crucial to identify factors that can predict such critical changes early on. One promising indicator of future changes in trait loneliness may be certain patterns of state loneliness fluctuations that might indicate maladaptive loneliness regulation. Therefore, this study aims to use interindividual differences in how loneliness is experienced from day to day, such as its variability, instability, or inertness as predictors of changes in trait loneliness over one year. For this, we use data from a pre-registered 14-day daily diary study (N ≈ 490) with two assessments of trait loneliness 1 year apart. To estimate the unique predictive value of different indicators of daily state loneliness fluctuations for future trait loneliness, we conduct a hierarchical regression analysis. Additionally, we consider neuroticism, a person's tendency towards emotional instability, as a moderator to examine potential between-person differences in predicting trait loneliness. This study will inform recommendations for interventions and prevention strategies to tackle persistent loneliness.

Background: Loneliness, a common phenomenon in the general population and clinical practice, is associated with several psychiatric disorders. Theoretically, cognitive biases and counterproductive behaviours in social situations contribute to maintaining loneliness. Interventions tackling maladaptive social cognitions are among the most effective in reducing loneliness. Due to loneliness stigma, internet-based self-help interventions (IBIs) hold promise, with studies indicating cognitive-behavioural IBIs can reduce loneliness. To increase the effectiveness of IBIs, a deeper understanding of how loneliness is reduced is needed. The aim of this secondary analysis is to identify how changes in psychopathological symptoms or cognitive model components impact loneliness after a cognitive-behavioural IBI.

Loneliness was measured with the 9-item UCLA Loneliness Scale. Psychopathological symptoms, cognitive bias, and counterproductive behaviours were assessed as potential mediators. Mediation analyses assessed how changes in potential mediators influenced loneliness in the two intervention groups at follow-up.
Results: Results are not available at the time of abstract submission.
Conclusion and Implications: Results will be discussed in relation to existing research. They will provide a deeper understanding of changes in loneliness following an IBI and help inform the improvement of existing and the development of future loneliness interventions.

Investigating Individual Differences in Actual Behavior in Psychological Science and Beyond
Chair(s) Dr. Simon Breil (University of Münster)
Niclas Kuper (University of Münster)
Room: LT
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Psychological science defines many of its core constructs in behavioral terms, yet empirical research relies predominantly on self-report measures that capture individuals’ experiences, beliefs, and memories rather than their actual behavior. This mismatch limits our understanding of individual differences, obscures behavioral mechanisms, and constrains integration across research domains.
This symposium brings together four contributions that address this challenge by focusing on individual differences in actual behavior in human and non-human animals. In the first presentation, Back discusses the implications of measuring personality mainly through self-reports. He argues for grounding psychological personality research in observable behavior by developing scalable behavioral assessment tools and strengthening collaboration with animal personality research. In the second presentation, Bhattacharjee and Massen demonstrate a behavioral approach to personality research in macaques. Using a cooperative loose-string paradigm, they examine how personality differences predict partner choice and dyadic cooperation.
The next two presentations focus on individual differences in humans. Kuper et al. investigate to what extent different personality trait measures predict later observed behavior, contrasting self- versus other-reports and global versus state measures. Breil et al. focus on social skills, an inherently behavioral construct that is typically assessed via self-reports. Using standardized interpersonal simulations, they examine how behaviorally expressed skills relate to skill self-concepts, the stability of skills over time, and their links to later outcomes.
Together, these talks underscore the limits of self-reports and, across human and animal research, outline concrete pathways for grounding personality research in observable behavior. Finally, Wrzus concludes the symposium with an integrative discussion.

Towards a Behavioral Assessment of Personality (Across Species)
Mitja Back | University of Münster | Germany
Show details
Author:
Mitja Back | University of Münster | Germany

Personality refers to individual differences in experience and behavior. Thus, to understand personality differences, we need to assess not only how much individuals feel frightened, strive for status, or derive optimistic interpretations; but also, how much they act nervously, show expressive gestures, engage in demanding tasks, explore their environment, actively approach, avoid or aggress against others. Despite repeated calls to focus more on actual behavior, personality measurements are still almost exclusively measurements of individuals' experiences and memories. Findings on the structure, momentary dynamics, development and consequences of personality mostly pertain to the personality self-concept. This seriously limits our understanding of personality and contradicts its conceptualization. To move towards a more mature personality assessment, we need to regularly incorporate actual behavioral measures of personality. This is burdensome and it hinges on the development of standardized and scalable behavioral assessment tools across laboratory and field contexts. I argue that close cooperation with research on animal personality, which has flourished in recent years, is a worthwhile way to (finally) anchor personality psychology research in actual behavior – the natural level of analysis for non-human species. This includes, for example, the joint derivation of trait-relevant contexts and situational triggers, behavioral indicators at various levels of abstraction, and automated tools for their assessment. In addition to the necessary expansion of our methodological repertoire, this allows for advances in the dynamic conceptualization of personality. Finally, such a behavioral approach fosters a cross-species understanding of personality, which includes overarching similarities and systematic differences between human and non-human animals.

Association Between Personality Differences and Dyadic Cooperation in Macaque Societies
Dr. Debottam Bhattacharjee | Utrecht University | Netherlands
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Debottam Bhattacharjee | Utrecht University | Netherlands
Jorg J. M. Massen | Utrecht University | Netherlands

Cooperation is widespread in the animal kingdom and consistent inter-individual behavioural differences, i.e., personality, may act as a key proximate mechanism shaping it. In humans, prosocial personality traits such as sociability and extraversion are positively associated with cooperation and are often conceptualised as “cooperative personality.” Similar patterns have been reported across non-human taxa, suggesting the phenomenon of personality-linked cooperation. Another prominent framework for understanding these dynamics is personality homophily, where individuals with similar personality traits preferentially associate, form social bonds, and cooperate. Indirect evidence for homophily-driven cooperation exists across humans, non-human primates, birds, and other taxa, with implications for friendship and reproduction. However, cooperation does not exclusively arise from personality similarity. In humans, individuals with dissimilar personalities can also cooperate effectively by contributing complementary skills or behavioural tendencies. Emerging evidence from non-human animals suggests that personality heterophily, particularly along non-social traits, such as boldness or exploration, may similarly facilitate cooperation, yet this remains comparatively understudied. While existing research has prioritised homophily as a predictor, the role of personality dissimilarity in cooperative decision-making is poorly understood. We conducted a cooperative loose-string paradigm to measure dyadic cooperation and used a multi-method approach combining repeated behavioural observations and experiments to assess personality in >100 macaques across six species (e.g., Macaca mulatta, M. fuscata). By integrating information on overall and individual-level social and non-social traits, we tested how personality similarity and dissimilarity influenced partner choice and cooperation, contributing to a critical understanding of the mechanisms underpinning cooperation.

Most personality research focuses on self-reported global trait ratings even when examining behavioral personality constructs. Several alternative approaches to trait measurement have been posited to be closer to behavior. These include, for instance, state reports from experience sampling, other-reports, and combinations of both. However, it remains unclear how well these different measures predict actual behavior. We provide initial evidence from a highly multi-methodological study (N = 88) in which actual behavior in the laboratory was predicted from six trait measures: global self-report, global informant-report, time-based self-reported states (fortnightly diaries), time-based peer-reported states, event-based self-reported states (after social interactions), and event-based peer-reported states. We focus on four behaviors (warmth, expressiveness, self-confidence, nervousness). Self-reported states were rarely incrementally predictive above global self-report and thus not as close to behavior as often suggested. Further, other-report was more consistently linked to behavior than self-report. Importantly, other-reported states were substantially predictive beyond global informant-report and self-reported states and thus represent an underused trait measure that is closer to behavior. Overall, our findings highlight the value of going beyond self-report in behavioral personality science.

In this study, we examine social skill expression using behavioral observations from brief interpersonal simulations. These simulations consist of standardized, observer-rated role-play tasks designed to systematically elicit the respective skills via structured interpersonal challenges. Our behavior-based assessment captures three predefined social skills: agency skill (getting ahead in social situations), communion skill (getting along in social situations), and interpersonal resilience (staying calm in social situations). Behavioral skill expressions and skill self-concepts were assessed twice, approximately two years apart. At a follow-up more than three years after the initial assessment, we additionally collected behavioral outcomes and self-reported life outcomes. We investigate (1) associations between expressed skills and individuals’ skill self-concepts (N > 900), (2) the longitudinal stability of expressed social skills (N > 500), and (3) links between expressed skills and later behavioral and life outcomes (N > 200). We report our findings and discuss the theoretical and practical implications of distinguishing skill self-concepts from actual skill expression, highlighting the value of behavior-based approaches in social skill research and assessment.

This meta-analysis synthesizes the quantitative evidence on the impostor phenomenon within academic work contexts. The impostor phenomenon has gained increasing scholarly and public attention as the experience of intellectual fraudulence accompanied by a fear of exposure. While the empirical studies on the impostor phenomenon and its correlates have grown markedly in recent years, conceptual frameworks as well as quantitative review work remain limited. For this first encompassing meta-analysis of the impostor phenomenon, we focus on articles that investigated the impostor phenomenon in academic researchers, doctoral students, graduate/master’s students, and undergraduate students across diverse disciplines. We specifically investigate the conceptual antecedents of the individual (i.e., demographics, personality aspects), in the social context (e.g., social support), and in the academic career context (e.g., academic rank). Next, we investigate the conceptual outcomes of the impostor phenomenon for the individual (i.e., mental health) and for the individual’s academic career (i.e., academic productivity, career aspirations). Our objectives are to (a) develop a conceptual overview of potential antecedents and consequences of the impostor phenomenon, (b) test these associations through correlational analyses, and (c) propose a research agenda to guide future work on the impostor phenomenon.

Grit is a construct that is conceptualized as perseverance and passion for long-term goals (Duckworth et al., 2007) and typically measured in two dimensions – consistency of interest and perseverance. Grit is viewed as a personality trait supporting academic and non-academic success. However, research has raised concerns regarding the construct validity of grit. While its dimensions can be differentiated from motivational constructs such as goal orientations, perseverance shows stronger associations than consistency of interest. This study examines the relations between grit dimensions and achievement goal orientations and explores whether consistency of interest and perseverance can be differentiated with respect to temporal perspective as an indirect test of potential state-like tendencies. In an online survey, 257 university students (Mage = 24,02 years) completed established measures of grit and goal orientations, as well as newly developed items assessing long-term and short-term self-perceptions of consistency of interest and perseverance. Comparative CFA models indicated that a two-factor structure of grit provided a better fit to the data than a single-factor model when examined alongside achievement goal orientations. Perseverance was positively associated with mastery goals, whereas consistency of interest showed no significant correlations. The grit dimensions were moderately correlated. Exploratory analyses further suggested that temporal perspective contributes to a more differentiated representation of grit dimensions.

Reference
Duckworth, A. L., Peterson, C., Matthews, M. D., & Kelly, D. R. (2007). Grit: Perseverance and passion for long-term goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 92(6), 1087–1101.

How to best practice a skill is a central question in many fields of psychology, including clinical, industrial-organizational, and educational psychology, as well as the performance sciences. Deliberate practice is a specific type of practice that, according to Ericsson and colleagues, leads to high performance levels across domains, including sports, music, and academic or professional education such as psychotherapy training. Questions about the role of deliberate practice within the expertise attainment process remain unresolved because inconsistent definitions and varying, often insufficient measures hinder the accumulation of knowledge across studies and domains. To address these issues, this study synthesized prevailing definitions of deliberate practice to develop a standardized, psychometrically validated instrument suitable for cross-domain research on skill acquisition. Reliability and validity of the instrument were assessed in a cross-domain sample of 1,594 people. Results indicated high reliability and internal consistency. Strong correlations with conceptually related learning measures and performance outcomes demonstrated the validity of the instrument. In sum, the Deliberate Practice Inventory provides a valid, multifaceted measure of practice quality and can be used across domains, including educational, performance-based, and professional training contexts.

Does even brief exposure matter? Cognitive costs of short video use on processing speed, mental fatigue, and time distortion in a comparative experiment

Show details
Authors:
Thorsten Otto | Technical University Braunschweig | Germany
Prof Barbara Thies | Technical University Braunschweig

Short videos have become a dominant form of digital media consumption, characterized by fast-paced, highly fragmented, and algorithmically personalized content. Prior research has focused on (problematic) long-term short video use and has paid little attention to the situational context of this use. Therefore, the present study aimed to examine how watching short videos affects time distortion, acute fatigue, and processing speed, which are central to effective cognitive functioning during learning. In line with memory-based and attentional models, watching short videos should lead to retrospective time overestimation due to increased temporal markers and frequent contextual changes, and to prospective time underestimation due to immersion, leaving fewer attentional resources to monitor time. Additionally, watching short videos can reduce acute fatigue through mood enhancement (mood management theory) or increase it through cognitive overload, thereby impairing processing speed. The study employed a laboratory experiment (N = 129) with a mixed between-within-subjects design, manipulating the type of activity across three groups: watching short videos for 10 minutes on a private smartphone, watching a 10-minute documentary on a laboratory monitor, or engaging in a non-media activity for 10 minutes. Before and after the activity, participants completed a questionnaire regarding acute fatigue and performed reaction-time tasks to assess processing speed. Retrospective (post-experiment) and prospective time distortion (post-activity) were computed with the difference between estimated and actual duration. Long-term short video use, time estimation ability, and chronic fatigue were statistically controlled to isolate situational effects. Limitations, implications, and future directions are discussed.

Interview data were analyzed using a qualitative approach informed by two theoretical frameworks. First, identity exploration and commitment were examined using process-oriented concepts. Second, Self-Determination Theory was applied to analyze participants’ self-perceptions with respect to autonomy, competence, and relatedness as basic psychological needs underlying identity development.

Participants emphasized the importance of these experiences for developing autonomous pathways toward a professional identity and for integrating this identity into their broader sense of self. The results further suggest that academic contexts supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness contribute to students’ self-development processes. Implications are discussed for higher education teaching aimed at strengthening students’ self-development as a contribution to mental health within the challenging developmental period of emerging adulthood.

Wirksamkeit von Interventionen zur Gesundheitsverhaltensänderung basierend auf dem Health Action Process Approach
Prof. Dr. Ralf Schwarzer | Freie Universitaet Berlin | Germany
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Ralf Schwarzer | Freie Universitaet Berlin | Germany

Hintergrund. Der Health Action Process Approach (HAPA) differenziert zwischen motivationalen und volitionalen Phasen der Verhaltensänderung. Das Modell integriert zentrale Konstrukte wie Risikowahrnehmung, Ergebniserwartungen, Selbstwirksamkeit, Intention und Planung.
Zielsetzung. Systematische Zusammenfassung der Evidenz HAPA-basierter Interventionen über verschiedene Gesundheitsverhaltensweisen hinweg mit Fokus auf deren Wirksamkeit und Identifikation zentraler Interventionskomponenten.
Methoden. Das erste Review umfasste 108 Stichproben über multiple Verhaltensdomänen, mit Analysen für körperliche Aktivität (41 Studien) und Ernährung (23 Studien). Das zweite Review identifizierte 74 randomisiert-kontrollierte HAPA-Studien zu 12 Gesundheitsverhaltensweisen, primär körperliche Aktivität und Ernährung.
Ergebnisse. Pfadanalysen bestätigten die theoretisch postulierten Zusammenhänge zwischen HAPA-Konstrukten. Risikowahrnehmung, Ergebniserwartungen und Selbstwirksamkeit erwiesen sich als Prädiktoren der Intentionsbildung. Handlungs- und Bewältigungsplanung sowie Selbstwirksamkeit überbrückten die Intentions-Verhaltens-Lücke. Die Interventionswirksamkeit variierte domänenspezifisch, wobei die stärksten Effekte für Mundhygiene, Impfverhalten sowie Obst- und Gemüsekonsum nachgewiesen wurden. Interventionen mit kombinierter motivationaler Unterstützung (Risikofeedback, Nutzen-Kosten-Bewertung, Selbstwirksamkeitsförderung) und verhaltensbezogener Unterstützung (Planung, Handlungskontrolle) zeigten günstige Outcomes.
Schlussfolgerungen. HAPA-basierte Interventionen fördern Gesundheitsverhaltensänderungen über multiple Domänen. Die praktische Implementation erfordert maßgeschneiderte Risikokommunikation, präzise Nutzenformulierung, spezifische Wenn-Dann-Pläne, systematische Barriereidentifikation mit entsprechenden Bewältigungsstrategien sowie Selbstbeobachtungsunterstützung.
Klinische Implikationen. Effektive Interventionen sollten beide Phasen des Veränderungsprozesses systematisch adressieren, wobei Planungs- und Selbstregulationsstrategien zur Überbrückung der Intentions-Verhaltens-Lücke besonders zu betonen sind. Weitere Forschung zu Langzeiteffekten und optimaler Interventionsdosierung ist erforderlich.

This study investigated whether variations in teachers' interpersonal behavior across students in their classes are systematically related to students' social group memberships and associated stereotypes. We integrate the complementarity principle of interpersonal theory (Sadler et al., 2011) with the stereotype content model (Fiske et al., 2002). Together, we predict that teachers' behavior is complementary to their perceptions of the communion and agency associated with students group memberships, such that higher perceived communion of a student's social group elicits more communal behavior from teachers.
We analyzed 325 elementary school teachers' descriptions of their communal and agentic behavior in dyads with 4,341 students. Students' standardized achievement scores in German and mathematics and their grades were included to control for their competencies. Multilevel regressions showed that students with an Arabic or Turkish immigrant backgrounds, low socioeconomic status, or social-emotional problem behaviors (affected by contemptuous stereotypes) received particularly low communion and strong agency, compared to their respective outgroup. Boys (affected by envious stereotypes) received less communion but, contrary to expectations, stronger agency than girls. Students with mental or physical difficulties (affected by paternalistic stereotypes) received higher communion and agency than students without such difficulties.
This study advances our understanding of stereotype-based educational inequity. By demonstrating that interpersonal complementarity operates in stereotype-consistent ways, this study extends interpersonal theory to educational contexts and identifies dyadic teacher-student interactions as a mechanism linking stereotypes to differential educational practices and student experiences.

Who Laughs, Who Sees, Who Knows? A Multi-Perspective Study of Teacher Humor in the Classroom
Dr. Hassan Banaruee | University of Education Weingarten | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Hassan Banaruee | University of Education Weingarten | Germany
Prof. Dr. Sonja Bieg | University of Education Weingarten | Germany

Teacher humor is increasingly recognized as an effective instructional tool that shapes students’ emotional, motivational, and cognitive experiences in the classroom, yet little is known about how humor is perceived across different classroom stakeholders. This study presents a multi-perspective investigation of teacher humor by integrating teacher and student self-reports, and observer assessments collected in authentic classroom settings. Four humor types (course-related, course-unrelated, self-disparaging, and aggressive) were examined across 15 high school classes (15 teachers; Mage = 39.9, SD = 7.8, 367 ninth-grade students; Mage = 14.2, SD = 0.5). Teacher humor in self-reported questionnaires was measured with the Teacher Humor from Students’ Perspective Scale (HUMLAS, Bieg & Dresel, 2016), and observed teacher humor was coded by two independent raters using a structured observation checklist derived from HUMLAS. Across all perspectives, correlation analyses revealed that humor types were moderately interrelated but empirically distinguishable. However, repeated-measures analyses demonstrated substantial perspective-dependent differences in perceived teacher humor. Observers consistently perceived significantly less course-related and self-disparaging humor than both teachers and students. Students reported higher levels of course-unrelated humor than observers and rated aggressive humor higher than teachers. These systematic discrepancies suggest that teacher humor is not uniformly perceived across perspectives and point to systematic perceptual differences in how different types of teacher humor are recognized. Our findings underscore the importance of considering multi-perspective approaches when studying instructional behaviors such as humor. Methodologically, this study highlights the added value of combining self-reports with observational data to capture how humor is perceived in classroom interactions.

Feeling capable, finding joy: reciprocal relationships between competence beliefs and intrinsic motivation in mathematics
Prof. Jeroen Lavrijsen | KU Leuven | Belgium
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Jeroen Lavrijsen | KU Leuven | Belgium
Prof. Karine Verschueren | KU Leuven | Belgium

Despite efforts to improve motivation for mathematics, secondary school students often report to not like their mathematics classes. Moreover, many students have low confidence in their mathematical capacities. Theoretically, intrinsic motivation and competence beliefs have been hypothesized to be mutually reinforcing: high intrinsic motivation may stimulate students to invest effort and thus enhance their competence, while experiencing success in learning would bring about feelings of accomplishment and positive affect. However, longitudinal evidence for these reciprocal processes remains limited and inconclusive, especially at the within‑student level (e.g., Paschke et al., 2025). This study examined reciprocal relationships between intrinsic motivation for and competence beliefs in mathematics in a large longitudinal sample of secondary school students (n = 3,409; 49.6% boys; Mage = 12.4 years), with four measurements across Grades 7 and 8. To distinguish between-student from within-student processes, both conventional Cross‑Lagged Panel Models and Random Intercept CLPMs were applied. Results revealed consistent positive cross-lagged effects from competence beliefs to intrinsic motivation, both at the between-student and within-student level, suggesting that students who feel more competent tend to subsequently enjoy mathematics better, both relative to their peers and relative to their usual level, controlling for prior enjoyment. By contrast, no robust evidence was found for a reverse path from intrinsic motivation to subsequent competence beliefs. These findings indicate that competence beliefs play a modest yet robust role in shaping students’ motivational development in mathematics, suggesting that strengthening students’ sense of competence may be an important avenue for fostering intrinsic motivation in the subject.

Expertise-Dependent Effects of Teachers’ Nonverbal Social Behavior on Learning: A Large-Scale Study Using Computer Vision
Jonas Frenkel | Universität Potsdam | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jonas Frenkel | Universität Potsdam | Germany
Uroš Petković | Technische Universität Berlin | Germany
Prof. Olaf Hellwich | Technische Universität Berlin | Germany
Prof. Rebecca Lazarides | Universität Potsdam | Germany

In social learning, learners’ motivation and cognitive performance are shaped not only by instructional content but also by the interpersonal cues through which it is conveyed. Yet it remains unclear to what extent the effects of instructors’ nonverbal social behaviors depend on learners’ individual differences. This study tests how the cognitive and motivational effects of nonverbal social behaviors - conceptualized as nonverbal immediacy (NVI) - interact with learner characteristics in naturalistic learning settings. Automated computer vision analysis of classroom videos was combined with large-scale survey and knowledge-test data from 1,070 students and 46 teachers to assess whether the benefits of NVI are uniform or moderated by prior knowledge and interest. Multilevel analyses showed that higher NVI consistently increased situational interest across students, regardless of initial interest. In contrast, NVI’s effect on knowledge acquisition depended on prior knowledge: students with higher baseline knowledge benefited from more expressive teachers, whereas those with lower prior knowledge showed diminished or negative effects. This interaction challenges the assumption of universal benefit, demonstrating that NVI’s motivational advantages coexist with expertise-contingent cognitive consequences. Furthermore, the findings underscore the need to distinguish social signals from functional nonverbal cues, as their expertise dependencies diverge. Methodologically, the work illustrates how integrating automated video analysis with survey data enables large-scale research on social learning in ecologically valid environments.

Executive Functions, Metacognition, Self-Regulation, and Self-Regulated Learning – What are We Talking About?
Chair(s) Jun. Prof. Dr. Julia Kerner auch Koerner (Universität Münster)
Prof. Dr. Friederike Blume
Room: AT
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

As students progress through school, they are expected to increasingly regulate their attention, behaviour and learning. While some meet these demands with ease, others experience persistent difficulties that may be associated with adverse educational outcomes. Research has identified four key constructs in this domain: executive functions (EF), metacognition (MC), self-regulation (SR), and self-regulated learning (SRL). Although conceptually related, these constructs have often been examined in isolation due to disciplinary and methodological divides, resulting in fragmented accounts that obscure their dynamic interrelations.
This symposium addresses this challenge by integrating theoretical and empirical perspectives on EF, MC, SR, and SRL. The first presentation provides a comparative conceptual overview and introduces the EMERGE model of learning, which situates these constructs along a continuum ranging from more biologically grounded mechanics (e.g., EF) to more culturally shaped regulatory pragmatics (e.g., strategy knowledge in SRL; https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/ug62w_v1). Four empirical contributions then examine different constellations of these constructs across developmental periods and methodological approaches. The first contribution presents data on the interplay of EF and SR strategies in three-year-olds in delay-of-gratification contexts. The second contribution reports analyses on the association between EF and SRL in fourth-grade students. The third contribution introduces a meta-analysis on the use of if–then plans in children. The fourth contribution examines the factorial structure of two questionnaire-based measures purported to assess EF and SR. All empirical contributions are discussed within the EMERGE framework, and the symposium concludes with a discussion of future research designs aimed at bridging fragmented research traditions on EF, MC, SR, and SRL.

A Review and Introduction of the EMERGE Model
Jun. Prof. Dr. Julia Kerner auch Koerner | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Jun. Prof. Dr. Julia Kerner auch Koerner | Germany
Jun. Prof. Dr. Maria Theobald
Dr. Friederike Blume

Executive functions (EF), metacognition (MC), self-regulation (SR), and self-regulated learning (SRL) are each robustly associated with academic achievement. However, despite substantial conceptual overlap, these constructs are frequently investigated in isolation, resulting in fragmented theoretical accounts and limited integration across research traditions. In this presentation, we report findings from a comprehensive review that systematically compares EF, MC, SR, and SRL with respect to their definitions, operationalisations, and the research designs commonly used to study them.
Based on this synthesis, we introduce the EMERGE model of learning, which conceptualises EF, MC, SR, and SRL as functionally distinct yet interconnected components arranged along a continuum from biologically grounded regulatory mechanics (e.g., EF) to culturally shaped, context-dependent pragmatics (e.g., strategy knowledge in SRL). Within this framework, SR in learning contexts is conceptualised as an integrative construct that links cognitive control processes with strategic and reflective components.
To guide empirical research, the model formulates two complementary hypotheses: a stage-setting hypothesis that emphasises long-term developmental relations among regulatory components, and a compensatory hypothesis that addresses short-term interactions between these components in predicting learning outcomes. We argue that testing these hypotheses requires longitudinal, experimental, and hybrid research designs capable of capturing both developmental change and dynamic regulation processes. The EMERGE model thus provides a conceptual foundation for integrating fragmented literatures and for advancing theory-driven diagnostics and interventions in educational contexts.

How do Inhibition and Strategy use Interact in the Prediction of Delay of Gratification Performance in 3-Year-Olds?
Anna Hessel | Institut für Psychologie in Bildung und Erziehung | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Anna Hessel | Institut für Psychologie in Bildung und Erziehung | Germany
Lea Penning
Julia Kerner auch Koerner

Delay-of-gratification tasks, such as the marshmallow task, show strong predictive validity for later academic achievement and are often treated as prototypical measures of self-regulation (Mischel et al., 1988; Moffitt et al., 2011). However, these tasks conflate multiple regulatory processes, most notably executive functions (particularly inhibition) and the use of self-regulatory strategies. Within the EMERGE framework, the compensatory hypothesis suggests that strategic behaviour may be especially relevant for children with lower inhibitory control.
In this study, three delay-of-gratification tasks (snack delay, attractive toy, and gift task) were administered to a sample of 159 children (72 girls) aged 3;0 to 3;11 years. Inhibition was assessed using three computerized tasks from a standardized executive function battery (EF Touch; Ulitzka et al., 2023), which load onto a single latent factor and provide excellent model fit (RMSEA = 0.000; CFI = 1.000; SRMR = 0.006). Self-regulatory strategies are currently being coded based on Gross’s (2015) process model of emotion regulation, distinguishing strategies according to the regulatory stage they target (e.g., distraction, reappraisal, soothing, response modulation), adapting an existing coding scheme (Lüken et al., 2025).
Data collection is complete and strategy coding is ongoing. A positive association between inhibition and strategy use would be consistent with a stage-setting account, although longitudinal data would be required for a direct test. In contrast, an interaction between inhibition and strategy use in predicting delay performance would provide support for the compensatory hypothesis.

The Relationship Between Self-Regulated Learning and Executive Functions – A Multimethod Approach
Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich
Show details
Authors:
Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich
Eric Klopp
Julia Ruhl
Julia Karbach
Franziska Perels

Self-regulated learning (SRL) describes a goal-oriented process in which learners monitor and regulate their behavior and comprises cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components (Perels et al., 2020). Similarly, executive functions (EF) support people in goal-setting, self-monitoring, and flexible adaptation of behaviour and comprise the components of working memory, inhibition, and shifting (Miyake et al., 2000). Despite both constructs focusing on goal-oriented behavior, they stem from different theoretical frameworks, leading to conceptual equivocality. Although previous studies show relationships between SRL and EF (Davis et al., 2021), a recent review underscores the influence of measurement methods (Dörrenbächer-Ulrich & Bregulla, 2024), with EF mostly measured in a contextualized, fine-grained manner, whereas SRL is mostly measured decontextualized. The previous study used a multimethod approach for SRL to examine the role of assessment granularity in the relationship between SRL and EF.
A sample of N = 107 fourth graders (M = 9.59, SD = 0.51, 45.8% female) was assessed for cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components of SRL using a decontextualized questionnaire, a contextualized microanalytical approach (Cleary & Callan, 2018), and a test to assess conditional SRL strategy knowledge. EF were measured with a Complex-Span-Task (working memory), an antisaccade task (inhibition), and the Wisconsin Card-Sorting-Test (shifting). The results showed few small-to-moderate correlations for single combinations of EF and SRL components, distributed across all three SRL instruments. These findings will be discussed in relation to their implications for assessment aspects in future studies on the relationship between SRL and EF.

Implementation Intentions: An Effective Self-Regulation Strategy for Children?
Jasmin Breitwieser
Show details
Authors:
Jasmin Breitwieser
Tilman Reinelt

The recently proposed EMERGE model (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/ug62w_v1) conceptualizes executive functions, metacognition, self-regulation, and self-regulated learning as hierarchically ordered along a continuum from biologically grounded processes (mechanics) to culturally shaped processes (pragmatics). Pragmatic processes are assumed to be amenable by explicit instruction of strategies. One prominent self-regulation strategy is the use of implementation intentions (Gollwitzer, 1999), which link a situational cue to a goal-directed action (e.g., “If/when situation X occurs, then I will perform behavior Y”). Due to their relative simplicity, they may be especially suitable for fostering self-regulation in children, whose self-regulation is still developing. However, little is known about the effectiveness of implementation intentions and moderating factors in children. Our pre-registered meta-analysis included 52 effect sizes from 42 studies (N = 12,957, Mage = 10.67 years). We found a small-to-medium effect of implementation intentions in children (Hedge’s g = 0.33, 95% CI [0.20; 0.46), with substantial heterogeneity (Q(51) = 183.47, p < .001). Moderator analyses revealed larger effects in younger children and in children with ADHD, lending tentative support to the compensatory hypothesis discussed in the EMERGE framework, which posits that self-regulation strategies may compensate for deficits in executive function. We conclude by outlining directions for future research, emphasizing a shift from teaching fixed plans toward supporting children in generating their own high-quality implementation intentions to foster adaptive self-regulation skills.

Questionnaire Measures of Executive Functions and Self-Regulation: Blurred Boundaries
Friederike Blume
Show details
Authors:
Friederike Blume
Dieter Baeyens | Belgium

Self-regulation (SR) is the capacity to adjust cognition, emotion, and behaviour in line with goals. Executive functions (EF), conceptualised as working memory, inhibition, and cognitive flexibility, are widely assumed to constitute the basis of SR. However, EF and SR are typically assessed using different approaches: EF via performance-based tasks and SR via behaviour rating scales. Responding concerns regarding the ecological validity of EF tasks, questionnaire-based measures such as the Behaviour Rating Inventory of EF (BRIEF) have been developed. The BRIEF includes subscales explicitly intended to reflect core EF domains. At the same time, their content overlaps conceptually with SR assessed by instruments such as the Strengths and Weaknesses of ADHD and Normal Behaviour scale (SWAN), raising the question of whether these BRIEF subscales capture EF or SR.
To address this issue, convergent and factorial validity of the BRIEF-2 core EF subscales and the SWAN were examined using parent reports of N=211 children (Mage=9.57 years, SD=1.01). Correlational analyses indicated convergence between conceptually related subscales (r=.68-.79). Structural equation models revealed two robust cross-instrument factors, combining BRIEF Working Memory with SWAN Inattention and BRIEF Inhibition with SWAN Hyperactivity–Impulsivity. In contrast, BRIEF Cognitive Flexibility emerged as a distinct factor without substantial SWAN loadings. All latent factors were correlated (r=.28-.54), and overall model fit was good.
Overall, although the BRIEF subscales were designed to operationalise core EFs, the findings suggest that rating-based measures of working memory and inhibition primarily reflect SR, highlighting the importance of measurement mode for the conceptual interpretation of regulatory constructs.
