Können Lehrkräfte bei der Interpretation von Lernverlaufsdaten durch Visualisierungen unterstützt werden?
Erika Lunowa | Pädagogische Hochschule Karlsruhe | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Erika Lunowa | Pädagogische Hochschule Karlsruhe | Germany
Dr. Sarah Bez | Pädagogische Hochschule Karlsruhe | Germany
Dr. Tom Rosman | Leibniz-Institut für Psychologie (ZPID) | Germany
Prof. Dr. Samuel Merk | Pädagogische Hochschule Karlsruhe | Germany

Bei formativem Assessment gilt die Einnahme der kriterialen Bezugsnorm und der individuellen Bezugsnorm bei der Interpretation als lernförderlich. Lehrkräfte scheinen jedoch Schwierigkeiten bei der Interpretation von Lernverlaufsdaten zu haben, die durch gezielte Visualisierungen gemindert werden könnten. Gleichzeitig wird angenommen, dass Lehrkräfte situationsübergreifend eine bestimmte Bezugsnorm bevorzugen. Daher besteht Forschungsbedarf, inwiefern die situationsübergreifende Bezugsnormorientierung die in einer spezifischen Bewertungssituation eingenommene Bezugsnorm einer Lehrkraft vorhersagen kann und ob die grafische Darstellung die eingenommene Bezugsnorm beeinflusst. In zwei Studien wird deshalb untersucht, welche Bezugsnormen (angehende) Lehrkräfte bei der Interpretation von Lernverlaufsdaten einnehmen (1), ob die situationsübergreifende Bezugsnormorientierung prädiktiv für die eingenommene Bezugsnorm in einer spezifischen Bewertungssituation ist (2) und ob die eingenommene Bezugsnorm von der grafischen Darstellung der Lernverläufe beeinflusst wird (3).

In einem randomisierten Mixed-Within-Between-Design (Studie 1) bewerteten N = 223 Lehramtsstudierende ökologisch valide Lernverläufe in einer neutralen und einer bezugsnormhervorhebenden Darstellung. Bei der neutralen Darstellung wurde häufig die individuelle oder kriteriale Bezugsnorm eingenommen. Die situationsübergreifende Bezugsnormorientierung war schwach prädiktiv. Bezugsnormhervorhebende Visualisierungen beeinflussten die eingenommenen Bezugsnormen signifikant (4.25 ≤ OR ≤ 11.17).

In einer konzeptuellen Replikation (Studie 2) mit N = 157 Lehrkräften nahmen diese bei der neutralen Darstellung häufig die individuelle Bezugsnorm ein. Die situationsübergreifende Bezugsnormorientierung war ebenso schwach prädiktiv. Die signifikanten Effekte der jeweiligen visuellen Bezugsnormhervorhebungen konnten repliziert werden (2.38 ≤ OR ≤ 7.05).

Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass gezielte Visualisierungen eine vergleichsweise einfache und kostengünstige Möglichkeit darstellen, Lehrkräfte bei der Interpretation von Lernverlaufsdaten, z.B. in Dashboards, zu unterstützen.

Vorliegende empirische Studien, die den Zusammenhang zwischen Langeweile und Kreativität untersuchten, erbrachten widersprüchliche Ergebnisse. Aus theoretischer Perspektive liegt es nahe, dass Zustände geringer Erregung und positiver Valenz kreative Prozesse fördern können. Deshalb haben Studien das Langeweileerleben von Schülerinnen und Schülern anhand von Valenz und Arousal differenziert und auf dieser Grundlage latente Profile identifiziert.
In dieser Studie untersuchten wir, ob latente Situations-Profile von Langeweile, die in früheren Untersuchungen an Studierendenstichproben beschrieben wurden, auch bei einer jüngeren Stichprobe im schulischen Kontext zu finden sind. Darauf aufbauend, überprüften wir, ob sich diese latenten Langeweileprofile hinsichtlich ihrer Ausprägung von Kreativität unterscheiden. Es wurde eine Experience-Sampling-Studie (N = 111 Schülerinnen und Schüler der Sekundarstufe, k = 1.712 momentane Assessments) durchgeführt, in der Langeweile, Valenz, Arousal und Kreativität im Klassenzimmer gemessen wurden.
Mit Latenten Profilanalysen konnten fünf Profile von Langeweile identifiziert werden, die sich hinsichtlich Valenz und Erregung unterscheiden. Wir fanden signifikante Unterschiede in der Kreativität zwischen den Langeweile-Profilen. Wie hypothetisiert, waren Profile, die durch positive Valenz und geringe Erregung gekennzeichnet waren, mit einer höheren Kreativität in Unterrichtsmomenten verbunden, während Profile, die durch negative Valenz und hohe Erregung gekennzeichnet waren, mit einer geringeren Kreativität verbunden waren. Momente, die nicht als langweilig empfunden wurden, hatten im Durchschnitt einen höheren Kreativitätswert als langweilige Momente.
Unsere Ergebnisse tragen dazu bei, die Kontroverse um den Zusammenhang zwischen Langeweile und Kreativität empirisch zu substantiieren. Die Implikationen für Forschung und Praxis werden diskutiert.

University faculty often pursue research and teaching goals simultaneously, which can lead to goal conflicts or synergies that shape emotional well-being. Based on literature on multiple goal-thriving, goal conflict can be assumed to undermine well-being, while synergy enhances it. Each morning, participants identified three work goals; each evening, they rated goal conflict, synergy, and emotions.

Multilevel structural equation modeling showed that higher-than-usual goal synergy predicted greater joy and pride, whereas higher-than-usual goal conflict predicted increased frustration.
Beyond these situational dynamics, we observed substantial and stable between-person differences (ICC₁ = .17–.52), indicating that some individuals consistently experienced more conflict or synergy across the study period. At the between-person level, higher overall goal conflict was associated with anger, anxiety, frustration, and nervousness. Higher overall goal synergy was related to pride, but also to anxiety, shame, and boredom.
Goal conflicts consistently predicted greater negative emotions within and between persons, underscoring the emotional costs of managing competing personal goals. Daily goal synergies aligned with hypotheses by enhancing emotional well-being, supporting theoretical assumptions that synergistic goal pursuit can foster positive emotions in work life, although stable synergy showed no comparable benefits. Together, our results indicate the strong relevance of motivation regulation navigating multiple goal-thriving as a foundation of faculty well-being.

Lehrergesundheit nach der Pandemie: Corona als Brandbeschleuniger für das Entstehen von Burnout
Dr. Udo Käser | Rheinische Friedrich Wilhelms Universität Bonn | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Julia Löher | Rheinische Friedrich Wilhelms Universität Bonn | Germany
Dr. Udo Käser | Rheinische Friedrich Wilhelms Universität Bonn | Germany

Bereits vor der Pandemie zeigten sich für Burnout im Lehrerberuf hohe Prävalenzen zwischen 16 und 28 Prozent. Durch die Pandemie waren Lehrkräfte mit zusätzlichen Anforderungen und Belastungen konfrontiert. Vor diesem Hintergrund wurde untersucht, in welchem Ausmaß Lehrerinnen und Lehrer durch Burnout gefährdet sind und inwieweit das Erleben der Pandemie als Belastung im Beruf mit ihrem aktuellen beruflichen Belastungserleben in Zusammenhang steht. Dabei wurden biographische, personen- und berufsbezogene Faktoren als mögliche Prädiktoren berücksichtigt.

Die Untersuchung wurde als Fragebogenstudie an allgemein- und berufsbildenden Schulen mit einer Stichprobe von 107 Lehrkräften (91 Frauen, 16 Männer) realisiert. Burnout wurde randomisiert mittels BAT (n = 53) oder MBI (n = 54) gemessen. Das Belastungserleben während der Pandemie und das aktuelle Belastungserleben wurden differenziert nach beruflichen Handlungsfeldern erhoben. Neben Alter, Berufserfahrung, Geschlecht, Familienstand, Arbeitszeit und Schulform wurden Selbstwirksamkeit, Berufszufriedenheit, Ängstlichkeit und Klima im Kollegium erfasst. Alle Skalen zeigen gute Reliabilitäten (> .7) und Trennschärfen (> .3).

BAT und MBI messen übereinstimmend Prävalenzen für Burnout von 20.8% bzw. 20.4%. Jeweils ist emotionale Erschöpfung als Teildimension am stärksten ausgeprägt. Die berufliche Belastung während der Pandemie wird im Vergleich zur aktuellen Belastung als signifikant stärker empfunden, wobei beides signifikant positiv miteinander korreliert. Selbstwirksamkeit sowie Familie als soziale Ressourcen bestätigen sich als protektive Faktoren, während mit Ängstlichkeit in Bezug auf Burnout Vulnerabilität einhergeht. Demgegenüber zeigen sich keine Unterschiede in Abhängigkeit von Geschlecht, Arbeitszeit und dem Klima im Kollegium. Letzteres steht im Widerspruch zu früheren Befunden, in denen sich soziale Unterstützung unter Lehrkräften als wichtiger protektiver Faktor erwies.

Socio-emotional development in adolescence: Unraveling the role of antecedents, long-term trends, and underlying processes
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Jenny Wagner (Universität Hamburg)
Dr. Larissa L. Wieczorek (Universität Hamburg)
Room: BG
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Adolescence is a critical period for socio-emotional development, marked by rapid growth of abilities and increased vulnerability to contextual affordances. This symposium sheds light on the socio-emotional skills, dynamics, and challenges of adolescence. Drawing on cross-sectional, longitudinal, and ambulatory assessment data, the five talks provide new insights into the antecedents, long-term trends, and underlying processes of socio-emotional development. The first set of talks explores broad research lines focusing on non-linear associations between trait personality and empathy in middle and late adolescence (Wieczorek et al.), the role of personal goals on personality development across the transition out of high school (Steinhage et al.), and the identification of theoretically and empirically derived causal predictors of students’ well-being across secondary school (Brandt et al.). The second set of talks moves into daily dynamics throughout the adolescent period, focusing on emotion regulation processes and flexibility in daily life (Warnholtz et al.) and testing nuanced daily affect-regulatory processes to understand developmental trajectories of risk and resilience factors across a one-year follow-up (Philippi et al.). Across all talks, this symposium integrates up-to-date research on socio-emotional characteristics in adolescence, focusing on both long-term development and short-term dynamics, as well as their interplay. Covering diverse adolescent populations and contexts, the research employs advanced statistical methods like multilevel models and lagged exposure-wide approaches. Taken together, these contributions deepen our understanding of inter-individual differences and dynamic developmental processes during this vibrant life stage.

Previous research highlights the relevance of agreeableness and neuroticism for individual differences in empathy, but previous studies mainly focused on (linear) main effects. Furthermore, knowledge regarding neuroticism remains inconclusive, as the trait has been linked to both lower and higher empathy. We address these research gaps by investigating the potential interplay of agreeableness and neuroticism in predicting individual differences in empathy based on self- and other-reports from two adolescent samples (overall N = 712). Using an information-theoretic approach combined with response surface analyses, we analyze linear, non-linear, and interaction effects of agreeableness and neuroticism while distinguishing the four empathy facets perspective taking, fantasy, empathic concern, and personal distress. At this point, data collection and a preregistration have been completed. The results will provide nuanced insights into the complex relationship between personality and empathy during the developmentally sensitive time of adolescence.

Understanding personality development in emerging adulthood is crucial, as this period offers the onset of diverse life paths that significantly impact young adults’ futures. While genetic and environmental factors may nudge individuals onto certain trajectories, they may also self-regulate their development through personal goals and intentions. While earlier research has provided little evidence for the explanatory power of major life goals in shaping the development of personality traits, more recent findings indicate that explicitly setting goals to change one’s own personality is associated with subsequent development in these traits. Both strands of research are, however, constrained by several limitations concerning timespans, -intervals, assessment tools, and analytic approaches. In this pre-registered study, we aim to examine predictive effects of changes in goal importance on changes in personality traits, applying structural equation modeling and incorporating a comprehensive assessment of global, yet personality-related goals. More specifically, we examine personality development in emerging adults as they transition out of secondary education into different post-school pathways. Using propensity score matching, we control for pre-transition differences and take advantage of the quasi-experimental nature of these transitions to distinguish between selection effects, environmental influences, and individuals’ personal goals across five measurement waves spanning a decade, using existing data from a large-scale German panel study (TOSCA; Nt1 ~ 4,500). With this study, we aim to gain a deeper understanding of whether, and to what extent, personality development unfolds in alignment with individuals’ personal goals during emerging adulthood.

Students’ school well-being is central to both immediate academic success and long-term life outcomes, underscoring the need to understand its determinants. Although prior cross-sectional and longitudinal studies have identified individual, social, and contextual correlates, three gaps remain. First, most studies consider only a few predictors, leaving other influential factors unexplored. Second, analyzing predictors in isolation limits comparisons of their relative importance. Third, varying definitions of well-being hinder cumulative knowledge. With the current pre-registered work, we aim to address these gaps by analyzing predictive effects of 64 theoretically and empirically selected candidate factors from six domains (1) students’ performance, (2) personality and motivation (3) health and general well-being, (4) aspects of teaching, homework and extracurricular involvement, (5) leisure time activities, and (6) parental attitudes towards their children’s learning efforts and school using a lagged exposure-wide approach. We use longitudinal data from a large sample of German students (NT1 3,500), assessed annually starting in grade 5. As our statistical approach is driven by the detection of novel effects, we refrained from formulating explicit hypotheses about the role of specific predictors, however we pre-registered the predictor sets under consideration, the control variables included, the statistical analyses to be conducted, inclusive robustness checks and sensitivity analyses. With the present study we aim to identify the most salient factors from a broad set of theoretically and empirically derived predictors. In doing so, it seeks to pinpoint promising leverage points for enhancing students’ well-being in schools and, consequently, their long-term educational success.

Adolescence is a sensitive developmental period marked by novel emotional challenges and shifting emotional dynamics, rendering the development of effective emotion regulation capabilities crucial for navigating these emerging demands. Recent theoretical advancements highlight the importance of emotion regulation flexibility —the ability to adjust regulatory efforts to situational demands—in supporting adaptive regulation. However, little is known about which contextual factors shape emotion regulation and whether flexibility contributes to adaptive psychological outcomes in the daily life of adolescents. The present study has two aims: first, exploring the role of contextual factors for the selection and effectiveness of four emotion regulation strategies: reappraisal, expressive suppression, social sharing, and reflection, and second, investigating whether the three components of emotion regulation flexibility (context sensitivity, repertoire, and feedback sensitivity) are associated with momentary affective outcomes in adolescence. To this end, ESM data from more than 400 adolescents aged between 14 to 18 years old have been collected and will be analyzed using different multilevel modeling approaches. Show details
Authors:

Adolescence is a sensitive developmental period characterized by substantial neurobiological and psychosocial changes that heighten vulnerability to mental health disorders. Affect regulation represents a central transdiagnostic factor in the emergence and maintenance of mental health problems, particularly internalizing and externalizing symptoms. However, the mechanisms by which situational and interindividual factors influence short-term dynamic affective processes in response to daily stressful events, and their prospective effects on mental health, remain insufficiently researched in adolescence. This study examines how situational and interindividual factors influence short-term affective responses to stressful events and to what extent these processes predict changes in internalizing and externalizing symptoms over one year. In a 14-day Ambulatory Assessment study, 288 adolescents aged 12 to 21 years (M = 17.6, SD = 2.6) were prompted 8 times daily via m-Path to report affective experiences and stressful events. When a stressful event was reported, participants received four additional follow-up prompts at 15-minute intervals over the next hour (microbursts), enabling high-resolution characterization of affective trajectories. Internalizing and externalizing symptoms were assessed at baseline and one-year follow-up using the Youth Self Report.
Multilevel growth curve models revealed that affective responses to stressful events are characterized by linear reactivity followed by linear and quadratic recovery. These dynamics are influenced by situational factors (event intensity, type) and interindividual factors (symptoms, event frequency). Predictive machine learning analyses are in progress. Results contribute to a nuanced understanding of daily affect-regulatory processes and the identification of risk and resilience factors, thereby supporting advances in just-in-time-adaptive interventions for adolescents.

States in context: Synergizing passive and subjective data using ambulatory assessment and sensor data in everyday life

Co-chair(s) Noémie Topalian (Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research (LISER))
Room: RO
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

The surge of sensors holds great promise in advancing our knowledge about everyday life experiences and symptom expression. The great advantages of sensors is their ability to passively capture data, thus, providing an unobtrusive and (semi-)continuous assessments of context information. In this symposium, we will present studies synergizing passive and subjective data.
Markus Reichert will introduce key methods for collecting and analyzing geolocation data in everyday life and demonstrate how integrating geospatial information with momentary psychological and sensor-based data enables fine-grained contextual analyses of human behavior. Since early experiences of childhood abuse are often associated with functional impairments in adulthood including restricted activity space in daily life, Philip Santangelo will present their findings on geospatial mobility patterns tracked via GPS for three times (seven days each) over the course of a 12-month psychotherapy program in N=181 patients with experiences of child abuse. Noémie Topalian will present a study in which she combines vocal, mobility, and environmental exposure features from a 15-day geographically explicit ecological momentary assessment study to build an long short-term memory neural network-based model for predicting momentary stress from passive smartphone and sensor data. Djenna Hutmacher will present the APAC project, a randomized controlled trial evaluating the feasibility, user engagement, and potential effects of the Go-Well app as an adjunctive, transdiagnostic aftercare intervention for patients transitioning from inpatient psychiatric treatment to everyday life. She will explore how passive smartphone data relate to well-being and post-discharge stability.

Prof. Dr. Markus Reichert | Austria
Show details
Author:
Prof. Dr. Markus Reichert | Austria

Human emotions, thoughts and behaviors are strongly shaped by the environments in which they occur. People respond differently when they are alone compared to being with others, at a funeral versus at a celebration, or in an urban landscape rather than in a natural setting. Although context can include many elements, it is often defined through characteristics of the geographic location at a given moment—such as access to green spaces, population density, or levels of air pollution. These contextual factors influence both healthy individuals and clinical populations alike, making them a topic of growing relevance in psychological research.
With the rise of geospatial technologies and location based services, large volumes of geodata have become available, providing the opportunity for fine grained contextual analysis. Modern geoinformatics offers powerful tools to integrate these spatial datasets with psychological research. Geolocation information—frequently collected via smartphone GPS—can be combined with repeatedly sampled data from daily life, such as electronic diary reports of affective states or physiological measurements from wearable sensors including accelerometers, known as Ecological Momentary Assessment and Ambulatory Assessment.
In this presentation, we will outline the fundamental methods for collecting and analyzing geolocation data in everyday contexts. We will also illustrate how these approaches can generate deeper insights into human behavior and which advances can be expected as these techniques continue to evolve within psychological research.

Living within a limited radius – and breaking free? Examining activity space in women with a history of child abuse using global positioning system tracking over the course of psychotherapy
Prof. Dr. Philip Santangelo | Luxembourg
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Philip Santangelo | Luxembourg
Johanna Rehder2 | Austria
Marvin Guth | Germany
Prof. Dr. Ulrich Ebner-Priemer | Germany

Experiences of childhood abuse are associated with long-term impairments in physical and mental well-being and can affect everyday behavior in adults with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Passive sensing using digital sensors, such as global positioning system (GPS) tracking, offers a promising approach to capture behavioral manifestations of psychopathology in daily life, including restricted activity spaces. However, this methodology has rarely been applied in psychotherapy research.
In this randomized controlled trial, we investigated whether treatment-related symptom improvements are reflected in changes in everyday mobility patterns over the course of outpatient psychotherapy. We analyzed spatial and temporal activity spaces of women with PTSD following childhood abuse (n = 166, Mage = 35.81, SDage = 10.98) at three one-week assessment periods: before treatment (t1), after six months of treatment (t3), and at the end of the intensive treatment phase after twelve months (t5). Participants were randomly assigned to either dialectical behavior therapy for PTSD (DBT-PTSD) or cognitive processing therapy (CPT).
Although both treatments have demonstrated clinical efficacy, with DBT-PTSD showing superiority over CPT in symptom reduction, these effects did not translate into changes in daily-life mobility. Linear mixed-effects models comparing t1 and t5 showed no significant effects of time or treatment condition on movement radius or time spent away from home. Thus, previously reported therapeutic improvements were not reflected in GPS-derived behavioral indicators.
Our findings indicate that, despite substantial reductions in self-reported symptom severity, patients’ everyday activity spaces remained restricted. This suggests that behavioral recovery in daily life may lag behind clinical symptom improvement and highlights the importance of integrating passive sensing measures into psychotherapy research to better capture real-world functioning.

Noémie Topalian | Luxembourg
Show details
Author:
Noémie Topalian | Luxembourg

Geographically-explicit Ecological Momentary Assessment (GEMA) studies offer a wide range of opportunities to derive contextual information from sensors, location tracking or novel technologies such as vocal biomarkers.
This study aims to combine several data modalities to build a predictive model of momentary stress. We use features computed from passively collected data and evaluate their contribution to stress forecasting.
We will use data from FragMent, a GEMA study examining how daily activities and exposure to environments affect daily and momentary stress in Luxembourg. The mobile survey consists of a 15-day assessment among 276 participants, with four prompts per day and continuous geolocation tracking. At each entry, participants self-reported their momentary stress and completed a vocal task.
We derive three main families of features: vocal, mobility and exposure features. Vocal features include linguistic and paralinguistic features extracted from the recordings; mobility features are extracted from GPS points (e.g, distance covered, speed, location changes); and exposure measures are computed by linking environmental attributes to participants’ tracks (e.g., green spaces, noise).
To account for the temporal structure of the data, we will use long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network models to predict stress. We will report the accuracy of the model, and the contribution of the feature sets.
Smartphone-embedded data sources can serve as proxies for mental states at fine-grained temporal scales. Integrating contextual information from multiple passive sensing sources is key to strengthening digital health monitoring solutions.

The transition from inpatient psychiatric treatment to everyday life represents a particularly vulnerable period for individuals with mental disorders, as it is associated with increased risks of suicide, self-harming behavior, and rehospitalization. The APAC project (App-based Psychiatric Aftercare) addresses this transition phase by means of a real-time self-monitoring application. Within this project, the application Go-Well was provided to transdiagnostic psychiatric patients at discharge to support their transition into everyday life. The aim of the study was to investigate the efficacy of an adjunctive transdiagnostic app-based aftercare intervention (IG) compared to a control group (CG), by using a randomized controlled trial design (RCT), based on a dataset of a multi-center recruitment in psychiatric clinics of Switzerland and Luxembourg.
The app was designed to structure daily routines through diary-based entries while allowing patients to document and reflect on personally relevant life domains, such as social relationships, occupational activities, well-being, psychological distress, daily functioning, and behavioral activation (captured by standardized questionnaires). In addition, usability-related aspects of the app-based aftercare intervention, including system usability, user satisfaction, and potential negative effects, were assessed. An exploratory analysis of passive smartphone data, such as GPS-based mobility indicators, call activity, application usage, and step counts, were furthermore conducted in relation to the well-being of participants during the transition from inpatient treatment to everyday life.
The symposium contribution presents the conceptual framework of the APAC project, the design and implementation of the Go-Well app, and first results regarding its feasibility, user engagement, and potential effects on post-discharge stability.

Toward a Holistic Understanding of Interpersonal Perception
Connecting Personality and Social Psychological Perspectives on Attitude and Judgment Formation
Chair(s) Nele Freyer (Technische Universität Dresden)
Moderator(s) Hans Alves (Ruhr Universität Bochum)
Room: DK
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Interpersonal perception is a highly complex process, involving characteristics of targets who are both individuals and members of social groups, limited information, evaluative attitudes, and the semantics of descriptive terms. Although this process is subject to both social and personality psychology, the two fields operate largely independently, relying on different theories, terminology, and methods. To foster a holistic understanding of person perception, this symposium links perspectives from both fields, highlighting how bottom-up influences of target characteristics and top-down influences of perceiver evaluations jointly shape judgments.
Nele Freyer opens by introducing a framework that specifies two pathways from target characteristics to judgments: the interpretation of target behavior in descriptive terms and the formation of evaluative attitudes reflected in the positivity of these terms. Focusing on trait expression and interpretation, Michael Dufner investigates how contextual factors shape both the behavioral expression of target characteristics and their interpretation as powerful by perceivers. Shifting the focus to evaluative attitudes, Anne Wiedenroth demonstrates to what extent positivity reflects target differences as opposed to perceiver-based bias in first impressions. Patrick Rothermund explores such target- versus perceiver-driven processes in attitude formation through stereotype emergence in group perception. Finally, Anne Weitzel presents a large-language-model approach to measure the semantic similarity and lexical diversity of person/group descriptors. Hans Alves will conclude as discussant, connecting the contributions and highlighting the potential of integrating social and personality psychological perspectives.

Accounting for the Complexity of Interpersonal Perception: A Formal Model of Judgment Accuracy
Nele Freyer | TU Dresden | Germany
Show details
Authors:
Nele Freyer | TU Dresden | Germany
Anne Wiedenroth | TU Dresden
Matthias Borgstede | Uni Bamberg
Daniel Leising

How do person judgments emerge from the complex interplay of target and perceiver influences? Despite extensive research in personality and social psychology, this question remains unresolved. We present a formal model of accuracy in person judgments that systematically examines how target information, its interpretation by the perceiver, and evaluative attitudes jointly shape evaluations. The model proposes two primary pathways from target characteristics to judgments: the interpretation of observed target characteristics in terms of judgment dimensions, and the formation of attitudes that influence the positivity of judgments. Its formal structure allows these pathways and their interactions to be systematically analyzed and their distinct contributions to be disentangled. By incorporating a clear criterion of accuracy, the model makes it possible to identify and differentiate several biases that can arise throughout the judgment process. Recognizing the inherent complexity of interpersonal perception, this framework provides a deeper understanding of the mechanisms that produce accurate or biased evaluations. The framework provides conceptual clarity in a highly fragmented theoretical landscape, integrates a variety of research strands, and fosters the development of testable hypotheses for future studies.

Who Attains Power in Small Groups? The Roles of Behavior and Valuation Contingency

Show details
Authors:
Michael Dufner | Universität Witten/Herdecke
Stathis Grapsas | Utrecht University | Netherlands

Studies have linked personality dispositions to important social evaluations, such as how much power individuals are granted. Yet, these links are not always consistent and seem to depend on the social context. We zeroed in on this issue, testing two mutually non-exclusive hypotheses on how the context might moderate the effects of personality dispositions on perceptions of power in newly formed groups. The behavior contingency hypothesis posits that the context moderates the extent to which a disposition is expressed in behavior. The valuation contingency hypothesis posits that the context moderates the extent to which disposition-specific behavior is valued. In a round-robin study, we found support for both hypotheses. The findings of multigroup SEM analyses reveal the importance of behavior expression and valuation in the processes underlying personality-situation interactions in power hierarchies. Implications for interactionist theories as well as potential practical implications for organizational settings will be discussed.

What’s in a Halo? Comparing Target and Perceiver Influences on Positivity in Personality Impressions
Anne Wiedenroth
Show details
Authors:
Anne Wiedenroth
Aline Bartlick | TU Dresden

Global evaluations are a central feature of person perception: Individuals who are rated positively on one attribute are often evaluated favorably across other characteristics as well. Such halo-like patterns have long occupied both social and personality psychology, raising the fundamental question of what they reflect. While halos are often conceptualized as perceiver-based biases, other accounts emphasize that positivity may also reflect substantive target differences. A challenge for integrating these perspectives is that standard designs based on judgments from individual perceivers make it difficult to disentangle perceiver and target influences. To address this issue, we examined the structure and role of positivity in target effects in a large dataset of behavior-based personality impressions and contrasted findings with earlier investigations of the respective perceiver effects. Targets (N=200) were filmed in 20 standardized situations. Perceivers (N=3,963) each observed and rated ten targets in one situation, resulting in approximately 200 independent ratings per target (ten per situation). Averaging across perceivers allowed us to derive reliable target effects and examine target-based positivity across situations. Our analyses show that beyond trait-specific impressions, a broad positivity factor captures substantial additional target variance: Across perceivers and situations, some individuals reliably elicit more positive evaluations than others. Further analyses examine the role of positivity in relation to situational differences, target characteristics, and perceiver-target interactions. We discuss implications for debates about accuracy and bias and for integrating perspectives on person perception.

Differentiation in Stereotype Formation: Top-down or Bottom-up?
Patrick Rothermund | Universität Würzburg
Show details
Authors:
Patrick Rothermund | Universität Würzburg
Roland Deutsch | Universität Würzburg

Attitude formation often highlights features that distinguish one object from another. While this differentiation process has been documented across a wide range of targets (e.g., individuals, brands, meals), social groups provide a particularly clear case differentiation, with stereotype formation being biased toward intergroup differences rather than similarities. Despite its ubiquity, it remains unclear whether intergroup differentiation arises from bottom-up responses to stimulus characteristics or from top-down processes driven by perceivers’ expectations and goals. Across three preregistered experiments, we addressed this question using a trait-learning paradigm. Specifically, participants learned social traits assigned to members of either one or two fictitious groups. Crucially, novel traits introduced in the second half of the learning phase were equally novel across conditions but only marked intergroup distinctiveness in the two-groups condition. Supporting a top-down account, recall for these novel traits was higher in the two-groups condition than in the single-group condition (Exp. 1). Novel traits were also judged as more typical for their group than initially learned traits, but again only in the two-groups condition (Exp. 2). Finally, differentiation effects varied systematically across different two-groups conditions depending on manipulations of participants’ expectations and goals regarding intergroup differences (Exp. 3). Together, these findings show that differentiation in group perception (and more broadly in attitude formation) is not merely a response to salience or recency of distinctive stimuli but reflects top-down mechanisms related to structure and meaning.

Anne Irena Weitzel | Universität zu Köln
Show details
Author:
Anne Irena Weitzel | Universität zu Köln

Large language models (LLMs) essentially create new semantic landscapes based on the massive text corpora they were trained on. Typically, these training materials originate in the human world (books, newspaper articles, movie subtitles, etc.), which is why the resulting LLMs are expected to reflect reality in the same way that humans perceive it. However, there is evidence that LLMs can and do introduce distortions to the mirror images they create, which can be tricky to detect, explain, and quantify. The first part of my talk examines several prominent LLMs’ semantic landscapes in terms of their match with human perceptions of the English language. To this end, I present a new benchmark of human semantic similarity ratings, consisting of 243,250 pairwise similarity ratings from N = 1,217 participants of six nationalities, stratified by gender, age, and education. I compare the performance of each model (incl. different Gemini, Qwen3, GloVe, GPT versions) in mirroring the semantic structure of this human-rated dataset, discussing strengths and weaknesses regarding their use in social cognition research. In the second part, I exemplify how LLMs can provide highly cost-efficient tools to measure the semantic similarity of person/group traits, unlocking the potential to test valence asymmetry predictions of the Evaluative Information Ecology Model (EvIE; Unkelbach et al., 2019) in a more fine-grained way.

Computational Metascience: AI and Automation for Robustness and Reproducibility in Psychological Science
Chair(s) Dr. Cassie Ann Short (Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg)
Room: IT
Topic: Digital Transformation and AI
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

Concerns about robustness and reproducibility continue to challenge cumulative psychological science, particularly as research increasingly relies on complex, high-dimensional data and flexible analytic pipelines. However, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and automation offer new opportunities to automate and scale metascientific practices that were previously labour-intensive. This symposium brings together complementary approaches developed within the DFG priority program META-REP that demonstrate how AI- and automation-supported tools can strengthen the feasibility and transparency of robustness assessments and reproducibility checks throughout the research workflow in psychology. The first two contributions focus on multiverse analysis as a framework for robustness assessment. Maximilian Frank introduces automation support for systematically defining and documenting defensible analytic choices in multiverse analyses, addressing transparency and reproducibility at the level of multiverse construction. Cassie Short examines how active learning can be used to generate representative robustness reports in large-scale multiverses that rely on pipeline sampling. The final two contributions focus on AI and automation for reproducibility checks and evidence synthesis. Johannes Breuer presents AI-based tools designed to proactively identify and address reproducibility and replicability during the submission and review process. Sana Hassan Imam reports on the use of large language models to automatically extract methodological decisions from the scientific literature, supporting automated meta-analyses and evidence synthesis. The symposium concludes with a moderated panel discussion exploring how AI and automation can be integrated into research workflows to improve reproducibility without introducing new sources of opacity or bias. Together, these contributions illustrate how AI and automation can be leveraged as valuable tools for advancing metascientific practice in psychology.

Automation Support in SMART 2.0 - Mapping Dimensions of Multiverse Analysis
Maximilian Frank | Ludwig-Maximimilans Universität München
Show details
Authors:
Maximilian Frank | Ludwig-Maximimilans Universität München
Dr. Cassie Ann Short | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Yusuf Cosku Inceler | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Prof. Dr. Andrea Hildebrandt | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg

Multiverse analysis improves robustness assessment by making analytic flexibility explicit, yet its benefits depend on how transparently and systematically the decision space is specified. In practice, constructing a multiverse is often the main bottleneck: researchers must identify relevant decision nodes, define defensible pipelines, and manage dependencies across choices - tasks that become impractical as multiverses grow in size and complexity. We present ongoing work on SMART 2.0, an extension of the Systematic Multiverse Analysis Registration Tool (SMART), an open-access Shiny application that guides users through a structured multiverse specification workflow and exports preregistration-ready records. SMART 2.0 targets large-scale multiverses by improving both automation and usability. First, instead of generating a full Cartesian product of all options, SMART 2.0 enables rule-based pipeline generation: users specify dependency constraints so that indefensible combinations are prevented by design, reducing effort while preserving transparent documentation of decision rationales. Second, SMART 2.0 adds scalable visualisation and navigation features to support real-time auditing of large decision spaces, helping users detect specification errors before finalizing the multiverse. Finally, we discuss future directions for development, including the potential role of large language models as assistants for drafting decision-node descriptions or running consistency checks within a machine-readable specification schema. While drawing from our application development process, we highlight more broadly how automation can improve metascientific workflows beyond multiverse preregistration. For example, by supporting literature search and screening, pooling and harmonising data across studies, and enabling scalable evidence synthesis and reporting.

Active Learning for Representative Robustness Reports in Large-Scale Multiverse Analyses
Dr. Cassie Ann Short | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Cassie Ann Short | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Prof. Dr. Andrea Hildebrandt | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Robin Bosse | Universität Hildesheim
Prof. Dr. Stefan Debener | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Metin Özyağcılar | Universität Hamburg
Dr. Katharina Paul | Universität Hamburg
Prof. Dr. Jan Wacker | Universität Hamburg
Dr. Daniel Kristanto | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg

The multiplicity of defensible data-processing and analysis pipelines is increasingly recognised as a major source of uncertainty and low replicability in psychological research. Multiverse analysis makes this uncertainty explicit by systematically reporting results across alternative defensible analytic pipelines. However, in data-processing-intensive domains such as psychophysiological research, the large number of defensible pipelines often renders exhaustive computation infeasible. Researchers therefore rely on sampling subsets of pipelines, implicitly assuming that the samples are representative of the full multiverse. Yet, different sampling strategies may produce systematically different robustness estimates, introducing what we term ‘multiverse sampling uncertainty’. Here, we present the first application of active learning to sample from and estimate a large EEG multiverse analysis. Using a 528-pipeline EEG-personality multiverse, we compared random, stratified, and active learning sampling approaches in terms of how well the sampled pipelines, and, in the case of active learning, estimated pipelines, approximate the distribution of model fits observed in the fully computed multiverse. The active learning sample most closely approximated the robustness patterns observed across the full computed multiverse when sample sizes were small. These findings highlight multiverse sampling uncertainty as an important but underreported source of variability in multiverse analyses, and demonstrate that active learning is a promising approach for obtaining representative multiverse results when only small proportional pipeline samples are feasible to compute. We provide an open-source tool to support the transparent reporting of multiverse sampling uncertainty and the application of active learning in future multiverse analyses.

Using AI for Automated Checks of Reproducibility and Replicability
Prof. Dr. Johannes Breuer | Center for Advanced Internet Studies (CAIS); University of Duisburg-Essen
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Johannes Breuer | Center for Advanced Internet Studies (CAIS); University of Duisburg-Essen
Prof. Dr. Mario Haim | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität Munchen
Philipp Knöpfle | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität Munchen

Discussions of replicability and reproducibility in the context of AI typically emphasise AI as a threat. While there certainly are risks involved and such concerns are warranted, AI can also be proactively used as a tool for improving the reproducibility and replicability of research. The project “Fostering Proactive Replicability in Computational Communication Science via Frontloading Effort and Automating Protocols” (AutoFrontCCS) employs this perspective by developing and testing AI-based solutions for checking and improving the reproducibility and replicability of research during the submission and review process. Specifically, building on prior insights into common barriers, the tools developed in the project seek to assist in identifying and addressing potential obstacles for reproducibility and replicability. Our talk will present the project’s pipeline and discuss first results from an implementation study to showcase how AI can be used for automated checks and as a tool for strengthening reproducibility and replicability.

Automating Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses in Graph Theory-Based fMRI Research
Dr. Sana Hassan Imam | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Sana Hassan Imam | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Dr. Daniel Kristanto | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Dr. Carsten Gießing | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Prof. Dr. Andrea Hildebrandt | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are the foundations for evidence-based science, yet their reliability and scalability are often limited by the manual, time-consuming, and error prone information extraction from articles describing primary studies. In a previous study, we manually extracted the preprocessing and analysis pipelines of 220 functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) graph theory-based studies. We identified 78 distinct analytical choices, for which we created an interactive web-based application, METEOR, which allows to explore the analytical design space of these pipelines. To ensure the app's sustainability, we aim to automatically update its knowledge space using a Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted framework. Here, we explore how LLMs can support automated information extraction of methodological decisions and results from scientific publications. We introduce an LLM-based pipeline for the structured extraction of preprocessing steps, analysis methods, and reported results from scientific articles that employ fMRI data to study the network topology of the human brain. The articles are drawn from major bibliographic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. The framework enables systematic benchmarking of methodological variability across studies and supports reproducible knowledge synthesis. The talk will focus on the pipeline, discussing initial findings, LLM-based annotations, and benchmarking with a human-in-the-loop review process, as well as future aspects of the project.

Moderated Panel Discussion: Responsible Research Practices for the Use of AI and Automation in Metascientific Workflows in Psychology
Dr. Cassie Ann Short | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Prof. Dr. Johannes Breuer | Center for Advanced Internet Studies (CAIS); University of Duisburg-Essen
Maximilian Frank | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität Munchen
Dr. Sana Hassan Imam | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Cassie Ann Short | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg
Prof. Dr. Johannes Breuer | Center for Advanced Internet Studies (CAIS); University of Duisburg-Essen
Maximilian Frank | Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität Munchen
Dr. Sana Hassan Imam | Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg

The symposium concludes with a moderated panel discussion focusing on responsible research practices for the use of AI and automation in metascientific workflows in psychology. Building directly on the presented tools, the panel will examine how such methods can be implemented without introducing new sources of opacity or bias. Discussion will center on questions of transparency and reporting standards for AI-supported analyses, including how assumptions and model-driven decisions should be communicated. The discussion will be opened to the audience to reflect on best practices for deploying AI and automation as supportive, accountable tools in psychological metascience.

Translational values of extinction learning
Chair(s) Prof. Dr. Christian Merz (Ruhr University Bochum)
Co-chair(s) Prof. Dr. Adriane Icenhour (Ruhr University Bochum)
Room: BE
Topic: Open Area
Form of presentation: Symposium
Duration: 90 Minutes

We preferentially learn, store, and remember aversive, interoceptive, and painful cues. Classical conditioning, therefore, holds substantial translational value, as it helps explain the development of mental and somatic disorders, including anxiety disorders, somatic complaints, or visceral pain along the gut-brain axis. Even more crucial for broadening translational knowledge is extinction learning, during which an initially acquired association is inhibited. The clinical analogue of extinction learning is exposure therapy, a cornerstone intervention for many of these conditions. In recent years, our understanding of the mechanisms, modulators, and predictors of conditioning and extinction processes in both healthy individuals and clinical populations has substantially advanced. The aim of this symposium is to integrate complementary perspectives on extinction learning to develop a comprehensive, unified framework. First, Christian Merz will present how stress hormones change extinction learning in healthy participants and explore boundaries regarding contextual cues. Second, Anna-Lisa Lipp will share recent data on how cognitive factors modulate success in extinction learning and exposure therapy in patients with anxiety disorders. Third, Katharina Schmidt will elucidate biases in pain-related learning and extinction processes characterized by a “better safe than sorry” strategy in individuals with chronic low back pain. Fourth, Adriane Icenhour will highlight the specificity of interoceptive sensations, especially visceral pain in shaping pain-related fear learning and extinction along the gut-brain axis. Fifth, Hanna Öhlmann will shed light on effects of acute and chronic inflammation in affecting pain-related learning and memory and their implications for post-inflammatory pain perception. Altogether, this symposium will leverage the translational relevance of stress, cognition, and interoception in shaping fear learning and extinction to advance mechanistic understanding and foster novel clinical approaches for patients with anxiety disorders and somatic or visceral pain.

Extinction learning and stress hormones: how cortisol changes extinction memories context-dependently
Prof. Dr. Christian Merz
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Christian Merz
Lianne Wolsink
Jaël Caviola
Leander Fester
Oliver Wolf
Dr. Valerie Jentsch

The stress hormone cortisol significantly changes episodic learning and memory processes. On the one hand, cortisol reduces memory retrieval, while on the other hand, cortisol enhances memory consolidation. These multifaceted effects of cortisol open a wide range of possibilities for harnessing stress hormones in the treatment of anxiety disorders, which are believed to stem from aversive learning experiences. Indeed, some successful attempts have been made with cortisol administration to support exposure therapy, the standard treatment in psychotherapy that relies on the principles of extinction learning. Furthermore, the influence of stress hormones on extinction learning in healthy humans has been investigated to uncover the underlying learning mechanisms and contextual boundaries. In these studies, standard fear conditioning designs were combined with acute psychosocial stress and physical exercise interventions, which are also capable of elevating stress hormone levels. This talk will provide an overview of how these interventions and the associated changes in stress hormone concentrations alter fear extinction memories and the role that context plays in this process.

Extinction learning and exposure therapy: modifying stimulus-outcome contingencies in anxiety disorders
Annalisa Lipp
Show details
Authors:
Annalisa Lipp
Beray Macit
Prof. Dr. Christian Merz
Prof. Dr. Oliver Wolf
Prof. Dr. Jürgen Margraf
Prof. Dr. Marcella Woud
Prof. Dr. Armin Zlomuzica

Impaired extinction learning is a key mechanism in the persistence of anxiety disorders (ADs) and might contribute to fear relapse following exposure-based treatments. Using two complementary studies, we investigated cognitive modulation of extinction processes in an laboratory study and a clinical trial.
The laboratory study examined how the timing of contingency instructions (CI) affects extinction learning in 240 participants (120 patients with ADs and 120 healthy controls) using a three-day sequential conditioning paradigm. Electrical shocks served as the unconditioned stimulus (US) and coloured lamps as conditioned stimuli (CS). CI before extinction training enhanced extinction learning across physiological (skin conductance responses) and subjective measures (CS valence, US expectancy). Post-extinction CI reduced fear relapse during extinction retrieval. The reinstatement test revealed complex, context-dependent effects of CI.
In a clinical proof-of-principle randomized controlled trial, we investigated whether adding a Cognitive Bias Modification-Interpretation (CBM-I) training to a single-session exposure therapy would further facilitate cognitive change in acrophobic patients (N = 81). Patients received either a single session of CBM-I or sham training following exposure therapy. CBM-I led to greater immediate reductions in negative interpretation bias compared to sham training, but these effects were not sustained at the 4-week follow-up. Both groups showed comparable improvements in symptoms, cognitive measures, and behavioural approach.
These findings demonstrate that cognitive interventions can modulate extinction processes in the laboratory, but translating effects into sustained clinical benefits remains challenging. Although CBM-I reduced interpretation bias immediately, effects were not sustained. Implications for optimizing exposure-based treatments will be discussed in the presentation.

Extinction learning and pain: a “better safe than sorry” approach
PD Dr. Katharina Schmidt
Show details
Authors:
PD Dr. Katharina Schmidt
Lea Busch
Jialin Li
Dr. Frederik Schlitt-Nguyen
Dr. Katarina Forkmann
Prof. Dr. Katja Wiech
Prof. Dr. Ulrike Bingel

Pain-related associative learning supports harm avoidance by linking predictive cues to painful outcomes. However, when threat associations persist despite updated environmental conditions, learning becomes maladaptive and may contribute to pain chronification. Insufficient extinction of pain-related fear and an exaggerated focus on safety are therefore considered key mechanisms limiting recovery and treatment success in patients with chronic pain.
Using experimental pain-related conditioning and extinction paradigms combined with psychophysiological measures and neuroimaging, we investigated pain-related threat, safety and reward learning in healthy individuals and patients with chronic back pain. Our findings demonstrate that in both groups painful outcomes are learned more robustly as indicated by incomplete extinction than non-painful aversive or pain-relieving events, likely driven by their high biological salience. Patients with chronic back pain further show impairments in discriminating between threat and safety cues, due to marked impairments in safety and reward learning. Moreover, in health and chronic pain, pain-related learning is shaped by internal and external factors, including pain-related fear, physiological stress and the anatomical relevance of pain, suggesting that biologically salient pain signals promote stronger and more persistent cue–pain associations. Neuroimaging findings indicate altered engagement of threat- and salience-processing networks and reduced flexibility within circuits supporting extinction and safety learning.
Together, these results support the notion that pain-related learning and chronic pain are characterized by a “better safe than sorry” strategy. Targeting biased pain-related learning and extinction processes may offer a promising translational avenue to improve long-term clinical outcomes.

Extinction learning and the gut-brain axis: how interoception governs visceral pain-related fear memories
Prof. Dr. Adriane Icenhour
Show details
Authors:
Prof. Dr. Adriane Icenhour
PD Dr. Franziska Labrenz
Prof. Dr. Sigrid Elsenbruch

The gut-brain axis is gaining increasing attention across scientific disciplines, including translational neuroscience. As captured by the evolving concept of interoception, the sensation, interpretation, and integration of signals from within the gut-brain system play a vital role in shaping learning and memory, with significant clinical implications. Aversive interoceptive signals related to visceral pain can particularly drive fear learning and behavioral adaptations, engaging the fear and salience networks of the human brain. However, neurobiological mechanisms underlying interoceptive learning and memory, particularly successful interoceptive fear extinction, and their clinical implications in conditions involving the gut-brain axis remain widely uncharted territories. Our research is dedicated to unraveling the role of pain-related learning and memory processes in the vicious circle of interoceptive hypervigilance, amplified sensitivity to interoceptive signals, and maladaptive avoidance as they characterize disorders of gut-brain interaction. This talk will address behavioral and neural mechanisms shaping visceral pain-related learning and memory processes in both health and disease. It will particularly highlight the specificity of interoceptive sensations, the role of contextual factors, and the impact of avoidance on fear learning and extinction. Finally, putative clinical implications translating these experimental findings into a therapeutic context will be discussed, focusing on fear extinction in the treatment of disorders of the gut-brain axis.

Extinction learning and inflammation: how inflammatory episodes shape fear processing and pain perception
Dr. Hanna Öhlmann
Show details
Authors:
Dr. Hanna Öhlmann
Dr. Robert Jan Pawlik
Dr. Laura Ricarda Lanters
Prof. Dr. Jost Langhorst
Prof. Dr. Adriane Icenhour
Prof. Dr. Harald Engler
Prof. Dr. Sigrid Elsenbruch

Inflammation plays a central role in numerous clinical conditions, including chronic inflammatory diseases, neuropsychiatric disorders, and chronic pain. Although inflammation is known to disrupt neuronal processes critical for learning and memory, its impact on fear extinction remains poorly understood, particularly in humans. Interoceptive processing along the gut-brain axis is strongly influenced by immune signals, and pain arising from visceral organs is closely linked to fear and stress. Studying pain-related fear extinction in patients with chronic visceral pain related to inflammatory processes, therefore, provides a unique opportunity to elucidate clinically relevant interactions between immune activity and extinction learning. In a translational research program, we first examined how acute inflammation affects pain-related fear extinction and subsequent pain perception in healthy individuals. To investigate the effects of chronic inflammation on these processes, we then compared patients with inflammatory versus non-inflammatory chronic interoceptive pain and healthy controls. Both after an experimentally induced episode of acute inflammation and in patients with cumulative clinical inflammatory burden, neural responses in key regions of the central fear network were enhanced during extinction training. Moreover, after extinction training, pain responses were elevated upon unexpected re-exposure. Together, these findings indicate that acute and particularly chronic inflammation may leave a ‘fingerprint’ in the fear network, shaping post-inflammatory pain perception. This highlights the need for tailored interventions that target conditioned fear, strengthen extinction learning, and reduce post-inflammatory pain.
